name: Mani
by_whom: Maniots under Petros Mavromichalis
basis: Greek Revolution; Messenian Senate / Peloponnesian Senate, then the provisional governments
event: Mani declared the revolt on 17/29 March 1821 and was never retaken: Ibrahim was beaten at Vergas (June 1826) and at Pyrgos Dirou and Polytsaravo, which ended his hopes of occupying Mani.
date_note: Start: Petros Mavromichalis declared war at Areopoli on 17 March 1821 (Julian) = 29 March (Gregorian). End: Mani passes to de_jure with the 1832 settlement (see 1832-kingdom-de-jure).
sources: en.wikipedia Greek War of Independence (Mani 17 March, Julian); en.wikipedia Timeline of modern Greek history (Battle of Vergas 24 June 1826); lychnos.org '1821 Independence Milestones' (Diros, Polytsaravo)
note: Vergas is dated 24 June 1826 in the en.wikipedia timeline without a calendar (if Julian, 6 July 1826).

name: Messenia (revolution-held, 1821-1825)
by_whom: Mavromichalis, Kolokotronis, Papaflessas and the Messenian revolutionaries
basis: Greek Revolution; Messenian Senate (Kalamata), then the Peloponnesian Senate and the provisional governments
event: Kalamata was the first town taken (23 March/4 April 1821). Modon and Koroni were never taken and became Ibrahim's base: he landed at Methoni on 26 February 1825, took Navarino in May and burned Kalamata.
date_note: Start: Kalamata taken 23 March 1821 (Julian, per Greek tradition; en.wikipedia gives 23 March without a calendar) = 4 April (Gregorian). End: lost in stages to Ibrahim between his landing at Methoni (26 Feb 1825) and the fall of Navarino (11 May 1825) and of Kalamata/Tripolitsa (June 1825); month only.
sources: en.wikipedia Greek War of Independence (Kalamata 23 March 1821; Ibrahim landed Feb 1825); en.wikipedia Ibrahim Pasha of Egypt (landing at Modon 26 Feb 1825); greece2021.gr timeline 'Ibrahim in the Peloponnese'; en.wikipedia Massacres in the Greek War of Independence (Kalamata burned)
note: Extent of Greek control between the fortresses is approximate. Ibrahim held Messenia from mid-1825 until the evacuation of Sept-Oct 1828 (see 1828-peloponnese-evacuated).

name: Navarino (Pylos): Neokastro and Old Navarino
by_whom: Maniot and Messenian forces (siege under Konstantinos Pierrakos Mavromichalis)
basis: Greek Revolution
event: Besieged from March 1821, the Ottoman garrison capitulated in the first week of August 1821 (gates opened 7/19 Aug) and was massacred. Ibrahim retook Navarino on 11 May 1825 after the Battle of Sphacteria.
date_note: Start: the gates opened on 7 August (Julian) = 19 August 1821 (Gregorian), per en.wikipedia. End: Ibrahim took Neokastro on 11 May 1825 (calendar not stated in en.wikipedia New Navarino fortress; if Julian, 23 May 1825).
sources: en.wikipedia Navarino massacre (7 Aug O.S. / 19 Aug N.S. 1821); en.wikipedia New Navarino fortress (11 May 1825); en.wikipedia Ibrahim Pasha of Egypt (Sphacteria 1825)
note: Sources disagree on the calendar of the 1825 date.

name: Arcadia (revolution-held, 1821-1825)
by_whom: Kolokotronis and the Peloponnesian chieftains
basis: Greek Revolution; Peloponnesian Senate
event: Victories at Valtetsi, Doliana and Vervena gave the Greeks control of most of the center and south of the Peloponnese in 1821. Ibrahim took and razed Tripolitsa in June 1825.
date_note: Start: siege camps around Tripolitsa from April 1821 (month only). End: Ibrahim retook Tripolitsa on 22 June 1825 (en.wikipedia timeline, calendar not stated; greece2021.gr: June 1825).
sources: en.wikipedia Siege of Tripolitsa; en.wikipedia Timeline of modern Greek history (22 June 1825); greece2021.gr timeline 'Ibrahim in the Peloponnese'
note: Kolokotronis kept guerrilla bands in the Arcadian mountains during 1825-1828, so parts of the interior were contested rather than held by Ibrahim; extent approximate.

name: Tripolitsa (Tripoli town)
by_whom: Kolokotronis
basis: Greek Revolution
event: The Ottoman capital of the Morea fell on 23 Sept/5 Oct 1821 after a siege from April 1821; Ibrahim retook and destroyed it in June 1825.
date_note: Start: Greeks entered on 23 September (Julian) = 5 October 1821 (Gregorian); en.wikipedia Siege of Tripolitsa gives both dates without explaining them, the en.wikipedia timeline gives 11 Sep. End: 22 June 1825 (calendar not stated).
sources: en.wikipedia Siege of Tripolitsa; en.wikipedia Greek War of Independence (23 Sep 1821, N.S. 5 Oct); en.wikipedia Timeline of modern Greek history
note: The en.wikipedia timeline's '11 Sep 1821' disagrees with all other sources.

name: Achaea and Elis (revolution-held, 1821-1825)
by_whom: Germanos of Patras, Achaean notables
basis: Greek Revolution; Achaean Directorate, then the Peloponnesian Senate
event: The rising began around Kalavryta and Patras in late March 1821; the Ottomans recaptured the town of Patras on 3 April 1821 and held Patras and Rio until October 1828. The north-west came under Ibrahim's control in 1825.
date_note: Start: the traditional declaration at Agia Lavra on 25 March (Julian) = 6 April 1821; Kalavryta was besieged from 21 March (Julian). End: by the end of 1825 most of the Peloponnese was under Egyptian control (month approximate).
sources: en.wikipedia Greek War of Independence (Kalavryta besieged 21 March; Patras recaptured by the Ottomans 3 April 1821; most of the Peloponnese under Egyptian control by the end of 1825); lychnos.org (Greeks controlled the countryside by the end of March 1821)
note: End date and extent of Egyptian control in Achaea and Elis are approximate; the mountain districts (Kalavryta) were contested.

name: Laconia outside Mani (revolution-held, 1821-1825)
by_whom: Laconian and Maniot revolutionaries
basis: Greek Revolution; Peloponnesian Senate
event: Laconia rose with the rest of the Peloponnese in spring 1821; the lowlands fell under Ibrahim's control after 1825.
date_note: Start: spring 1821 (month only). End: approximate; Ibrahim's forces dominated the Laconian lowlands from late 1825 (no exact date found).
sources: en.wikipedia Greek War of Independence (countryside held by end of March 1821; most of the Peloponnese under Egyptian control by end 1825); lychnos.org
note: No fetched source gives the date Ibrahim took Mystras/Sparta; end date approximate.

name: Monemvasia fortress
by_whom: Garrison under Tzannetakis Grigorakis after the surrender
basis: Greek Revolution
event: Besieged from March/April 1821, the Ottoman garrison surrendered on 23 July 1821, the first major fortress to fall.
date_note: Surrender on 23 July 1821 (en.wikipedia Siege of Monemvasia, calendar not stated; taken as Julian = 4 August Gregorian). End: passes to de_jure in 1832.
sources: en.wikipedia Siege of Monemvasia (1821) (siege from 15 March or after 25 March; surrender 23 July 1821)
note: No fetched source records Monemvasia being retaken by Ibrahim; treated as held throughout. If 23 July is Gregorian, start = 1821-07-23.

name: Argolis (revolution-held)
by_whom: Provisional governments
basis: Greek Revolution; seat of the provisional governments (Argos, Nafplio, Kranidi)
event: Held for most of the war. Dramali's army overran the Argos plain in July 1822 and was destroyed at Dervenakia (26 July 1822, calendar not stated; = 7 Aug if Julian); Ibrahim was stopped at the Mills of Lerna (June 1825) before Nafplio.
date_note: Start: spring 1821 (month only). End: passes to de_jure in 1832.
sources: en.wikipedia Timeline of modern Greek history (Dervenakia 26 July 1822); fhw.gr Chronos 1821-1833, War index (operations against Dramali secured most of the Peloponnese in summer 1822); greece2021.gr (Mills, after June 1825); lychnos.org
note: The brief Ottoman presence in the Argos plain in July 1822 and Ibrahim's raids in 1825-26 are not modeled as separate events.

name: Nafplio and Palamidi
by_whom: Staikos Staikopoulos (Kolokotronis' forces)
basis: Greek Revolution
event: Greek forces under Staikos Staikopoulos took Palamidi on 30 Nov/12 Dec 1822 and the town surrendered. Nafplio became the seat of the revolutionary government on 18 January 1823 and was the capital until 1834; it was never retaken.
date_note: Palamidi stormed on 30 November 1822, St Andrew's day (Julian church calendar) = 12 December 1822 (Gregorian). End: de_jure 1832.
sources: castleroute.culture.gov.gr Palamidi (30 November 1822, St Andrew's day); en.wikipedia Timeline of modern Greek history (seat of government 18 Jan 1823); en.wikipedia First Hellenic Republic

name: Acrocorinth and Corinth town (first Greek tenure)
by_whom: Revolutionary forces
basis: Greek Revolution
event: Acrocorinth surrendered on 14 Jan 1822; Dramali's army took Corinth in July 1822 on its way to Argos.
date_note: Start: Ottoman garrison surrendered 14 January 1822 (en.wikipedia, calendar not stated; taken as Julian = 26 Jan). End: abandoned on Dramali's advance in July 1822 (month only; no exact date in the fetched sources).
sources: en.wikipedia Greek War of Independence (Acrocorinth surrendered 14 Jan 1822); fhw.gr Chronos War page 07 (Dramali's advance, late June/July 1822)
note: Corinthia outside the citadel: see 1821-corinthia.

name: Corinthia outside Corinth and Acrocorinth
basis: Greek Revolution; Peloponnesian Senate
event: Revolution-held except for the passage of Dramali's army in July-August 1822 (destroyed at Dervenakia); the Ottoman remnant held Corinth and Acrocorinth until 1823.
date_note: Start: spring 1821 (Corinth was under siege by August 1821). End: de_jure 1832.
sources: en.wikipedia Siege of Tripolitsa (Corinth under siege, August 1821); en.wikipedia Timeline of modern Greek history (Dervenakia 26 July 1822); fhw.gr War index
note: Dramali's brief presence in 1822 is not modeled as a gap.

name: Acrocorinth and Corinth town (second Greek tenure)
by_whom: Revolutionary forces
basis: Greek Revolution
event: The Ottoman garrison left in Acrocorinth by Dramali's army surrendered again in 1823; Corinth then stayed Greek.
date_note: Start: year only. The garrison left by Dramali capitulated again in late 1823; no fetched source gives the day.
sources: UNVERIFIED: standard histories (e.g. Dakin, The Greek Struggle for Independence); not confirmed in the fetched sources
note: Check the date of the second surrender (late 1823) before drawing.

name: Peloponnese evacuated by Ibrahim (1828)
by_whom: Greek government of Kapodistrias; French expeditionary corps (General Maison) with the Greek government's consent
basis: Convention of Alexandria (6 August 1828, Codrington and Muhammad Ali) on the Egyptian evacuation; Ibrahim accepted on 7 September, effective 9 September 1828
event: After Navarino and the landing of Maison's corps (Navarino Bay 29-31 Aug 1828, Petalidi 22 Sept), the Egyptians evacuated the Morea; the Ottoman-held fortresses were taken by the French in October 1828 and the whole Peloponnese passed to the Greek government.
date_note: Start: Ibrahim sailed on 5 October 1828 with the last Egyptian transport (the first Egyptian division left on 16 Sept); the last Turks and Egyptians had left the Morea by 5 November 1828. Dates from French accounts, Gregorian.
sources: en.wikipedia Morea expedition (Alexandria convention 6 Aug 1828; evacuation 7/9 Sept to 5 Oct; Morea clear 5 Nov 1828); en.wikipedia Ibrahim Pasha of Egypt (capitulation 1 Oct 1828)
note: French troops (an occupation brigade under Schneider, then Guéhéneuc) stayed in the Peloponnese with the Greek government's consent until August 1833: not an occupation.

name: Patras (town and castle)
by_whom: French 3rd brigade (Maison's corps), on behalf of the Allies; then the Greek government
basis: Capitulation of the Pasha of Patras to the French Morea expedition
event: Ottoman since the recapture of 3 April 1821; the French 3rd brigade landed on 4 October 1828 and the Pasha signed the capitulation on 5 October.
date_note: Capitulation signed on 5 October 1828 (Gregorian).
sources: en.wikipedia Morea expedition; en.wikipedia Greek War of Independence (Patras recaptured by the Ottomans 3 April 1821)
note: French troops with Greek consent until 1833.

name: Castle of the Morea (Rio)
by_whom: French expeditionary corps (Maison); then the Greek government
battle: Siege of the Castle of the Morea (1828)
basis: Surrender to the French Morea expedition
event: Last Ottoman fortress in the Peloponnese; surrendered after a breach on 30 October 1828.
date_note: Bombardment opened and the aghas surrendered on 30 October 1828 (Gregorian).
sources: en.wikipedia Morea expedition

name: Navarino (Pylos) fortresses
by_whom: French expeditionary corps (Higonet); then the Greek government
basis: Surrender of the Egyptian/Ottoman garrison to the French
event: Held by Ibrahim since May 1825; handed to the French in October 1828.
date_note: General Higonet marched on 6 October 1828 and the fort surrendered after a breach; the exact day is not given (about 6-7 October 1828, Gregorian).
sources: en.wikipedia Morea expedition; en.wikipedia New Navarino fortress (handed to Maison's troops in October 1828)
note: French garrison with Greek consent until 1833.

name: Methoni (Modon)
by_whom: French expeditionary corps; then the Greek government
basis: Surrender to the French
event: Ottoman throughout the war and Ibrahim's landing place (26 Feb 1825); taken by the French on 7 October 1828.
date_note: The French appeared on 7 October 1828 and took the fort at the gate the same day on the same terms as Navarino (Gregorian).
sources: en.wikipedia Morea expedition; en.wikipedia Ibrahim Pasha of Egypt
note: French garrison with Greek consent until 1833.

name: Koroni
by_whom: French expeditionary corps (Sébastiani); then the Greek government
basis: Surrender to the French
event: Ottoman throughout the war; entered by the French on 9 October 1828.
date_note: Sébastiani appeared on 7 October and the French entered on 9 October 1828 (Gregorian).
sources: en.wikipedia Morea expedition

name: Eastern Roumeli (revolution-held, 1821-1826)
by_whom: Athanasios Diakos, Odysseas Androutsos, Ioannis Gouras and the armatoles
basis: Greek Revolution; Areopagus of Eastern Continental Greece, then the provisional governments
event: Phocis and Boeotia rose in late March 1821 (Julian). Control was contested: Omer Vrioni won at Alamana (23-24 April 1821) and retook Livadeia (10 June 1821), but was checked at Gravia and left Attica in September 1821 after Vasilika; Dramali passed through in July 1822 and burned Thebes; in 1823 neither side gained full control. After Missolonghi (April 1826) Kiutahi reconquered the region.
date_note: Start: Salona rose on 27 March (Julian) = 8 April 1821; Livadeia was taken by Diakos on 31 March (Julian) = 12 April; Thebes about 2 April (Julian). End: Reşid Mehmed Pasha (Kiutahi) occupied Eastern Roumeli after the fall of Missolonghi; month approximate (he was in Athens by August 1826).
sources: en.wikipedia Greek War of Independence (Phocis 24 Mar, Salona 27 Mar, Livadeia 31 Mar, Thebes c. 2 Apr; Livadeia retaken by Vrioni 10 Jun 1821; Vasilika); en.wikipedia Timeline of modern Greek history (Alamana 23-24 Apr 1821); fhw.gr Chronos War pages 06-07 (Dramali burned Thebes 1 July 1822; 1823 campaigns; Ottoman control of central Greece after Missolonghi)
note: The en.wikipedia dates for 1821 are given in the Julian calendar in that article's chronology; Vrioni's dates (Alamana, Livadeia) are uncalendared. Extent approximate: this was a contested zone, not a front.

name: Athens town (first Greek tenure, 1821)
by_whom: Attic insurgents
basis: Greek Revolution
event: The Athenians rose and took the town without a fight in late April 1821 and besieged the Acropolis; Vrioni relieved it in July 1821.
date_note: Start: Greeks took the town on 25 April 1821 (ancientathens3d; en.wikipedia gives 28 April and 25 April for the start of the siege), probably Julian = 7 or 10 May (month given). End: Omer Vrioni and Omer Bey of Karystos entered Athens on 20 July 1821 (calendar not stated; taken as Julian = 1 August).
sources: en.wikipedia Siege of the Acropolis (1821-1822); ancientathens3d.com 'Ottoman Athens 1458-1833'

name: Athens and Attica (1821-1826)
by_whom: Androutsos, Gouras
basis: Greek Revolution; Areopagus of Eastern Continental Greece
event: After Vrioni's departure the Greeks held Attica; Kiutahi (Reşid Mehmed Pasha) took the town in summer 1826 and besieged the Acropolis.
date_note: Start: Vrioni left Attica in September 1821 and the siege of the Acropolis resumed (month only). End: Kiutahi took the town in August 1826; the siege of the Acropolis began on 25 August 1826 (Julian per en.wikipedia) = 6 September (Gregorian). Month only.
sources: en.wikipedia Siege of the Acropolis (1821-1822); lychnos.org (Turks abandoned Attica, September 1821); en.wikipedia Siege of the Acropolis (1826-1827) (siege from 25 Aug 1826 O.S.); ancientathens3d.com
note: Megaris (West Attica) is included by assumption; no fetched source describes it separately.

name: Acropolis of Athens
by_whom: Gouras (garrison commander from 1823), later Fabvier's reinforcements
battle: Siege of the Acropolis (1821-1822); Siege of the Acropolis (1826-1827); Arachova; Kamatero; Phaleron (Analatos)
basis: Greek Revolution
event: The Ottoman garrison capitulated in June 1822 (Dramali did not retake it). Besieged by Kiutahi from August 1826; after the relief army was routed at Phaleron (24 April/6 May 1827) the garrison surrendered on 24 May/5 June 1827, leaving the Ottomans in control of all Roumeli.
date_note: Start: capitulation on 10 June 1822 (fhw.gr) or 9 June 1822 (en.wikipedia, Old Style) = 22 or 21 June (Gregorian). End: surrender on 24 May 1827 (Old Style) = 5 June 1827 (Gregorian).
sources: en.wikipedia Siege of the Acropolis (1821-1822) (9 June 1822 O.S.); fhw.gr Chronos War page 07 (10 June 1822); en.wikipedia Siege of the Acropolis (1826-1827) (25 Aug 1826 - 24 May 1827 O.S.; Phaleron 24 April); protothema.gr (surrender 24 May 1827); fhw.gr War index
note: The two sources differ by one day on the 1822 capitulation (9 vs 10 June Julian).

name: Parnassus area recovered by Karaiskakis (1826-1827)
by_whom: Georgios Karaiskakis
basis: Greek Revolution
event: Karaiskakis' winter campaign of 1826-27 temporarily recovered parts of the Parnassus region behind Kiutahi's lines.
date_note: Start: Greek victory at Arachova, November 1826 (calendar not stated). End: after the defeat at Phaleron (6 May 1827 Gregorian) and the fall of the Acropolis (5 June 1827); month approximate.
sources: en.wikipedia Siege of the Acropolis (1826-1827) (Arachova, November 1826); fhw.gr War index (the Acropolis' fall in 1827 gave the Ottomans control of all Roumeli)
note: Extent and duration are approximate; no fetched source maps Karaiskakis' gains.

name: Western Roumeli (revolution-held, 1821-1825)
by_whom: Alexandros Mavrokordatos, Markos Botsaris and the armatoles of Aetolia-Acarnania
battle: Peta (1822); first and second sieges of Missolonghi (1822-23, 1823)
basis: Greek Revolution; Senate of Western Continental Greece
event: Western Roumeli rose in May-June 1821. Ottoman offensives in 1822-23 failed before Missolonghi (second siege ended December 1823). In 1825 Kiutahi broke through at Makrynoros and overran the region except Missolonghi and Anatoliko.
date_note: Start: Missolonghi rose on 25 May 1821 (en.wikipedia, calendar not stated); month given as June to cover the rising of Vrachori and Acarnania. End: Kiutahi took Makrynoros at the end of March 1825 and began the siege of Missolonghi on 15 April 1825 (Old Style) = 27 April (Gregorian).
sources: en.wikipedia Greek War of Independence (Missolonghi 25 May 1821; second siege ended Dec 1823); fhw.gr Chronos War page 06 (Makrynoros end of March 1825; siege from end of April 1825); en.wikipedia Third siege of Missolonghi (15 April 1825, O.S.)
note: Contested zone. Evrytania (Karpenisi, Agrafa) is left out: it was a battleground (Botsaris fell attacking the Ottoman camp at Karpenisi in 1823) and no fetched source shows it held by the revolution. Extent approximate.

name: Missolonghi
by_whom: Garrison of Missolonghi
basis: Greek Revolution; Senate of Western Continental Greece
event: Besieged by Kiutahi from 15/27 April 1825 and by Ibrahim from early 1826; Vasiladi fell on 9 March 1826, Dolmas and Poros on 12 March; the town fell after the exodus of 10/11 (22/23) April 1826.
date_note: Start: rising of 25 May 1821 (calendar not stated). End: exodus on the night of 10/11 April 1826 (Old Style) = 22/23 April (Gregorian); Ibrahim's page gives 24 April 1826.
sources: en.wikipedia Third siege of Missolonghi (10 April [N.S. 22 April] 1826; Vasiladi 9 March 1826); fhw.gr Chronos War page 06 (night of 10/11 April 1826); en.wikipedia Ibrahim Pasha of Egypt (24 April 1826)
note: Vasiladi and Dolmas dates in en.wikipedia are presumably Old Style like the rest of that article.

name: Anatoliko (Aitoliko)
basis: Greek Revolution
event: The island town surrendered when the Ottomans controlled the lagoon in early 1826.
date_note: End: Anatoliko surrendered during the blockade of February-March 1826 (fhw.gr: by February; en.wikipedia: during the March events); no exact day.
sources: fhw.gr Chronos War page 06; en.wikipedia Third siege of Missolonghi

name: Acarnania recovered (Vonitsa, Xiromero, Karvasaras, Valtos)
by_whom: Richard Church; Souliote corps under Athanasios Koutsonikas
basis: Greek government of Kapodistrias (campaign of Sir Richard Church and Augustinos Kapodistrias)
event: Church's campaign in Western Greece recovered Acarnania; Vonitsa castle surrendered in March 1829 and the Souliotes blocked Reşid Pasha at Koronisia (5 March 1829).
date_note: Start: Vonitsa 'became Greek again' on 5 March 1829 (en.wikipedia Battle of Koronisia; calendar not stated; if Julian, 17 March); castleroute.culture.gov.gr: the castle surrendered in March 1829. Church's forces were in Acarnania from late 1828 (no exact date found).
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Koronisia (1829); castleroute.culture.gov.gr Vonitsa (castle surrendered March 1829; Aetolia-Acarnania incorporated by the 1832 treaty); en.wikipedia Richard Church (partisan war in western Greece)
note: This area lay outside the 1830 (Aspropotamos-Spercheios) award but stayed in Greek hands 1829-1832; Kapodistrias asked for Acarnania to be included, and it became de_jure Greek only with the 1832 settlement.

name: Nafpaktos (Lepanto) and Antirrio (Castle of Roumeli)
by_whom: Greek Army of Western Greece (Augustinos Kapodistrias)
basis: Surrender of the Ottoman garrison to the Greek forces
event: Lepanto, Ottoman throughout the war, was recovered in spring 1829.
date_note: Sources disagree: en.wikipedia Nafpaktos says it became part of Greece in March 1829; en.wikipedia Morea expedition says it was recaptured in April 1829. Month only.
sources: en.wikipedia Nafpaktos (March 1829); en.wikipedia Morea expedition (April 1829)
note: The fate of Antirrio is assumed to follow Nafpaktos; no fetched source dates it separately.

name: Missolonghi, Aitoliko and Aetolia recovered
by_whom: Greek Army of Western Greece (Augustinos Kapodistrias)
basis: Greek government of Kapodistrias
event: Missolonghi and Anatoliko were retaken in May 1829, completing the recovery of Western Roumeli.
date_note: Missolonghi recaptured in May 1829 (en.wikipedia Morea expedition); day not given.
sources: en.wikipedia Morea expedition (Messolonghi recaptured May 1829)
note: Agrinio and the area north of lakes Trichonida/Lysimachia lay outside the 1830 award; held de facto until 1832.

name: Evrytania and Agrafa (Greek authority 1829-1832)
basis: Greek government of Kapodistrias
event: Evrytania lay north of the 1830 line; its status in 1829-1832 is not documented in the fetched sources.
date_note: Year only: no fetched source dates the establishment of Greek authority in Evrytania.
sources: No direct source; inferred from the recovery of Western and Eastern Roumeli in 1829 (en.wikipedia Morea expedition; en.wikipedia Battle of Petra) and its inclusion in the 1832 kingdom
note: UNVERIFIED: check whether Karpenisi and the Agrafa were under Greek or Ottoman control between 1829 and 1832 before drawing.

name: Western Boeotia and Phocis recovered (Livadeia, Salona)
by_whom: Demetrios Ypsilantis (army of Eastern Greece)
basis: Greek government of Kapodistrias
event: Ypsilantis took Livadeia in early November 1828; a counter-attack by Mahmud Pasha from Euboea was repulsed in January 1829.
date_note: Livadeia taken in early November 1828 (en.wikipedia Morea expedition; Gregorian). The date for Salona and Phocis is not given.
sources: en.wikipedia Morea expedition (Livadeia early Nov 1828; Mahmud Pasha repulsed Jan 1829)
note: Extent approximate.

name: Thebes and eastern Boeotia
by_whom: Demetrios Ypsilantis
basis: Greek government of Kapodistrias
event: Thebes was recaptured on 21 May 1829.
date_note: Thebes recaptured 21 May 1829 (en.wikipedia Morea expedition; presumably Gregorian).
sources: en.wikipedia Morea expedition
note: lamia.gr chronology: Ottoman authority remained in parts of Attica, Boeotia, Euboea and Phthiotis until 1832-33 (probably the districts bordering Attica and the Euripus, e.g. Tanagra/Oropos); extent approximate.

name: Eastern Roumeli from Livadeia to the Spercheios (Petra capitulation)
line: Northern limit: the Spercheios river to its mouth in the Malian Gulf; Lamia (north bank) stayed Ottoman.
by_whom: Demetrios Ypsilantis, Georgios Dyovouniotis, Nikolaos Kriezotis
basis: Capitulation/truce after the Battle of Petra: the Ottomans surrendered all lands from Livadeia to the Spercheios in exchange for safe passage out of Central Greece
event: Aslan Bey and Osman Aga, marching from Athens towards Thrace, were stopped at Petra between Livadeia and Thebes; the last battle of the war, fought after the Treaty of Adrianople (14 Sept 1829).
date_note: The Battle of Petra was fought on 12 September 1829 (en.wikipedia, evidently Julian = 24 September Gregorian); the Ottoman force capitulated on 25 September 1829 (Gregorian; the truce was agreed the day after the battle).
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Petra (12 Sept 1829; capitulation 25 Sept 1829; lands from Livadeia to the Spercheios); 200years.mfa.gr (Adrianople 2/14 Sept 1829)
note: Athens (Acropolis garrison), Euboea and Lamia remained Ottoman until 1833. Whether the Ypati (Patratziki) district on the south bank was handed over in 1829 is unclear (it was disputed in 1832, see 1833-lamia-handover).

name: Spetses
by_whom: Spetsiot shipowners (Bouboulina)
basis: Greek Revolution
event: One of the three naval islands (with Hydra and Psara); held throughout the war.
date_note: Spetses raised the flag on 3 April 1821 (Julian) = 15 April (Gregorian): traditional date, not confirmed in the fetched sources. End: de_jure 1832.
sources: lychnos.org (Hydra, Spetses and Psara gave the Greeks control of the sea, early 1821); en.wikipedia Greek War of Independence (Hydra and Spetses as naval bases); date: standard chronologies (unverified here)

name: Hydra
by_whom: Hydriot shipowners (Kountouriotis, Miaoulis)
basis: Greek Revolution
event: Main naval base of the revolution; held throughout.
date_note: Hydra joined on 16 April 1821 (Julian) = 28 April (Gregorian): traditional date, not confirmed in the fetched sources. End: de_jure 1832.
sources: lychnos.org; en.wikipedia Greek War of Independence; date: standard chronologies (unverified here)

name: Psara
by_whom: Psariot shipowners (Kanaris, Papanikolis)
basis: Greek Revolution
event: Koca Hüsrev Mehmed Pasha's fleet captured and destroyed the island; it stayed deserted and Ottoman until the Greek Navy took it on 21 October 1912.
date_note: Start: Psara joined on 10 April 1821 (en.wikipedia, calendar not stated; taken as Julian = 22 April). End: destroyed on 20-21 June 1824 (Old Style) = 2-3 July 1824 (Gregorian).
sources: en.wikipedia Destruction of Psara (10 April 1821; 20-21 June (2-3 July N.S.) 1824; 1912); en.wikipedia Timeline of modern Greek history (21 June 1824)
note: Psara was not included in the 1830 or 1832 settlements (Kapodistrias asked for it); its refugees founded Nea Psara in Euboea.

name: Kasos
by_whom: Kasiot shipowners
basis: Greek Revolution
event: The semi-autonomous island joined the revolution and raided the coasts; Muhammad Ali's fleet destroyed it in June 1824. It stayed Ottoman (Italian 1912, Greek 1947).
date_note: Start: year only (no date in the fetched sources). End: the Egyptian landing behind Agia Marina on the night of 19/20 June 1824 (en.wikipedia Kasos Massacre, Gregorian; the en.wikipedia timeline gives 7-8 June, i.e. Julian).
sources: en.wikipedia Kasos Massacre (fleet off Kasos 2 June, landing night of 19 June 1824); en.wikipedia Timeline of modern Greek history (7-8 June 1824); en.wikipedia Massacres in the Greek War of Independence (27 May 1824, calendar not stated)
note: Three different dates appear in the sources (27 May, 7-8 June, 19-20 June 1824); 7-8 June Julian = 19-20 June Gregorian reconciles two of them.

name: Samos
by_whom: Lykourgos Logothetis
basis: Greek Revolution; Samian autonomous administration under Lykourgos Logothetis; part of the Eastern Sporades province of the Greek state 1828-1830
event: Samos rose in 1821, beat off Ottoman and Egyptian landing attempts (Battle of Samos, 5-17 Aug 1824, Julian) and held out to the end of the war; excluded from Greece in 1830 and 1832, it kept its own regime until the Principality was imposed in 1834 (batch GB2).
date_note: Start: 1821 (month not given in the fetched sources; the rising under Lykourgos Logothetis was in spring 1821). End: year only; the 3 February 1830 protocol excluded Samos, and First Hellenic Republic shows the 'Military-Political System of Samos' as a successor state from 1830.
sources: en.wikipedia Principality of Samos; en.wikipedia Battle of Samos (5 Aug 1824, Julian); en.wikipedia First Hellenic Republic (Samos part of the Eastern Sporades province 1828-1830); en.wikipedia London Protocol (1830) (Samos not included)
note: 1830-1834 (Samian self-rule outside the Greek state) is not de_facto Greek; leave it to GB2.

name: Cyclades
basis: Greek Revolution; Aegean provinces of the provisional governments
event: The Cyclades were part of the revolutionary state throughout and were included in every Great-Power award (1828, 1829, 1830, 1832).
date_note: Year only: the islands joined in stages in spring and summer 1821; the Catholic communities (Syros, parts of Tinos and Naxos) were reluctant. No fetched source gives dates.
sources: fhw.gr War index (the revolution had taken root in the Aegean islands by 1822); en.wikipedia London Protocol (1829) (Cyclades included); en.wikipedia Aspropotamos-Spercheios line (Cyclades incl. Amorgos); lamia.gr chronology (Nov 1828 protocol: Peloponnese and Cyclades)
note: Start date approximate.

name: Saronic islands and Troizinia
basis: Greek Revolution
event: Held throughout. The government moved to Aegina on 11 November 1826 and Kapodistrias governed from Aegina in 1828; the 1827 assembly met at Troezen and the ambassadors' conference at Poros (Dec 1828).
date_note: Month approximate.
sources: en.wikipedia Timeline of modern Greek history (government to Aegina 11 Nov 1826); en.wikipedia First Hellenic Republic (Troezen 1827); solarspell mirror of en.wikipedia Greek War of Independence (Poros protocol 21 Dec 1828)

name: Northern Sporades and Skyros
basis: Greek Revolution
event: Refuge and base for the Thessalian and Macedonian fighters; included in the 1830 and 1832 settlements.
date_note: Year only: no fetched source dates their adhesion.
sources: en.wikipedia Aspropotamos-Spercheios line (Northern Sporades and Skyros included 1830); 200years.mfa.gr (Sporades included 1830)
note: Start approximate.

name: Euboea countryside (revolt, 1821-1823)
by_whom: Angelis Govios, Nikolaos Kriezotis; later Fabvier
basis: Greek Revolution
event: Euboea rose in 1821 but Chalkis and Karystos were never taken; the island stayed Ottoman until 1833 (Mahmud Pasha still attacked Boeotia from Euboea in January 1829).
date_note: Both dates approximate: the rising of 1821 under Angelis Govios and Kriezotis did not break Ottoman resistance; the revolutionaries repeatedly failed against Chalkis and Karystos in 1823-1824.
sources: archaeology.wiki (Chalkida article: 1821 rising under Govios, Kriezotis and Fabvier did not break Ottoman resistance); fhw.gr Chronos War page 07 (failed attacks on Chalkis and Karystos 1823-24); en.wikipedia Morea expedition (Mahmud Pasha from Euboea, Jan 1829)
note: Extent and duration of rebel control in Euboea are poorly documented in the fetched sources; draw faintly or omit.

name: Chios (1822 rising)
by_whom: Lykourgos Logothetis, Antonios Bournias
basis: Greek Revolution (Samian expedition)
event: Short-lived rising crushed in April 1822; Kanaris destroyed the Ottoman flagship on 18 June 1822. Chios stayed Ottoman until 1912.
date_note: The rising followed the landing of Samian forces under Logothetis in March 1822; the Ottoman fleet arrived on 11 April 1822 (en.wikipedia, calendar not stated) and the massacre followed. Months only.
sources: en.wikipedia Greek War of Independence (Ottoman fleet at Chios 11 April 1822; flagship destroyed 18 June 1822); en.wikipedia Massacres in the Greek War of Independence
note: A second expedition under Fabvier (late 1827 - early 1828) held parts of the island for some months; not confirmed in the fetched sources, so not recorded as an event.

name: Eastern Aegean islands of the revolutionary state (Patmos, Leros, Kalymnos, Astypalaia)
basis: Greek Revolution; Eastern Sporades province (1828-1830)
event: These islands joined the revolutionary administration and were returned to Ottoman rule under the 1830/1832 settlements (the 1830 award stopped at Amorgos).
date_note: Years only; no fetched source gives dates.
sources: UNVERIFIED in the fetched sources; inferred from en.wikipedia First Hellenic Republic (Eastern Sporades province 1828-1830) and en.wikipedia Aspropotamos-Spercheios line (Cyclades included up to Amorgos)
note: UNVERIFIED: confirm which Dodecanese islands were in the provisional state and when Ottoman authority returned (1830 or 1832) before drawing.

name: Crete (revolt, 1821-1824)
by_whom: Sfakians and Cretan revolutionaries
basis: Greek Revolution; Cretan provisional administration (commissioner Emmanouil Tombazis, 1823)
event: The Christians drove the Muslims into the fortified north-coast towns; Muhammad Ali's forces landed in 1822 and crushed the revolt by 1824.
date_note: Start: June 1821 (the Heraklion massacre of 24 June 1821 followed the outbreak); month approximate. End: year only; the Egyptian forces (fleet at Souda 28 May 1822) suppressed the revolt by 1824 (sources disagree on 1824 or 1825 for Ibrahim's role).
sources: en.wikipedia Ottoman Crete (24 June 1821; Muslims driven into the fortified towns; Egyptian intervention); en.wikipedia Greek War of Independence (Egyptian fleet at Souda 28 May 1822); en.wikipedia Gramvousa (Tombazis 1823); solarspell mirror of en.wikipedia Greek War of Independence (1824 Egyptian army landed)
note: The requested page 'Cretan revolt (1821-1828)' could not be fetched (url_not_found). Extent and dates approximate.

name: Gramvousa fort (Imeri Gramvousa)
by_whom: Dimitrios Kallergis and Emmanouil Antoniadis
basis: Greek Revolution
event: Cretans disguised as Turks took the fort; besieged for over two years, it became a pirate base until Mavrokordatos' expedition with British and French ships (1828). Hatzimichalis Dalianis landed there on 5 January 1828.
date_note: Start: captured on 9 August 1825 (en.wikipedia, calendar not stated; taken as Julian = 21 August). End: year only; after the Allied anti-piracy expedition of early 1828 the fort came under British control.
sources: en.wikipedia Gramvousa; en.wikipedia Greek War of Independence (Gramvousa 9 Aug 1825; Kissamos also captured)
note: When the fort was finally handed to the Ottoman/Egyptian authorities (c. 1830-31) is not in the fetched sources.

name: Sfakia and Frangokastello (1828 revolt)
by_whom: Hatzimichalis Dalianis
basis: Greek government of Kapodistrias (expedition to revive the Cretan revolt)
event: The attempt to revive the revolt in Crete failed at Frangokastello in May 1828. Crete was excluded from Greece in 1830 and administered for Egypt by Mustafa Naili Pasha until 1840.
date_note: Dalianis took Frangokastello in March 1828; Mustafa Naili Pasha arrived on 13 May 1828 and the castle fell after several days (calendar not stated). Months only.
sources: en.wikipedia Hatzimichalis Dalianis (5 Jan 1828; March 1828; 13 May 1828); en.wikipedia Ottoman Crete (1830 settlement; Mustafa Naili Pasha); en.wikipedia Greek War of Independence (Frangokastello, March 1828)
note: The en.wikipedia infobox gives Dalianis' death as 17 March 1828, which conflicts with the May siege in the text. Cretan resistance in the mountains continued into 1829-30; not modeled.

name: Chalkidiki rising (Kassandra, Mount Athos)
line: Insurgent lines across the Potidaea (Kassandra) isthmus; extent beyond Kassandra and Athos uncertain.
by_whom: Emmanouil Pappas
basis: Greek Revolution
event: Emmanouil Pappas raised Chalkidiki and Athos; the rebels failed to hold the Rentina pass in June and were crushed at Kassandra on 30 October 1821.
date_note: Start: Polygyros rose on 17 May 1821 (calendar not stated; = 29 May if Julian). End: Ottoman victory at Kassandra on 30 October 1821 (calendar not stated; = 11 Nov if Julian); Sithonia, Mount Athos and Thasos then surrendered on terms (dates not found).
sources: solarspell mirror of en.wikipedia Greek War of Independence (Polygyros 17 May 1821; Rentina June 1821; Kassandra 30 Oct 1821; Sithonia, Athos, Thasos surrendered on terms); en.wikipedia Greek War of Independence

name: Naoussa, Vermio and Olympus rising (1822)
by_whom: Anastasios Karatasos, Aggelis Gatsos, Zafeirakis Theodosiou
basis: Greek Revolution
event: The rising in western Macedonia ended with the sack of Naoussa in April 1822, ending the revolution in Macedonia.
date_note: The armatoles chose Naoussa, Kastania and Siatista as bases at the beginning of 1822; Mehmed Emin (Ebu Lubut) won at Kolindros and Kastania in March 1822 and entered Naoussa on 6 April (en.wikipedia Massacres) or 9 April 1822 (en.wikipedia timeline); calendars not stated. Months only.
sources: solarspell mirror of en.wikipedia Greek War of Independence (beginning of 1822 bases; March 1822 Kolindros and Kastania; April 1822 Naoussa); en.wikipedia Massacres in the Greek War of Independence (14 March arrival; 6 April 1822); en.wikipedia Timeline of modern Greek history (9 April 1822)
note: The revolution held little ground outside the towns and mountain villages; draw faintly.

name: Morea and Cyclades under the Powers' guarantee (London Protocol of 16 Nov 1828)
line: No land line north of the Isthmus of Corinth: the protocol covered the Peloponnese and the islands only.
basis: London Protocol of 4/16 November 1828 (Britain, France, Russia)
event: The Powers placed the Peloponnese and the Cyclades provisionally under their guarantee, limiting the new state to them, which alarmed Kapodistrias.
date_note: London Protocol of 4/16 November 1828; superseded by the protocol of 22 March 1829.
sources: lamia.gr chronology (xronologio 2013): '4/16 Nov 1828: a London protocol limits the new state to the Peloponnese and the Cyclades'
note: A provisional guarantee rather than a frontier award; include only if the film shows the diplomatic sequence. The Poros conference of the ambassadors (protocol of 21 Dec 1828) proposed a larger state (Arta-Volos, the Cyclades and Sporades, Samos and perhaps Crete) but was a recommendation, not an award.

name: Autonomous Greece, Arta-Volos line (London Protocol of 22 March 1829)
line: From the Gulf of Arta to the Pagasetic Gulf: in Özkan's quotation of the protocol, 'a line that would advance from the Gulf of Arta to the passes of Macrinoros on the one side, and on the other to Mount Othrys, near the entrance of the Gulf of Volos'. Arta and Volos outside. See 1832-kingdom-de-jure for the demarcated course of the same line.
basis: London Protocol of 22 March 1829 (Aberdeen, Polignac, Lieven): an autonomous tributary state under Ottoman suzerainty, with a hereditary Christian prince and a tribute of 1.5 million piasters; accepted by the Porte in the Treaty of Adrianople, Art. 10
event: First Great-Power frontier for Greece: autonomy within the Arta-Volos line; never carried out.
date_note: Protocol of 10/22 March 1829; accepted by the Porte in Art. 10 of the Treaty of Adrianople (2/14 September 1829); superseded by the protocol of 3 February 1830.
sources: en.wikipedia London Protocol (1829); 200years.mfa.gr International Treaties and Protocols (10/22 March 1829; Adrianople 2/14 Sept 1829 Art. 10); Özkan, 'The Final Phase of the Greek Revolution', in Stamatopoulos (ed.), European Revolutions and the Ottoman Balkans (2020), ch. 6 (academia.edu 19704198)
note: Included: the Peloponnese, Continental Greece and the Cyclades; excluded: Crete, Samos and the other Aegean islands then under Greek control (en.wikipedia). The fetched sources do not say whether Euboea and the Northern Sporades were in the 1829 award. Ottoman suzerainty means this was autonomy, not sovereignty.

name: Independent Greece, Aspropotamos-Spercheios line (London Protocol of 3 Feb 1830)
line: From the mouth of the Achelous (Aspropotamos) up the river, then east through a series of lakes (identified with Lysimachia and Trichonida; the protocol names the lakes of Angelokastro, Vrachori and Saurovitza), to Mount Artotina, then along the crest of the Axos and of Mount Oeta, reaching the Malian Gulf (Gulf of Zitouni) at the mouth of the Spercheios, passing south of Zitouni (Lamia), which stayed Ottoman. (The lake and Axos/Kalouri names are recalled from the French text of the protocol; the fetched sources confirm only the Achelous mouth, the lakes, Artotina, the Oeta ridge and the Spercheios mouth.)
basis: London Protocol of 3 February 1830 (Aberdeen, Montmorency-Laval, Lieven): Greece an independent sovereign state; second protocol of the same day chose Leopold of Saxe-Coburg as sovereign
event: The first act recognizing Greek independence gave it a smaller frontier than 1829. The Sultan accepted; Kapodistrias accepted on condition that the Ottomans evacuate Attica and Euboea; Leopold renounced the throne over the frontier. Never carried out: replaced by the Arta-Volos line in 1832.
date_note: Protocol of 22 January / 3 February 1830; notified to the Porte and to Greece on 27 March / 8 April 1830. Superseded by the Arrangement of Constantinople of 9/21 July 1832 (and, for the Lamia district, the London Protocol of 18/30 August 1832).
sources: en.wikipedia London Protocol (1830); en.wikipedia Aspropotamos-Spercheios line (Achelous mouth, Artotina, Oeta ridge, Spercheios mouth, south of Zitouni; Euboea, Northern Sporades, Skyros, Cyclades incl. Amorgos); en.wikipedia Territorial evolution of Greece (two rivers, a series of lakes and mountain summits); 200years.mfa.gr (Acheloos-Spercheios; Sporades and Euboea included; delivered to the Porte 8 April 1830)
note: Excluded: Crete, Samos (and Psara, Kasos, Chios, Astypalaia and the other eastern islands); on the mainland Acarnania, Agrinio, Evrytania and Phthiotis north of the Oeta. Greece held Acarnania, Aetolia north of the lakes and (from 1829) the land to the Spercheios de facto throughout 1830-32 (see the 1829 de_facto events). The Porte's acceptance of the protocol (April 1830) could be read as making the area within the line de_jure from 1830; per the brief it is coded as awarded. The MFA copy of the French text (mfa.gr .doc) could not be read; verify the quoted course against it.

name: Arta-Volos line restored (London Protocol of 26 Sept 1831)
line: Ambracian Gulf - Pagasetic Gulf (Arta-Volos) line, as in 1829; see 1832-kingdom-de-jure for the demarcated course.
basis: London Protocol of 14/26 September 1831 (Britain, France, Russia)
event: The Powers, noting the drawbacks of the Achelous-Spercheios line, proposed again the Ambracian-Pagasetic line.
date_note: Protocol of 14/26 September 1831; replaced by the treaty settlement of 21 July / 30 August 1832.
sources: lamia.gr chronology (14/26 Sep 1831; the Porte did not accept it); en.wikipedia London Protocol (1830) (protocol of 14/26 September 1831 extended the border; 'Turkey accepted these terms')
note: Sources disagree: en.wikipedia says Turkey accepted these terms, the lamia.gr chronology says the Porte did not, and the line was only agreed with the Porte at Constantinople in July 1832.

name: Kingdom of Greece, Arta-Volos line (1832 settlement): areas already in Greek hands
line: Arta-Volos (Ambracian-Pagasetic) line, set by the Arrangement of Constantinople (9/21 July 1832) and, for the Lamia (Zitouni) and Ypati (Patratziki) districts, by the London Protocol of 18/30 August 1832; demarcated in autumn 1832 by a commission (General A. de Scalon for Russia, Colonel J. Barthélemy for France, Colonel George Baker for Britain; the Ottoman commissioner Hüseyin Bey of Vonitsa, who met them at Preveza in late August 1832, withdrew); about 137 miles long, marked by 95 stone pyramids; survey and maps revised until spring 1835. Course west to east: from the Gulf of Arta at the foot of Mount Makrynoros, the Makrynoros pass going to Greece (a stream called Karitsa served as the boundary; the islet of Vouvala in the gulf was disputed in 1842); along the mountain crests of Valtos and the Agrafa (markers at Zacharaki Vrisi, the meeting of three ranges, moved from Mount Veluchi/Tymfristos, and at Graditza), then along Mount Othrys to the Gulf of Volos near its entrance. Arta and Volos stayed Ottoman. In present-day terms the line is close to the boundary between the Western Greece and Central Greece regions and the Epirus and Thessaly regions (Aetolia-Acarnania vs Preveza and Arta; Evrytania vs Karditsa; Phthiotis vs Karditsa, Larissa and Magnesia), except that Domokos municipality (now Phthiotis), north of the Othrys crest, stayed Ottoman until 1881 (Domokos exception not confirmed in the fetched sources).
basis: Treaty of London (7 May 1832, the Powers and Bavaria: Otto king, Arta-Volos frontier); Arrangement (Treaty) of Constantinople, 9/21 July 1832 (the Powers and the Porte; indemnity 40 million piasters); London Protocol of 18/30 August 1832; Ottoman acceptance 14/26 December 1832
event: The Kingdom of Greece came into being with the Arta-Volos frontier; Acarnania, Aetolia, Evrytania and the land to the Spercheios, held de facto since 1829 but outside the 1830 award, became Greek by right. King Otto landed at Nafplio in January (Julian) 1833 with Bavarian troops, who then took over the Ottoman-held districts (see 1833 events).
handover: no handover needed for these areas (already held)
date_note: Start = the London Protocol of 18/30 August 1832, which ratified the Constantinople arrangement and completed the frontier; the Porte formally accepted the demarcated borders on 14/26 December 1832. Alternative start: the signature of the Arrangement with the Porte, 9/21 July 1832.
sources: en.wikipedia London Conference of 1832; en.wikipedia Treaty of Constantinople (1832); 200years.mfa.gr (Constantinople 9/21 July 1832, Lamia referred to London; London Protocol 18/30 Aug 1832 gave the Lamia region to Greece); lamia.gr chronology (commission Sep-Nov 1832; Ottoman acceptance 14/26 Dec 1832); Özkan 2020 (commission, Makrynoros, Zacharaki Vrisi, Graditza, 137 miles, 95 pyramids, Karitsa, Vouvala); Hertslet, Map of Europe by Treaty, plates 10-11 'Boundary between Greece and Turkey 21 July 1832' (maproom.org); castleroute.culture.gov.gr Vonitsa
note: Excluded: Crete (to Egyptian administration), Samos (principality 1834, GB2), Psara, Chios, Kasos and the Dodecanese, the Ionian Islands (British protectorate until 1864). The MFA's English text of the Constantinople treaty (mfa.gr .doc) could not be read; verify the exact wording of the line against it or Hertslet.

name: Mainland Attica, awarded but still Ottoman-held (1832-1833)
basis: Arrangement of Constantinople (21 July 1832) and London Protocol (30 August 1832)
event: Attica was Greek by treaty but the Ottoman garrison held the Acropolis until April 1833.
date_note: From the entry into force of the 1832 settlement to the Ottoman evacuation of the Acropolis.
sources: see 1833-attica-handover
note: Attica was also within the 1830 award (1830-02-03-aspropotamos-spercheios).

name: Athens, the Acropolis and mainland Attica
by_whom: Bavarian battalion under Lt-Col Herbst (left Nafplio 28 February 1833); Major Paligen received the fortress; Christophoros Neezer garrison commander
basis: Arrangement of Constantinople (21 July 1832) and London Protocol (30 August 1832); Regency order of 16 February 1833 (Julian) to occupy all positions within the borders of the Kingdom; Royal Decree of 22 February 1833 (Julian) = 6 March 1833 placing Attica, Boeotia, Euboea and Phthiotis under the full sovereignty of the Kingdom
event: Osman Aga's garrison of about 250 men, which had refused to leave without orders from Constantinople, lowered the Ottoman flag on 31 March (Julian) 1833; the Ottoman governor (Egiup Aga) left for Chalkis. Athens had been Ottoman since 1826-27.
date_note: The Turkish garrison left the Acropolis on 31 March 1833 (Greek sources, Julian) = 12 April 1833 (Gregorian); St Clair gives 'April 1833', which fits the Gregorian reading. The Greek flag was raised on 1/13 April 1833.
sources: protothema.gr 'I apochorisi ton Tourkon apo tin Athina to 1833' (31 March 1833; Osman Aga; Herbst; Paligen; Neezer; Regency decree 16 Feb 1833); ancientathens3d.com (31 March 1833); St Clair, Who Saved the Parthenon? (Open Book Publishers 2022), ch. 15 ('by April 1833, when the Greek state took over from the Ottoman army'); lamia.gr chronology (Royal Decree 22 Feb 1833)
note: Neither web source states the calendar of 31 March; Julian is assumed (Greek usage, and consistent with St Clair and with the Lamia dating, see 1833-lamia-handover). Athens became the capital on 18 September 1834.

name: Euboea, awarded but still Ottoman-held (1832-1833)
basis: Arrangement of Constantinople (21 July 1832) and London Protocol (30 August 1832)
event: Euboea was Greek by treaty but Ottoman troops stayed until April 1833.
date_note: End = handover (Chalkis 7 April 1833, calendar uncertain).
sources: see 1833-euboea-handover
note: Euboea was also within the 1830 award.

name: Euboea (Chalkis, Karystos)
by_whom: Representative of King Otto and Bavarian/Greek troops
basis: Arrangement of Constantinople (21 July 1832) and London Protocol (30 August 1832); Royal Decree of 22 February 1833 (Julian)
event: The Ottomans handed the island over only to Otto's representative in 1833; the local agas had demanded unpaid wages before withdrawing. A Muslim community remained in Chalkis until 1881.
date_note: Chalkis was 'liberated on 7 April 1833' (odigostoupoliti.eu, calendar not stated; = 19 April 1833 if Julian, as Greek sources normally are). The date for Karystos is not in the fetched sources. Month given.
sources: odigostoupoliti.eu 'Chalkida. Ston porthmo tou Evripou' (7 April 1833); archaeology.wiki Chalkida article (handed over only to Otto's representative in 1833); protothema.gr (agas' wage demands); skroutz listing of 'O echthros entos ton teichon: I mousoulmaniki koinotita tis Chalkidas (1833-1881)'
note: Calendar of 7 April uncertain; Karystos handover date not found.

name: Lamia (Zitouni) and Ypati districts, awarded but still Ottoman-held (1832-1833)
line: Between the Spercheios (south) and the Othrys crest (north, the 1832 frontier).
basis: London Protocol of 18/30 August 1832
event: Zitouni (Izdin) and Patratziki (Ypati, Ottoman Padracık) were the main points of dispute in 1832 and went to Greece.
date_note: The Constantinople arrangement (21 July 1832) left the Zitouni district open; the London Protocol of 18/30 August 1832 gave it to Greece.
sources: see 1833-lamia-handover
note: This district was also in the 1829 award but outside the 1830 award.

name: Lamia (Zitouni), Ypati and Phthiotis north of the Spercheios
line: Between the Spercheios and the Othrys crest (1832 frontier).
by_whom: Interior and Church minister Iakovakis Rizos-Neroulos with Bavarian Lt-Col Albert
basis: London Protocol of 18/30 August 1832; Royal Decree of 22 February 1833 (Julian) placing Phthiotis under full sovereignty
event: No formal handover took place: the Ottoman commander left through the north gate and the Greek civil and military authorities moved in; most Muslim families had already left for Larissa.
date_note: The Turkish commander left and Lamia was taken over on 28 March 1833, which the source calls Holy Tuesday with Easter on 2 April: Orthodox Easter 1833 fell on 2 April Julian, so 28 March is Julian = Tuesday 9 April 1833 (Gregorian). Greek and Bavarian troops had taken the fortress of Agios Loukas in late March (Julian).
sources: lamia.gr chronology (xronologio 2013) (28 March 1833, Holy Tuesday; Rizos-Neroulos; Albert; Royal Decree 22 Feb 1833; London Protocol 18/30 Aug 1832); allovergreece.com Kastro Lamias (liberated 1832-33); Özkan 2020 (Izdin and Padracık to Greece by the 30 August 1832 treaty); 200years.mfa.gr
note: Whether the Ypati district was still Ottoman-held until 1833 or had passed to Greece in 1829 is not clear; it is grouped here with Lamia.

name: South Epirus insurgent zone 1854 (Arta, Peta, Pente Pigadia, Radovizi)
line: No defined line. The insurgents held the villages around Arta and Peta (their headquarters) and Pente Pigadia. en.wikipedia says Karaiskakis 'captured' Arta with 2,500 irregulars and that Ottoman troops (1,600 men plus 3,000 reinforcements with heavy artillery) later retook it; the date, and whether the castle of Arta fell, are not given. In 1854 all of this lay north of the 1832 frontier (Gulf of Arta between Kopraina and Menidi), i.e. in Ottoman territory.
by_whom: Irregulars and volunteers under Spyridon Karaiskakis (a Greek Army lieutenant), Kitsos Tzavelas and Theodoros Grivas (a Greek general), with officers who had resigned from the Greek Army to join (Nikolaos Zervas, Notis Botsaris, Athanasios Koutsonikas, Kitsos Tzavelas, Lambros Zikos). Not the Greek Army as such: unofficial, covertly supported by the Greek state.
battle: Peta (13 April 1854); Plaka; Voulgareli, Skoulikaria and Kleidi (12 May 1854)
basis: Insurrection during the Crimean War (Russo-Ottoman war of 1853–56), encouraged by King Otto's government; no Greek declaration of war.
event: Revolt began around Peta on 30 January 1854; Peta was the rebels' headquarters. A 6,000-strong Ottoman force with British and French artillery support attacked Peta on 13 April and Tzavelas withdrew behind the Greek border; after Voulgareli, Skoulikaria and Kleidi (12 May) the Epirotes retreated into Greece. The Anglo-French blockade of Piraeus cut off supplies and forced the Greek government to recall its officers.
date_note: en.wikipedia gives 30 January 1854 for the start (Karaiskakis's speeches in villages east of Arta, Peta region) and 12 May for the battle of Kleidi, after which the Epirotes withdrew behind the Greek border; the article does not say whether these dates are Julian or Gregorian.
sources: en.wikipedia Epirus revolt of 1854; en.wikipedia Greek Volunteer Legion (the Greek government sponsored the uprisings of early 1854).
note: Show as an unofficial insurgent zone, not as Greek state control: the Greek state did not enter the war, and its officers took part only after resigning. en.wikipedia flags the claim of Greek state support with 'citation needed'.
editorial: Status changed from 'de_facto' to 'rising'.

name: Metsovo (Grivas, March 1854)
line: Town only: held by Grivas's volunteers for a few weeks.
by_whom: Volunteers under General Theodoros Grivas. Unofficial.
basis: 1854 insurrection (Crimean War).
event: Grivas took Metsovo in early March 1854 (his men looted it); Ottoman troops from Ioannina retook it after three days of fighting; 400 houses were burned. Grivas retreated on 27 March.
date_note: en.wikipedia: captured 'in early March 1854', Grivas retreated on 27 March after repeated Ottoman attacks supported by Albanian irregulars. The Metsovo Museum timeline gives March 1854 for the three-day fight in which Ottoman forces from Ioannina drove Grivas out. Neither says which calendar it uses.
sources: en.wikipedia Epirus revolt of 1854; metsovomuseum.gr timeline '1854'.
editorial: Status changed from 'de_facto' to 'rising'.

name: Insurgent districts of central and northern Epirus 1854 (Paramythia, Souli, Tsamantas, Chimarra)
line: No line; en.wikipedia lists these places as 'under full rebel control' without dates or limits.
by_whom: Local insurgents and irregulars; unofficial.
basis: 1854 insurrection (Crimean War).
event: Reported rebel control of Paramythia, Souli, Tsamantas, Chimarra and some villages around Ioannina.
date_note: No dates in the sources; spring 1854, ending with the general collapse of the revolt in May 1854. Month values are estimates from the overall chronology.
sources: en.wikipedia Epirus revolt of 1854.
note: Weakly sourced; treat as a faint, approximate extent at most.
editorial: Status changed from 'de_facto' to 'rising'.

name: Thessalian insurgent districts 1854
line: Not determinable from the sources seen. en.wikipedia (Epirus revolt of 1854) says only that the revolt was 'in full swing' in parts of Thessaly. The standard accounts associate General Christodoulos Hatzipetros with the Thessalian rising and the area of Kalambaka, but the places and dates could not be verified.
by_whom: Irregulars led by Greek officers (Hatzipetros, unverified); unofficial.
basis: 1854 insurrection (Crimean War).
event: Rising in parts of Thessaly in 1854; fighters from Thessaly and Magnesia also joined the Olympus rising in Macedonia.
date_note: Months are estimates from the overall chronology of the 1854 risings (Epirus January–May, Macedonia April–June); no Thessaly-specific dates were found.
sources: en.wikipedia Epirus revolt of 1854; en.wikipedia 1854 Macedonian rebellion; en.wikipedia Greek Volunteer Legion.
note: Placeholder with no reliable extent: needs a Greek source (e.g. Istoria tou Ellinikou Ethnous vol. 13, or Hellenic Army General Staff) before drawing.
editorial: Status changed from 'de_facto' to 'rising'.

name: Tempe, southern Pieria and the western Pindus (Grevena) 1854
line: No line: Olympus chieftains with fighters from Greece, Thessaly and Magnesia took the Vale of Tempe and parts of Pieria; Theodoros Ziakas, after defeating the Ottomans at Karpero (May 1854), took the western Pindus, attacked the Grevena area and dug in at Spilaio.
by_whom: Irregular bands (Olympus chieftains, Theodoros Ziakas) with fighters from the Greek kingdom; unofficial.
basis: 1854 Macedonian rebellion (Crimean War).
event: Rising in Tempe and Pieria; Ziakas's victory at Karpero; armistice on 31 May under Anglo-French diplomatic pressure; withdrawal into Greece in June 1854.
date_note: en.wikipedia: April to June 1854; the rebels repulsed an Ottoman offensive on 28 May and an armistice was agreed on 31 May; the chieftains left for Greece in June.
sources: en.wikipedia 1854 Macedonian rebellion.
editorial: Status changed from 'de_facto' to 'rising'.

name: Sithonia and Mount Athos (Karatasos, 1854)
line: No line: landing on Sithonia, failed attack on the Ottoman camp at Ormylia, retreat to Athos and brief capture of Karyes.
by_whom: About 500 irregulars under Tsamis (Dimitrios) Karatasos, a former aide-de-camp of King Otto; unofficial.
basis: 1854 Macedonian rebellion.
event: Karatasos's landing on Sithonia; brief hold on Karyes; defeat on 28 May 1854.
date_note: en.wikipedia: landing in April 1854, attack on Ormylia on 22 April, retreat to Athos in mid-May, defeat on 28 May and withdrawal to Dafni; the rebels were taken back to Athens on the French ship Solon (date not given).
sources: en.wikipedia 1854 Macedonian rebellion.
note: The monks of Athos did not support the revolt.
editorial: Status changed from 'de_facto' to 'rising'.

name: Piraeus (Anglo-French occupation, Crimean War)
line: No defined line. The occupying troops held the port and town of Piraeus, the port of Athens, with camps in Piraeus; the sources seen do not say that Athens itself was garrisoned. The Anglo-French navy also blockaded Piraeus and other Greek ports.
basis: Anglo-French intervention to force Greek neutrality in the Crimean War after the 1854 incursions into Ottoman Epirus, Thessaly and Macedonia.
event: Anglo-French squadron blockaded Piraeus and landed troops; King Otto had to recall his officers and declare neutrality; the Kriezis government was replaced by one under Alexandros Mavrokordatos (with Kallergis as minister of war) acceptable to the British and French legations. Cholera spread from the occupation troops to Athens in 1854. The occupation lasted until 1857.
date_note: The sources seen give only '1854–1857' (Metsovo Museum timeline: occupied and blockaded 1854 to 1857; the Lausanne Project: troops deployed in April 1854; a letter from Greece of 2 June 1854 (Julian) is the earliest French military mail). The standard accounts give a landing in May 1854 and an evacuation in February 1857; the days could not be verified. Greek dates of the time are Julian (12 days behind).
sources: en.wikipedia Epirus revolt of 1854 (blockade of Piraeus); en.wikipedia Kingdom of Greece ('During the Crimean War the British occupied Piraeus'); en.wikipedia Greek Volunteer Legion; metsovomuseum.gr timeline 1854; thelausanneproject.com 'The Foreigner in Piraeus' (2025); efo.gr philatelic exhibit 'Greece French Military Mail' (Arvanitis); skai.gr article on the 1854 cholera and Mavrokordatos.
note: The sources disagree on the occupier: en.wikipedia Kingdom of Greece names only the British, the efo.gr exhibit only the French, the others both. the exact landing and departure days are not in the sources read.

name: Corfu and Paxoi with their dependencies (neutralized)
line: Islands only. Treaty of London of 29 March 1864, Art. II: Corfu and Paxo, 'after their union to the Hellenic Kingdom', shall enjoy 'the advantages of perpetual neutrality', and Greece undertakes to maintain it. (The Treaty of 14 November 1863, Art. II, had given perpetual neutrality to all the Ionian Islands; a Protocol of 25 January 1864 restricted it to Corfu and Paxo and their dependencies.) The fortifications of Corfu were to be demolished, and the UK kept the use of the port of Corfu.
basis: Treaty of London of 29 March 1864 (Great Britain, France, Russia and Greece), following the Treaty of 14 November 1863 among the Powers and the Ionian Parliament's vote for union (19 October 1863).
event: Britain gave up the protectorate (1815–1864); the islands became three Greek provinces.
handover: 1864-05-28 (Protocol at Corfu ending the British Protectorate; proclamation of the Lord High Commissioner) / 1864-06-02 (= 21 May Julian: the Greek authorities took over and the British departed)
date_note: Union with Greece on 21 May 1864 (Julian) = 2 June 1864 (Gregorian). en.wikipedia (Treaty of London 1864, infobox of the United States of the Ionian Islands) gives '21 May 1864', the Julian date; the body of the United States of the Ionian Islands article gives 2 June 1864 for the formal union and 28 May for the Lord High Commissioner's proclamation. Holland: a Protocol signed at Corfu on 28 May 1864 recorded the end of the British Protectorate.
sources: en.wikipedia Treaty of London (1864); en.wikipedia United States of the Ionian Islands; T. E. Holland, The European Concert in the Eastern Question (1885), ch. 2 (en.wikisource), for the 1863 and 1864 treaty texts and the Corfu protocol of 28 May 1864; en.wikipedia Territorial evolution of Greece.
note: Ratification date not found (Holland: ratifications of the 1863 treaty were to be exchanged within six weeks). Sources disagree on the parties: en.wikipedia Treaty of London (1864) lists Greece, Prussia, Russia and the UK; the United States of the Ionian Islands article lists the UK, Greece, France and Russia. en.wikipedia Territorial evolution of Greece gives '2 May 1864' as the signature date, which conflicts with 29 March. Neutrality matters later (e.g. the 1916 Allied occupation of Corfu, the 1923 Italian occupation).

name: Lefkada, Ithaca, Kefalonia, Zakynthos, Kythira and their dependencies
line: Islands only. The United States of the Ionian Islands consisted of Corfu, Paxo, Santa Maura (Lefkada), Ithaca, Cephalonia, Zante and Cerigo (Kythira) with 'the smaller islets'. The small islands named here are listed from their present attachment and are not named in the sources seen.
basis: Treaty of London of 29 March 1864.
event: Union of the Ionian Islands with Greece.
date_note: As for Corfu: 21 May 1864 Julian = 2 June 1864 Gregorian.
sources: en.wikipedia Treaty of London (1864); en.wikipedia United States of the Ionian Islands; Holland (1885) ch. 2.
note: Not verified: whether all the Echinades, Atokos and Arkoudi were Ionian dependencies, and whether Elafonisos (Cervi) was Ionian (Britain claimed Cervi and Sapienza as Ionian in 1850; they probably stayed Greek, so they are not counted in 1864). The mainland dependencies of the Venetian period had long gone (Parga was sold to Ali Pasha in 1819).

name: Southern Thessaly up to Domokos (Greek Army, February 1878)
line: From the 1832 frontier on the Othrys northwards to Domokos; the exact ground held is not described in the sources seen.
by_whom: Greek regular army under General Skarlatos Soutsos (official, ordered by the government).
basis: Greek government decision (Koumoundouros) to send the army into Ottoman Thessaly at the end of the Russo-Turkish War, to protect the Thessalian rebels.
event: The army entered Ottoman Thessaly and within two days liberated villages up to Domokos; it withdrew within days or weeks under Great Power pressure.
date_note: Crossing on 21 January 1878 (Julian) = 2 February 1878 (Gregorian): skai.gr 'on this day, 21 January' and en.wikipedia 1878 Macedonian rebellion ('2 February 1878'). The withdrawal date was not found: en.wikipedia says the forces 'returned to their bases shortly after' because of Great Power intervention (and San Stefano, 3 March 1878).
sources: skai.gr 'Σαν σήμερα 21 Ιανουαρίου' (1878 entry); en.wikipedia 1878 Macedonian rebellion; en.wikipedia Epirus Revolt of 1878 ('in February 1878 groups of irregulars entered Thessaly and Epirus').
note: Sources disagree on formality: en.wikipedia says 'Greece declared war on the Ottoman Empire on 2 February 1878'; skai.gr says the army invaded 'without a declaration of war'. Extent and end day need a Greek military history (Hellenic Army General Staff) before drawing.

name: Western Thessaly insurgent districts 1878 (Agrafa, Mouzaki)
line: No line: Thanassis Ziakas's Agrafa band rose at Vounista, Granitsa and Mesenikolas; a committee of Greek officers, sent secretly, had its headquarters at Loutro (Karditsa).
by_whom: Irregulars, with a committee of Greek officers sent secretly; at Mouzaki Lieutenants Georgios Alexandris and Takis Stournaris led the Greeks, 'with cover support from the Greek Army'. Semi-official at most.
basis: Thessalian revolt of 1878 during the Russo-Turkish War.
event: Rising in the Agrafa; victory at Mouzaki (the Ottoman commander Moussa Gkeka captured); suppression soon after.
date_note: en.wikipedia (Battle of Mouzaki): by early March 1878 the bands had risen; battle of Mouzaki on 4 May 1878 (calendar not stated). End month estimated: the Ottomans 'soon' suppressed the rising and the Powers pressed Greece to stop supporting it.
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Mouzaki.
note: Other 1878 Thessalian foci (e.g. Pelion) are not in the sources seen.
editorial: Status changed from 'de_facto' to 'rising'.

name: Epirus insurgent districts, February–March 1878 (Tzoumerka, north of Preveza, Radovizi)
line: No line.
by_whom: Irregulars (Epirote unit under Hristos Mitsios at Plaka); the Greek government had stopped Spyromilios and Botsaris from leading it. Unofficial.
basis: Epirus revolt of 1878.
event: First areas to join: Tzoumerka, the region north of Preveza and Radovizi; declaration of union at Botsi on 12 March 1878; retreat.
date_note: en.wikipedia: irregulars crossed in February 1878; on 12 March 1878 representatives at Botsi declared the union of Epirus with Greece, after which Ottoman troops arrived by sea and the revolutionaries retreated to the Greek border.
sources: en.wikipedia Epirus Revolt of 1878.
note: en.wikipedia places Tzoumerka 'west of Arta', which seems to be a slip (it lies north-east); Botsi is not identified.
editorial: Status changed from 'de_facto' to 'rising'.

name: Agioi Saranta–Delvino (Epirote volunteers, 1878)
line: No line: the volunteers held Agioi Saranta town, Vurgut, Delvino, Gjashta, Lekuresi and the St George monastery.
by_whom: About 150 Epirotes under Minoas Lappas and Georgios Stephanou, joined by about 700 volunteers, mostly refugees from Corfu. Unofficial.
basis: Epirus revolt of 1878.
event: Landing at Agioi Saranta; positions held until 6,000 Ottoman regulars and Albanian irregulars marched from Ioannina; 20 villages of the Delvino region were burned in reprisal.
date_note: Dates approximate. en.wikipedia says the revolt ended 'At March 4', which conflicts with the 12 March Botsi declaration and is probably an error.
sources: en.wikipedia Epirus Revolt of 1878; en.wikipedia Battle of Lëkurës (search result, not fetched).
note: Faint at most: an insurgent landing, not Greek state control.
editorial: Status changed from 'de_facto' to 'rising'.

name: Olympus (Litochoro) and Vourinos risings 1878
line: No line.
by_whom: Irregulars (Kosmas Doumpiotis at Olympus, Anastasios Pichion at Vourinos). Unofficial.
basis: 1878 Macedonian rebellion.
event: Risings at Litochoro (destroyed 4 March) and Vourinos.
date_note: en.wikipedia: Provisional Government of Macedonia formed on 18 February 1878 at Vourinos; the Olympus revolt began at Litochoro on 19 February and Litochoro was destroyed on 4 March 1878; the infobox ends the rebellion on 13 July 1878 (the text speaks of the winter). Calendar not stated.
sources: en.wikipedia 1878 Macedonian rebellion.
note: Outside the brief's Epirus and Thessaly focus; included for completeness, with Litochoro as the only firmly held point (19 February – 4 March 1878).
editorial: Status changed from 'de_facto' to 'rising'.

name: Thessaly and southern Epirus (1880 Berlin Conference line, Kalamas–Olympus)
line: As described in the US dispatch on the Conference (FRUS 1880): starts at the northern branch of the Kalamas delta and follows the river north to 'Poadhoniani' (unidentified); turns north-east through Kalpaki (Kalbaki), splitting Zagori, so that Greece gets the valleys of the Zagoritikos and Metsovitikos with Metsovo and Ioannina; follows the watershed north of the Salamvrias (Peneus), i.e. the Peneus–Aliakmon divide (Kamvounia), touching the 'Demirkapón' and 'Tahapka' peaks; crosses the Olympus range at its highest peak ('Mount Ilias'); and runs east to the Aegean at the mouth of the Mavrolongos river. de.wikipedia: the French proposal adopted 'ran from the mouth of the Mavrolongos to that of the Kalamas'. About 22,000 km² and about 300,000 inhabitants (FRUS).
basis: Berlin Conference of 16 June – 1 July 1880 (the six Powers), under Art. 24 of the Treaty of Berlin (13 July 1878) and Protocol 13 of the Congress of Berlin (5 July 1878).
event: The Powers adopted unanimously the French line drawn on the recommendation of the British technical delegate General Sir Lintorn Simmons; Greece accepted it and the Porte refused it. Greece mobilized; in April 1881 the Powers offered a smaller line, which became the 1881 settlement (about two-thirds of the Berlin award, per Lord Granville).
date_note: The Conference opened on 16 June 1880 and its last sitting was on 1 July 1880, when the ambassadors signed the final act / collective note (de.wikipedia, FRUS). It was presented to Greece and Turkey by the collective note of 15 July 1880; the Porte objected on 26 July. The Powers gave up the line on 7 April 1881 (offer of a reduced line) and it was superseded by the Convention of 24 May 1881 (Powers–Porte); 24 May 1881 is used as the end.
sources: FRUS 1880, doc. 281 (history.state.gov/historicaldocuments/frus1880/d281); de.wikipedia Berliner Konferenz 1880; Hansard (Lords) 30 June 1881 'Address for a paper'; Holland (1885) ch. 2 (en.wikisource), for the 1880–81 chronology; 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica 'Greece' (en.wikisource): the line 'would have given Greece Thessaly and southern Epirus, extending to the river Kalamas'.
note: Protocol 13 of 1878 only suggested a line following 'the valley of the Selmyrias (the ancient Peneus)' on the Aegean side and 'that of the Calamas' on the Ionian side; it was a recommendation, not an award. The Olympus/Kamvounia crest belongs to this 1880 line; the 1881 line ran further south, leaving Elassona and the Meluna pass Ottoman. The Thessaly part became de_jure in 1881 (event 1881-thessaly-arta); the rest (Ioannina, Metsovo, Preveza, Elassona, Thesprotia) lapsed in 1881. 'Poadhoniani', 'Demirkapón' and 'Tahapka' are as transcribed in the dispatch; they are not identified.

name: Thessaly and the Arta district (1881 line)
line: Article I of the Convention of 24 May 1881 (Powers–Porte), taken over by the Greek–Ottoman Convention of 2 July 1881 (Holland's text, summarized in order from east to west): from a point near the defile of Karalik-Dervend, 'between the mouth of the Salamvrias and Platamona' (about 4 km south of Platamon), west along a mountain crest between Krania and Avarnitza; between Nezeros and Analipsis to the summit of Mount Godaman; then along the Olympus crest to the summit of Kokkinopetra; west along the crest between Ligara and Derveni-Melona (the Meluna pass, left Ottoman) to the summit of Mount Kritiri; to the right bank of the Xeraghis (Xerias) and along the watershed south-west to the heights north of Zarko (the line passes north of Zarkos); north-west along the watershed towards Diminitza, then west, leaving Elevtherokhorion (Eleftherochori) to Turkey; along the watershed by Flamouristi, Gavronon and Georgitza to the summit of Mount Kratchovo; south along the crest by the summits of Zygos, Dokini and Peristeri; down the stream that 'carries off by the shortest way the rainfall' of Peristeri to the River Arta (Arachthos), passing near Kalarrhytes and Mikalitzi (left Ottoman); then the thalweg of the Arachthos to its mouth in the Gulf of Arta. 'This delimitation will be fixed on the spot by a Commission composed of the Delegates of the Six Powers'. Elassona and the Meluna pass, Metsovo, Kalarrytes and Syrrako, Ioannina and Preveza remained Ottoman.
basis: Convention of Constantinople of 2 July 1881 (Greece–Ottoman Empire, signed by Andreas Koundouriotis and Mahmud Server Pasha and ratified the same day), executing the Convention of 24 May 1881 between the six mediating Powers and the Porte (ratified 14 June 1881), under Art. 24 of the Treaty of Berlin.
event: Peaceful transfer of Thessaly (apart from Elassona) and the Arta district; Greek troops crossed on 6 July 1881; Chilil Pasha handed over Larissa and the mayor Etem Effendi gave up the keys of the city. About 13,400 km² and about 300,000 people (poimin.gr); Lord Granville in the Lords: 'more or less 5,000 square miles', about two-thirds of the Berlin award.
handover: 1881-07-06 to c. 1881-11 (in sections; Larissa 31 August 1881, calendar not stated)
date_note: Start = 6 July 1881, when Greek troops crossed the old frontier (Holland). The territory was then handed over 'section by section' under officers of the Powers, under an Act annexed to the Convention, to be finished within five months (Hansard, 30 June 1881), i.e. by about November–December 1881. The only town date found: Larissa was handed over on 31 August 1881 (poimin.gr; calendar not stated; if Julian, 12 September Gregorian), the army under Skarlatos Soutsos coming from the Othrys via Trikala. Dates for Arta, Volos, Trikala, Karditsa and the other towns were not found. Delimitation protocol: 28 November 1881.
sources: Holland, The European Concert in the Eastern Question (1885), ch. 2, on en.wikisource (Article I text, 6 July 1881 crossing, 28 November 1881 protocol, 1882 dispute); en.wikipedia Convention of Constantinople (1881); en.wikipedia Congress of Berlin; Hansard (Lords) 30 June 1881; poimin.gr (Larissa, 31 August 1881); 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica 'Greece' (the boundary 'traced in 1881' from the Aegean near Platamona to the mouth of the river Arta).
note: From 4 December 1897 this area is reduced by the strips ceded to the Ottoman Empire (event 1897-frontier-rectification-strips); the four points disputed in 1881–82 are in event 1881-82-disputed-frontier-points. The Olympus/Kamvounia crest of the 1880 line does not apply here. The el.wikipedia URL given for the convention returned 'not found', and the Greek MFA text of the convention (web.archive.org copy of mfa.gr 1881_constantinople_convention.doc) was blocked by the permission system, so the zone-by-zone handover dates are still missing. Where Holland's text (as summarized) says the line turns west 'about 18 km short of Diminitza', check the original.

name: Punta (Aktio) at the entrance of the Gulf of Arta
line: Convention of 24 May 1881, Art. II: Punta and its territory are ceded to Greece; the forts covering the entrance of the Gulf of Arta on both the Preveza and the Punta sides to be disarmed within three months and kept disarmed in peacetime; free navigation of the gulf. Under the 1832 arrangement the fort of Punta had stayed Ottoman with a surrounding radius of 'not less than half an hour, nor more than an hour'.
basis: Convention of 24 May 1881, Art. II; Convention of Constantinople of 2 July 1881.
event: The Ottoman enclave of Punta, on the Acarnanian shore of the Preveza strait, passed to Greece.
date_note: Handover date not found; within the 1881 section-by-section transfer (6 July 1881 onwards).
sources: Holland (1885) ch. 2 (en.wikisource): texts of the 1832 arrangement and of the 1881 Convention, Art. II.
note: A small enclave of 1832–1881 that the map can easily miss.

name: The four points disputed in 1881–82 (Karalik-Dervend, Nezeros/Analipsis, Kritzovali, Gounitza)
line: Small strips along the 1881 line where the Turks signed the Delimitation Commission's final protocol (28 November 1881) 'under reserve', objecting to giving them up: Karalik-Dervend, Nezeros (or Analypsis), Kritzovali and Gounitza. After fighting near Karalik-Dervend in August 1882, a protocol of 9 November 1882 settled the matter by 'accepting the frontier as it had been laid down by the international Commission', so the points went to Greece.
basis: Final protocol of the Delimitation Commission, Constantinople, 28 November 1881; Greek–Ottoman protocol of 9 November 1882.
event: Dispute over four points of the 1881 line; Greek–Ottoman fighting at Karalik-Dervend in August 1882; armistice 6 September 1882; settlement 9 November 1882.
date_note: Start = protocol of 9 November 1882 (armistice of 6 September 1882 after the August fighting); the actual handover date was not found. End: some or all of these heights were probably among the strategic points returned to the Ottomans in 1897 (not verified); if not, end should be null.
sources: Holland (1885) ch. 2 (en.wikisource).
note: Kritzovali and Gounitza could not be located. Who held these points between July 1881 and November 1882 is not stated (probably Ottoman troops, given the fighting).
editorial: Status changed from 'de_jure' to 'note'.

name: Western Crete outside the towns (Vassos's expeditionary corps)
line: No line.
