Vassos landed at Kolymbari, set up his headquarters at Platanias–Alikianos, and declared that he would not enter the four cities where the European fleets were present but intended 'to occupy the rest of Crete'. Voukolies was taken on 19 February 1897 by about 600 Cretan rebels, volunteers and Greek soldiers. The corps did not approach Chania and 'accomplished little'.
by_whom: About 1,500 men (two battalions) of the Greek Army under Colonel Timoleon Vassos. Official.
basis: Greek government decision (Deligiannis) to send the army to annex Crete; Vassos proclaimed the union of Crete with Greece on landing.
event: Landing and proclamation of union; the Powers' ultimatum (18 February / 2 March 1897), the blockade from 21 March and the Powers' proclamation of Cretan autonomy under Ottoman suzerainty (20 March 1897) followed; Vassos was recalled in May.
date_note: Landing date varies: en.wikipedia Greco-Turkish War (1897): 14 February (2 February Julian) at Platanias; en.wikipedia Cretan Revolt (1897–1898): 16 February at Kolymbari; Foundation of the Hellenic World (fhw.gr, Julian dates): 3 February = 15 February Gregorian, at Kolymbari Bay. 15 February is used. End: Vassos returned to Greece with the volunteers on 9 May 1897 (en.wikipedia Cretan Revolt).
sources: en.wikipedia Greco-Turkish War (1897); en.wikipedia Cretan Revolt (1897–1898); fhw.gr chronos 1833–1897 foreign policy, fact 08.
note: International troops of five Powers (Germany sent none) occupied the main Cretan towns from late March–April 1897.

name: Greek advance across the Arachthos to Philippiada and Pente Pigadia (April 1897)
line: From the Arachthos at Arta north-west to Philippiada and north to Pente Pigadia.
by_whom: Greek Army of Epirus under Colonel Thrasyvoulos Manos. Official.
basis: Greco-Turkish War of 1897 (war declared 18 April 1897).
event: The Greek Army crossed into Ottoman Epirus, took Philippiada and Pente Pigadia, and was thrown back to Arta at the end of April.
date_note: 1911 Britannica (Gregorian dates): the Turks bombarded Arta from 18 April for three days and withdrew towards Philippiada on the night of 21 April; on 23 April Colonel Manos occupied Philippiada and advanced to Pente Pigadia; on 28–29 April the advanced force near 'Homopulos' was attacked and driven back towards Arta. en.wikipedia: Manos captured Pente Pigadia about 23 April. istorikathemata.com (Julian dates, presumably): Ottoman victory at Pente Pigadia on 11 April (= 23 April Gregorian), Greeks fell back to Koumoutzades. End 29 April is approximate.
sources: 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica 'Greco-Turkish War, 1897' (en.wikisource); en.wikipedia Greco-Turkish War (1897); istorikathemata.com 'Ο ατυχής ελληνοτουρκικός πόλεμος του 1897' (2016).
note: The sources disagree on whether the fight at Pente Pigadia around 23 April was a Greek capture or an Ottoman victory.

name: Second Greek incursion towards Preveza (May 1897)
line: No line. On 12 May the Greeks began a new incursion and tried to cut off Preveza; fighting at Strevina on 13–14 May and an attack on Gribovo (Grimbovo) repulsed; retreat ordered on the night of 15 May; Epirote volunteers landed at the mouth of the Louros and were routed. At the armistice of 19 May Greek troops were still, if only just, on Ottoman soil in Epirus.
by_whom: Greek Army of Epirus (Manos) and Epirote volunteers. Official.
basis: Greco-Turkish War of 1897.
event: Failed attempt to cut off Preveza; heavy Greek casualties; retreat.
date_note: Gregorian dates from the 1911 Britannica and en.wikipedia; istorikathemata gives 2 May (Julian = 14 May) for the repulse at Grimbovo and 7 May (Julian = 19 May) for the armistice. End = night of 15 May, when the retreat was ordered; the small foothold still held at the armistice was presumably given up by the peace (date not found).
sources: 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica 'Greco-Turkish War, 1897'; en.wikipedia Greco-Turkish War (1897); istorikathemata.com (2016).

name: Villages of the Grevena district entered by Greek forces in 1897
line: No line: en.wikipedia lists the villages Gkrintades (now Aimilianos), Kipoureio, Pigaditsa, Plesia (now Melissi), Sitovo and Zalovo as entered 'without major difficulties', and Baltinon (now Kallithea), where local Aromanian fighters resisted.
by_whom: 'Greek forces' (en.wikipedia); probably irregular bands with some army officers, since about 2,600 Greek irregulars had crossed into Ottoman Macedonia on 24 March 1897. Officialness unclear.
basis: Greco-Turkish War of 1897.
event: Greek incursion into the Grevena district; Aromanian resistance at Baltinon.
date_note: No dates given; presumably April–May 1897, before the armistice of 20 May. Months are estimates.
sources: en.wikipedia Greco-Turkish War (1897).
note: en.wikipedia puts this in its Epirus section, but the villages are in the Grevena district (West Macedonia). Confirm against a Greek source before drawing.

name: Frontier zone and Tyrnavos (Ottoman occupation 1897–98)
line: From the 1881 line (Meluna pass) south to Tyrnavos and Deleria.
basis: Greco-Turkish War of 1897.
event: After the Greek defeat at Mati the Greek Army withdrew from the frontier and Tyrnavos.
date_note: 1911 Britannica (Gregorian): Edhem Pasha ordered the general advance from Elassona on 18 April; the Meluna pass was occupied on 19 April; fighting at Mati on 21–22 April; the Turkish left column reached Deliler on 23 April. fhw.gr: Tyrnavos taken 12 April (Julian) = 24 April. tirnavospress.gr (Julian, presumably): Ottomans descended from Meluna towards Mati on 8 April (= 20 April); Deleria and Mousalar occupied on the night of 11 April (= 23 April). End: see 1897-ottoman-occupation-larissa.
sources: 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica 'Greco-Turkish War, 1897'; fhw.gr; tirnavospress.gr 'Ο ελληνοτουρκικός πόλεμος του 1897 σε θεσσαλικό έδαφος'; en.wikipedia Greco-Turkish War (1897) (fighting outside Tyrnavos on 21–22 April).
note: Greek irregulars crossed the frontier on 9–10 April and Greek regulars took part in fighting on 16–17 April (1911 Britannica), but no Greek-held ground across the Thessalian frontier is described.

name: Larissa and the eastern Thessalian plain (Ottoman occupation 1897–98)
line: The Larissa plain north of Farsala and west of Velestino; the dates for Agia and Tempi were not found.
basis: Greco-Turkish War of 1897; evacuation under the Treaty of Constantinople (4 December 1897) once the indemnity was secured.
event: General Greek retreat from Larissa to Farsala; Ottoman entry into Larissa.
date_note: Larissa was abandoned by the Greek Army on 24/25 April (istorikathemata: 13 April Julian = 25 April; fhw.gr: taken on Easter Day, 13 April Julian = 25 April); the Turkish commander-in-chief entered on 27 April (1911 Britannica; en.wikipedia 'Larissa fell on 27 April'; istorikathemata: Edhem entered two days after the abandonment). Evacuation: fhw.gr 'Ottoman troops did not withdraw from Thessaly until May 1898'; tirnavospress.gr 'end of April or early May 1898' (calendar not stated); gaiaelliniki.gr 'until February 1898'. End = May 1898 (month only).
sources: 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica 'Greco-Turkish War, 1897'; en.wikipedia Greco-Turkish War (1897); istorikathemata.com (2016); fhw.gr; tirnavospress.gr; gaiaelliniki.gr (2021).
note: The day of the evacuation (and whether it was staged town by town) is not pinned down; the sources disagree (February vs April/May vs May 1898).

name: Western Thessaly: Trikala, Kalambaka, Karditsa (Ottoman occupation 1897–98)
line: The Greek part of western Thessaly, from the 1881 line to the Agrafa.
basis: Greco-Turkish War of 1897.
event: Ottoman occupation of western Thessaly after the Greek retreat.
date_note: The Ottoman entry dates for Trikala, Kalambaka and Karditsa were not found in any source seen; they were given up when the Greek Army fell back from Larissa to Farsala and Domokos (late April – May 1897). Start = May 1897 (estimate; could be late April). End as for Larissa.
sources: Inference from the chronology in the 1911 Britannica and en.wikipedia Greco-Turkish War (1897); FHW and tirnavospress for the evacuation.
note: Needs town dates from a Greek source.

name: Velestino, Volos, Farsala and Magnesia (Ottoman occupation 1897–98)
line: South-eastern Thessaly down to Almyros and the Othrys.
battle: Velestino (27–30 April and 5 May 1897); Farsala (5–6 May 1897)
basis: Greco-Turkish War of 1897.
event: After Farsala and Velestino the Greek Army fell back to Domokos; the Ottomans entered Volos without damage.
date_note: 1911 Britannica: on 5 May the Greeks were driven from their positions before Farsala and Velestino was abandoned that evening (Smolenskis retiring to Almyros); on 6 May the army withdrew from Farsala to Domokos. en.wikipedia and fhw.gr (26 April Julian): Volos fell on 8 May. Almyros was left when Smolenskis went to Thermopylae (he arrived on 18 May); its occupation date was not found. End as for Larissa.
sources: 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica 'Greco-Turkish War, 1897'; en.wikipedia Greco-Turkish War (1897); fhw.gr; istorikathemata.com; tirnavospress.gr.
note: Magnesia south of Volos (Pelion, Almyros) is included on the assumption that all of Thessaly was occupied; dates there were not found.

name: Domokos, the Othrys passes and the approaches to Lamia (part of Phthiotis)
line: Front at the armistice (approx.): the Ottoman vanguard at the outposts of Palioukoulia, Kamilovrysi and Taratsa just outside Lamia, the Greek Army at Lamia and Thermopylae. From Domokos south over the Othrys by the Furka pass (Derven Furka, now Kalamaki) to Taratsa.
basis: Greco-Turkish War of 1897; armistice of 20 May 1897 after the intervention of Tsar Nicholas II.
event: Domokos was the last battle; the Ottoman army crossed the Othrys and stopped just north of Lamia; Smolenskis was ordered to hold Thermopylae.
date_note: Battle of Domokos on 17 May 1897; the Greeks left Domokos during the night of 17/18 May and the Furka pass the following night (1911 Britannica). gaiaelliniki.gr (Julian, apparently): fighting at Derven Furka on 6 May (= 18 May); on 7 May (= 19 May) the Ottoman vanguard reached the outposts of Palioukoulia, Kamilovrysi and Taratsa, and the Turks camped at Taratsa. Ceasefire 19 May in Epirus and 20 May in Thessaly (en.wikipedia). End as for Larissa (May 1898); when the Ottomans left the ground south of the 1832 line was not found.
sources: 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica 'Greco-Turkish War, 1897'; en.wikipedia Greco-Turkish War (1897); en.wikipedia Battle of Domokos; gaiaelliniki.gr 'Ο ατυχής ελληνοτουρκικός πόλεμος του 1897 και η μάχη του Δομοκού' (2021); fhw.gr.
note: Disagreement: en.wikipedia Battle of Domokos says Edhem Pasha advanced about 40 km and 'captured' the Thermopylae pass; the other sources say the Greeks held Thermopylae and the Ottomans stopped at Taratsa outside Lamia. Taratsa = Roditsa and Derven Furka = Kalamaki are given by gaiaelliniki; coordinates are approximate.

name: Frontier strips of Thessaly returned to the Ottoman Empire in 1897
line: Not pinned down. The treaty gave the Ottomans 'some strategical points on the frontier possessing no geographical importance' (1911 Britannica), 'small changes in the pre-war border line in favour of the Ottomans' (en.wikipedia). tirnavospress.gr: the Ottomans gained strategic heights, not inhabited areas, except the village of Koutsoufliani west of Elassona; Greece evacuated the area 'between Olympus and the Kamvounia'. Area ceded: 152 square miles (about 394 km²) (1911 Britannica, 'Greece', area section). Likely candidates, not verified: the 1881–82 disputed points (Karalik-Dervend, Nezeros/Analipsis, Kritzovali, Gounitza), the Meluna–Kritiri heights, the heights north of Zarkos.
basis: Treaty of Constantinople of 4 December 1897 (Greece–Ottoman Empire), after the Great Powers' mediation; Greece also paid an indemnity of 4,000,000 Turkish pounds and accepted the International Financial Commission.
event: Greece ceded strategic frontier points in Thessaly to the Ottoman Empire.
handover: In fact never handed back after the 1897 occupation; the new line was marked out after the treaty (details not found)
date_note: Greek de jure from the 1881 cession (or 1882 for the disputed points) until the Treaty of Constantinople, signed 22 November 1897 (Julian) = 4 December 1897 (in.gr). The preliminary peace was signed in September 1897 (en.wikipedia: 20 September; usually given as 18 September; not verified). Held by the Ottoman army since April 1897 and kept by it at the evacuation of May 1898.
sources: 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica 'Greece' (en.wikisource): 'some strategical points on the frontier' and 152 sq. m.; en.wikipedia Treaty of Constantinople (1897); en.wikipedia Greco-Turkish War (1897) (infobox: 'Small parts of Thessaly ceded'); tirnavospress.gr; in.gr (22 November 2020) on the treaty.
note: The main gap in the research: the treaty's Article 1 and the 1898 delimitation protocol must be found to draw the strips (try the treaty text in Martens, Nouveau Recueil Général, 2e série, t. 28, or Hellenic Army General Staff). Koutsoufliani's present name was not found. The 1897 losses were recovered in 1912 (next batch).
editorial: Status changed from 'de_jure' to 'note'.

name: Cretan State (under Prince George and Zaimis)
line: The whole island. The Powers kept troops in the main towns (international occupation since March–April 1897) and their flags on the Souda fortress islet.
basis: Autonomy under Ottoman suzerainty proclaimed by the Powers on 20 March 1897; Cretan State set up under the four protecting Powers (Britain, France, Italy, Russia) with Prince George of Greece as High Commissioner (1898–1906), then Alexandros Zaimis (1906–).
event: The Admirals' Council was dissolved on 26 December 1898; the Theriso revolt began on 23 March 1905; Prince George was replaced by Zaimis in September 1906, after which the withdrawal of the foreign troops began; a constitution followed in February 1907.
date_note: Prince George arrived as High Commissioner on 9 December (Julian) = 21 December 1898 (Gregorian) (en.wikipedia Cretan State; the same article also says '13 December' in one place). The Ottoman troops had been expelled in November 1898 after the Powers' ultimatum of 17 October 1898 (30 days). End = the Cretan Assembly's declaration of union on 7 October 1908 (24 September Julian).
sources: en.wikipedia Cretan State; en.wikipedia Cretan Revolt (1897–1898).
note: The occupation sectors (in the standard accounts: British at Heraklion, French in Lasithi, Russian at Rethymno, Italian in the Chania district, with Chania town shared) are not given in the sources seen. Brief: show faintly.

name: Crete after the declaration of union (self-governing, union not accepted by Greece)
line: The whole island; the Powers' flags stayed on the Souda fortress until 14 February 1913.
basis: Unilateral declaration of union (enosis) by the Cretan Assembly, not recognized by Greece or the Powers until 1912–13.
event: Crete governed itself in the name of the King of the Hellenes; the international troops left in 1909; Venizelos became Greek prime minister in 1910.
date_note: Start: declaration of union by the Cretan deputies on 24 September (Julian) = 7 October 1908 (en.wikipedia Cretan State infobox), after the Young Turk Revolution of July 1908. Withdrawal of the international troops: July 1909 in the standard accounts (not verified; en.wikipedia says only that the withdrawal began after September 1906). End: in October 1912, with the First Balkan War, Greece admitted the Cretan deputies to its parliament and sent Stephanos Dragoumis as governor-general (en.wikipedia gives no day; often given as 1/14 October 1912, not verified). In May 1912 the Cretan deputies had been kept out of the Greek parliament by the police.
sources: en.wikipedia Cretan State; en.wikipedia Kingdom of Greece.
note: For the next batch: the Great Powers lowered their flags at Souda on 14 February 1913; the Treaty of London (30 May 1913) ended the Sultan's rights; the formal union ceremony was on 1 December 1913 at the Firka fortress in Chania.

name: Principality of Samos
line: The island of Samos. Ikaria was part of the same metropolitan district but not, as far as the sources seen say, of the principality.
basis: Tributary principality under Ottoman suzerainty set up after the London Protocol and the Treaty of Constantinople of 1832 left Samos to the Ottoman Empire.
event: Autonomous principality with Christian princes appointed by the Porte, from Stefanos Vogoridis (1834–1850) to Grigorios Vegleris (April–August 1912).
date_note: Start: 1834 (en.wikipedia infobox and lead; the officeholders table gives Stefanos Vogoridis from January 1833, and the firman setting up the principality is usually dated December 1832; year only). End: on 11/24 November 1912 the Samian parliament declared union with Greece after Themistoklis Sofoulis landed and the Ottoman garrison withdrew; the union took effect on 2 March 1913 (en.wikipedia, citation needed); en.wikipedia Kingdom of Greece says the island was not occupied by Greek forces until 13 March 1913 and was securely Greek by 16 March.
sources: en.wikipedia Principality of Samos; en.wikipedia Kingdom of Greece.
note: Whether Fournoi or other islets belonged to the principality was not checked. Brief: show faintly. The union of 1912–13 belongs to the next batch. In July 1912 Ikaria rose and formed a short-lived Free State (not covered here).
editorial: The principality's government declared union on 24 Nov 1912 but Samos stayed self-governing until the Greek landing of 13 Mar 1913 (GB3).

name: Free State of Icaria
by_whom: Ikarian insurgents (Ioannis Malachias)
basis: Local uprising; independence proclaimed until the Greek Navy took over
event: Ikarians expelled the Ottoman garrison and proclaimed a Free State, ended when Greece occupied the island on 4 November 1912 (Julian).
date_note: Revolt 16-18 July 1912 (Ottoman administrator surrendered 18 July); FOTW gives the Free State as 17-7-1912 to 4-11-1912 without calendar; these are Greek (Julian) dates, converted +13 days. If the sources meant Gregorian, start 1912-07-17 and end 1912-11-04.
sources: fotw.info/flags/gr-ai-ik.html; thecollector.com 'How one tiny island took on the Ottoman Empire'; Hellenic Navy (averof.hellenicnavy.gr/?p=8034) for 4 November
note: Starts before this batch's period (October 1912). Greek-populated entity outside the Greek state, comparable to Samos and Crete; show faintly. (Julian 17 July – 4 November 1912)

name: Ikaria
by_whom: Greek Navy
basis: Greek naval occupation in the First Balkan War at the invitation of the Free State
event: Greek forces took over Ikaria from the Free State of Icaria.
date_note: Hellenic Navy and FOTW give 4 November 1912, calendar not stated; Greek naval dates of 1912 are Julian, so 4 Nov Julian = 17 Nov Gregorian. FOTW adds 'union with Greece June 1913'.
sources: Hellenic Navy, 'Liberation of the North Aegean islands' (averof.hellenicnavy.gr/?p=8034): Mount Athos and Ikaria 'on November 2 and 4 respectively'; fotw.info gr-ai-ik
note: (Julian 4 November 1912). Becomes de_jure with the Great Powers' decision of 13 February 1914 (see 1914-aegean-islands-de-jure).

name: Crete
by_whom: Greek government (Governor-General Stephanos Dragoumis)
basis: Greek administration of the autonomous island, then cession by the Ottoman Sultan 'to their Majesties the Allied Sovereigns' in the Treaty of London (30 May 1913)
event: Greece administered Crete from October 1912; the Ottoman Empire ceded it to the Balkan allies on 30 May 1913 and recognized Greek sovereignty on 14 November 1913.
date_note: Start: Greek governor and Cretan deputies in the Greek parliament from 1/14 October 1912 (brief; standard histories). End: formal union ceremony, see 1913-crete-union.
sources: en.wikipedia Treaty of London (1913) (quote: 'cedes to their Majesties the Allied Sovereigns the island of Crete'); en.wikipedia Treaty of Athens; batch brief
note: (Julian 1 October 1912).

name: Crete
basis: Treaty of London (30 May 1913): Ottoman cession of Crete to the Allied Sovereigns; Treaty of Athens (14 November 1913): Ottoman recognition of Greek sovereignty over Crete
event: Formal union of Crete with Greece; Greek flag raised at the Firkas fortress in Chania in the presence of King Constantine and Venizelos.
in_force: 1913-11-14 (Treaty of Athens; ratification date not found)
date_note: The flag was raised at Firkas on '1 December 1913'. Greece was still on the Julian calendar and Greek sources (and the annual commemoration on 1 December) use the Julian date, so 1 Dec Julian = 14 Dec 1913 Gregorian. Some English sources give 1 December as if Gregorian. If you prefer the treaty date, use 1913-11-14.
sources: en.wikipedia Treaty of London (1913); en.wikipedia Treaty of Athens (Ottomans acknowledged 'Greek sovereignty on the island of' Crete); batch brief (flag raised 1 December 1913)
note: (Julian 1 December 1913).

name: Samos
by_whom: Greek Army and navy
basis: Greek military occupation, First Balkan War
event: Greek forces landed on Samos and had removed the Ottoman garrison by 16 March 1913.
date_note: en.wikipedia: attacked 13 March 1913, secured by 16 March (Gregorian); sansimera: 'liberated 2 March 1913' (Julian = 15 March).
sources: en.wikipedia First Balkan War; sansimera.gr articles/840; in.gr 2019-10-05 'Α΄ Βαλκανικός Πόλεμος'
note: (Julian 28 February – 2 March 1913). De jure from the Great Powers' decision of 13 February 1914.

name: Elassona and Deskati (north of the 1881 line)
line: From the 1881 Greek–Ottoman border north to the Sarantaporo pass and the Kamvounia range.
by_whom: Greek Army of Thessaly (Crown Prince Constantine)
basis: Military occupation, First Balkan War
event: Greece declared war 5/18 October 1912; the Army of Thessaly crossed the border the same day and took Elassona and Deskati on 6/19 October.
date_note: Army of Thessaly crossed the border 5/18 October 1912; Ottoman units at Elassona and Deskati driven back on 6 October 1912 (Julian) = 19 October Gregorian.
sources: stratistoria.wordpress.com 'Μάχη Σαρανταπόρου (9-10 Οκτ 1912)' (border crossed 5 Oct; 'στις 6 Οκτωβρίου, τα εγκαταστημένα στην Ελασσόνα και Δεσκάτη τμήματα του εχθρού'); sansimera.gr articles/840 (Elassona 6 October)
note: (Julian 6 October 1912). De jure from 1913-08-30, see 1913-macedonia-de-jure.

name: Sarantaporo pass and Servia
by_whom: Greek Army of Thessaly
basis: Military occupation, First Balkan War
event: After the Battle of Sarantaporo the Ottomans abandoned the pass in the night of 9/10 October; Greek forces entered Servia.
date_note: Battle of Sarantaporo 9-10 October 1912 Julian = 22-23 October Gregorian; Servia entered on the afternoon of 10 October Julian = 23 October; the 4th Division took the Aliakmon bridge intact on 10 October.
sources: stratistoria.wordpress.com 'Μάχη Σαρανταπόρου'; sansimera.gr articles/840 ('Σέρβια 10 Οκτωβρίου, entered in the afternoon'); en.wikipedia First Balkan War (Sarantaporo, undated)
note: (Julian 9-10 October 1912).

name: Kozani
by_whom: Greek Cavalry Brigade (Army of Thessaly)
basis: Military occupation, First Balkan War
event: Kozani was taken by parts of the Cavalry Brigade.
date_note: 11 October 1912 Julian = 24 October Gregorian.
sources: sansimera.gr articles/840; in.gr 2019-10-05
note: (Julian 11 October 1912).

name: Grevena and Siatista
by_whom: Greek Army of Thessaly (Evzone detachment)
basis: Military occupation, First Balkan War
event: Greek detachments occupied the Grevena and Siatista area after Kozani.
date_note: Month only. Stratistoria mentions an Evzone detachment assigned to 'the area of Grevena' after the liberation of Kozani (i.e. after 11/24 October 1912). No day was found in the sources read; local commemorations (not verified) put both in the second half of October 1912 (Julian).
sources: stratistoria.wordpress.com 'Μάχη των Γιαννιτσών' (Evzone detachment to 'την περιοχή Γρεβενών')
note: Day not found; do not use a precise day.

name: Eordaia and Amyntaio (Sorovich)
by_whom: Greek 5th Division; later the Center Group of the Greek Army
battle: Sorovich (Greek defeat); Vevi (15 November 1912, Greek defeat)
basis: Military occupation, First Balkan War
event: Advance of the 5th Division to Sorovich, its defeat and retreat, and reoccupation in November 1912.
date_note: The 5th Division was in the Amyntaio–Xyno Nero area on the afternoon of 18 October 1912 Julian (= 31 October). It was then routed at Sorovich (late October 1912; exact days not in the pages read) and fell back; by the evening of 6 November Julian (= 19 November) the Center Group again held the line Xyno Nero – Amyntaio – Arnissa.
sources: stratistoria.wordpress.com 'Μάχη των Γιαννιτσών' (disposition of 18 October) and 'Απελευθέρωση Φλώρινας' (line Xyno Nero–Amyntaio–Arnissa on 6 November); en.wikipedia First Balkan War (Vevi 15 November 1912 N.S. / 2 November O.S., Greek 5th Division forced to retreat)
note: Short interruption of control after Sorovich (about late Oct – mid Nov 1912 Gregorian) not dated precisely.

name: Pieria (Katerini)
by_whom: Greek Army of Thessaly
basis: Military occupation, First Balkan War
event: Katerini liberated.
date_note: 16 October 1912 Julian = 29 October Gregorian.
sources: sansimera.gr articles/840; in.gr 2019-10-05
note: (Julian 16 October 1912).

name: Imathia (Veria, Naousa)
by_whom: Greek Army of Thessaly
basis: Military occupation, First Balkan War
event: Veria and the Imathia plain taken.
date_note: Veria 16 October 1912 Julian (= 29 October) per sansimera; stratistoria says the Cavalry Brigade reached Veria only on the afternoon of 18 October Julian (= 31 October). Naousa: no date found (same days).
sources: sansimera.gr articles/840; stratistoria.wordpress.com 'Μάχη των Γιαννιτσών'
note: (Julian 16-18 October 1912). Sources disagree by two days.

name: Edessa (Vodena) and western Pella
by_whom: Greek Army
basis: Military occupation, First Balkan War
event: Edessa taken ('κατέλαβε την Έδεσσα').
date_note: 18 October 1912 Julian = 31 October Gregorian (title of a Nea tis Pellas article seen in search results; stratistoria confirms the capture without date).
sources: neapellas.gr '18 Οκτωβρίου 1912: η Απελευθέρωση της Έδεσσας' (title in search results; page itself could not be read); stratistoria.wordpress.com 'Μάχη των Γιαννιτσών'
note: (Julian 18 October 1912). Almopia: no date found.

name: Giannitsa and eastern Pella
by_whom: Greek Army of Thessaly
basis: Military occupation, First Balkan War
event: Greek victory at Giannitsa opened the road to Thessaloniki; the army crossed the Loudias on 20 October (Julian).
date_note: Battle 19-20 October 1912 Julian = 1-2 November Gregorian (en.wikipedia: 2 November N.S. / 20 October O.S.).
sources: en.wikipedia First Balkan War; stratistoria.wordpress.com 'Μάχη των Γιαννιτσών (19-20 Οκτ 1912)'; sansimera.gr articles/840
note: (Julian 19-20 October 1912).

name: Thessaloniki
joint_with: Bulgarian troops (a Bulgarian division entered the city after the Greek surrender and stayed until the Greek–Bulgarian clash of late June 1913)
by_whom: Greek Army of Thessaly (Crown Prince Constantine)
basis: Capitulation of the Ottoman garrison to the Greek Army
event: Hasan Tahsin Pasha surrendered Thessaloniki and its garrison to the Greek Army.
date_note: Surrender protocol signed on 26 October 1912 Julian (= 8 November, late evening); en.wikipedia gives the surrender of the city and its 26,000-man garrison as 9 November N.S. / 27 October O.S., the day the Greek Army entered.
sources: en.wikipedia First Balkan War; sansimera.gr articles/840 ('26 Οκτωβρίου 1912' surrender signed)
note: (Julian 26-27 October 1912). Bulgarian co-presence in the city from about 10 November 1912 to the expulsion of the Bulgarian garrison on 17-18 June 1913 Julian (30 June – 1 July Gregorian): these dates are from standard histories, not from the pages read; treat as approx.

name: Chalkidiki (without Mount Athos)
by_whom: Greek Army
basis: Military occupation after the surrender of Thessaloniki
event: Chalkidiki came under Greek control after the fall of Thessaloniki.
date_note: Month only: the Ottoman capitulation at Thessaloniki covered the region; no dates for the Greek entry into the Chalkidiki towns were found.
sources: en.wikipedia First Balkan War (surrender of Thessaloniki); no specific source for Chalkidiki
note: Extent and date approximate.

name: Mount Athos
by_whom: Greek Navy
basis: Greek naval landing, First Balkan War
event: Greek naval forces took Mount Athos.
date_note: Hellenic Navy: liberated on 2 November 1912 (Julian) = 15 November Gregorian.
sources: Hellenic Navy, averof.hellenicnavy.gr/?p=8034 ('Mount Athos ... on November 2')
note: (Julian 2 November 1912). END LEFT OPEN: the Treaty of London (1913) is usually summarized as leaving the title to the Aegean islands and to the peninsula of Mount Athos to the Great Powers (its Art. 5; not verified in the page read). Greek sovereignty over Athos was not settled by any treaty in this batch; the recognition at Lausanne is the record '1924-mount-athos'.
editorial: Greek-held from Nov 1912; Greek sovereignty (with the monastic autonomy) recognized at Lausanne (in force 6 Aug 1924).

name: Florina
by_whom: Greek Army (Center Group, Cavalry)
battle: Vevi (15 November 1912, Greek defeat); Ottoman withdrawal after the Serbs took Monastir
basis: Military occupation, First Balkan War
event: Florina liberated after the Ottoman retreat from Monastir.
date_note: Cavalry entered on the afternoon of 7 November 1912 Julian (= 20 November); the commander-in-chief entered on 8 November Julian (= 21 November).
sources: stratistoria.wordpress.com 'Απελευθέρωση Φλώρινας (8 Νοε 1912)' ('Την επομένη, 8 Νοεμβρίου 1912, μπήκε στην Φλώρινα'); sansimera.gr articles/840 (7 November); en.wikipedia First Balkan War (Vevi)
note: (Julian 7-8 November 1912).

name: Kastoria
by_whom: Greek Army
basis: Military occupation, First Balkan War
event: Kastoria liberated.
date_note: sansimera gives 10 November 1912 (Julian) = 23 November; the town's own commemoration is on 11 November (Julian) = 24 November.
sources: sansimera.gr articles/840; in.gr 2019-10-05
note: (Julian 10/11 November 1912). One-day disagreement between sources.

name: Philippiada and the Louros valley
by_whom: Greek Army of Epirus (Konstantinos Sapountzakis)
basis: Military occupation, First Balkan War
event: The Army of Epirus advanced from Arta and took Philippiada.
date_note: en.wikipedia First Balkan War says Philippiada was captured '30 September (N.S.) / 12 October (O.S.)', which is inconsistent; 12 October Julian = 25 October Gregorian is used. The Army of Epirus crossed the Arta border on 5/18 October 1912.
sources: en.wikipedia First Balkan War; en.wikipedia Battle of Bizani (Gribovo)
note: (Julian 12 October 1912). Coordinates of Gribovo are approximate.

name: Preveza
by_whom: Greek Army of Epirus
basis: Military occupation, First Balkan War
event: After the Battle of Nicopolis, Greek forces entered Preveza.
date_note: Preveza liberated 21 October 1912 Julian = 3 November Gregorian. en.wikipedia First Balkan War writes '8 October (N.S.) / 21 October (O.S.)', which is a mis-conversion; Battle of Bizani article gives 'October 21, 1912'.
sources: sansimera.gr articles/840 (21 October); en.wikipedia Battle of Bizani; en.wikipedia First Balkan War
note: (Julian 21 October 1912).

name: Chimarra
by_whom: Major Spyros Spyromilios with local insurgents and about 200 Cretan volunteers
basis: Local uprising with a Greek officer and a landing from Corfu
event: The Ottoman garrison was expelled; the area remained under Greek control until the end of the Balkan Wars despite Albanian attacks after 28 November 1912.
date_note: Revolt 18 November [O.S. 5 November] 1912. End: the Greek Army's evacuation of Northern Epirus was completed on 28 April 1914; Spyromilios' local force then joined the Autonomous Republic.
sources: en.wikipedia Himara revolt of 1912; en.wikipedia Autonomous Republic of Northern Epirus; en.wikipedia Battle of Bizani ('November 5, 1912')
note: (Julian 5 November 1912). Exact extent of the Chimarra enclave not given.

name: Metsovo
by_whom: Greek forces (detachment from Thessaly)
battle: Driskos (fighting on the Metsovo–Ioannina road, late November – December 1912; Lorentzos Mavilis killed)
basis: Military occupation, First Balkan War
event: Metsovo captured; the Ottomans held the Driskos heights east of Ioannina.
date_note: sansimera: Metsovo captured 10 November 1912 (Julian) = 23 November. Not cross-checked; local sources may give an earlier date.
sources: sansimera.gr articles/840; in.gr 2019-10-05
note: (Julian 10 November 1912). The Driskos dates are from general knowledge, not from a page read; approx.

name: Southern Epirus up to the Bizani front (Dec 1912 – Mar 1913)
line: Front line from west to east: Ionian coast area of Parga/Margariti (extent in Thesprotia not established) – south of Ioannina at Bizani and Manoliasa – Driskos heights – Metsovo. Ioannina, Bizani and the Driskos ridge stayed Ottoman until 6 March 1913.
by_whom: Greek Army of Epirus
basis: Front line, First Balkan War
event: Snapshot of the Epirus front before the fall of Ioannina.
date_note: Start: first Greek attack on the Bizani fortress area 14 December 1912 (Gregorian; Julian 1-3 December); second attack 20 January 1913 (Julian 7-10 January); the front held until the final assault of 5 March 1913.
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Bizani; stratistoria.wordpress.com 'Απελευθέρωση Ιωαννίνων' (attacks 1-3 December 1912 and 7-10 January 1913)
note: Front line snapshot; Thesprotia extent not established.

name: Korytsa district
by_whom: Greek Army (from western Macedonia)
basis: Military occupation, First Balkan War
event: Greek troops entered Korytsa, cutting Ioannina's last supply route.
date_note: 7 December 1912 Julian = 20 December Gregorian (Battle of Bizani article: 'December 20, 1912'; sansimera '7 Δεκεμβρίου'). en.wikipedia First Balkan War says 20 November 1912, which is an error. End: the Greek Army left Korytsa during the evacuation of March 1914 (day not found); by 22-27 March 1914 Epirote irregulars were fighting the Albanian gendarmerie for the town.
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Bizani; sansimera.gr articles/840; en.wikipedia Autonomous Republic of Northern Epirus (fighting at Korytsa, 22-27 March 1914)
note: (Julian 7 December 1912). Exact extent of the Greek-held Korytsa district (Pogradets probably not included) not established.

name: Ioannina
by_whom: Greek Army of Epirus (Crown Prince Constantine)
basis: Capitulation of the Ottoman garrison
event: Esad Pasha surrendered Ioannina and the forts; Greek troops entered on 7 March 1913.
date_note: Assault began 5 March 1913 [O.S. 20 February]; Esad Pasha agreed to unconditional surrender at 23:00 on 6 March [O.S. 21 February] (stratistoria: protocol signed at 04:30 of 21 February Julian at Emin Aga Han); Greek troops paraded into the city on 7 March 1913.
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Bizani; en.wikipedia First Balkan War; stratistoria.wordpress.com 'Απελευθέρωση Ιωαννίνων – Παράδοση Οχυρού Μπιζάνι (21 Φεβ 1913)'; sansimera.gr articles/840
note: (Julian 20-22 February 1913). Konitsa: no separate date found. Emin Aga Han coordinates approx.

name: Thesprotia (Chameria)
by_whom: Greek Army of Epirus
basis: Military occupation, First Balkan War
event: Thesprotia came under Greek control by the end of the Epirus campaign.
date_note: Taken in stages between November 1912 and March 1913; no dates found in the sources read. The month of the fall of Ioannina is used as the latest likely date.
sources: en.wikipedia Autonomous Republic of Northern Epirus (Greek forces held most of Epirus by war's end); en.wikipedia Treaty of London (1913) (Chameria assigned to Greece)
note: Dates not found; approximate.

name: Argyrokastro and Delvino
by_whom: Greek Army
basis: Military occupation, First Balkan War
event: After Ioannina, Greek troops advanced north and entered Argyrokastro and Delvino.
date_note: Entered on 16 March 1913 [O.S. 3 March]. End: Greek evacuation of Northern Epirus began in March 1914 and ended on 28 April 1914 (per-town dates not found).
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Bizani; en.wikipedia Autonomous Republic of Northern Epirus (evacuation ended 28 April 1914)
note: (Julian 3 March 1913). The Protocol of Florence (17 December 1913) assigned this area to Albania.

name: Tepeleni
by_whom: Greek Army
basis: Military occupation, First Balkan War
event: Tepeleni taken.
date_note: Taken 'the next day' after Argyrokastro and Delvino, i.e. 17 March 1913 (Julian 4 March). End as for the rest of Northern Epirus.
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Bizani
note: (Julian 4 March 1913).

name: Premeti and Kolonia (Leskoviki, Erseka)
by_whom: Greek Army
basis: Military occupation, First Balkan War
event: Premeti and Kolonia came under Greek control.
date_note: No date found for Premeti or Leskoviki; Greek forces held the whole line Ceraunian mountains – Lake Prespa by the end of the war, so March 1913 is the latest likely month (Kolonia may have been taken from Korytsa in December 1912).
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Bizani (furthest extent); en.wikipedia Autonomous Republic of Northern Epirus (Kolonia, Colonel Kontoulis)
note: Dates not found.

name: Agioi Saranta
by_whom: Greek Army/navy
basis: Military occupation, First Balkan War
event: Agioi Saranta came under Greek control.
date_note: No date found; presumably with Delvino (16 March 1913).
sources: en.wikipedia Autonomous Republic of Northern Epirus (Greek Navy blockaded Agioi Saranta 9 March 1914, i.e. after the Greek withdrawal from the port)
note: Date not found.

name: Northern Epirus, Greek-held extent (Mar 1913 – Apr 1914)
line: Northern limit: from the Ceraunian (Akrokeraunia) mountains above Chimarra on the Ionian coast, east via Tepeleni and the Aoos gorge, north of Premeti and Frasheri, to Moschopolis and north of Korytsa, ending at Lake Prespa, where Serbian-held territory began. Southern limit: the Protocol of Florence line (= present Greece–Albania border).
by_whom: Greek Army
basis: Military occupation; assigned to Albania by the Protocol of Florence (17 December 1913)
event: Greek-held Northern Epirus at the end of the First Balkan War, until the evacuation of spring 1914.
date_note: Envelope of the town events above. Evacuation: the Great Powers' ambassadors asked Greece on 21 February 1914 to evacuate; the slow withdrawal began in March 1914 and ended on 28 April 1914.
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Bizani ('a line from the Ceraunian mountains ... to Lake Prespa'); en.wikipedia Autonomous Republic of Northern Epirus (21 February 1914 request, evacuation March – 28 April 1914)
note: Line between the named points is approximate; the exact course is not given in the sources.

name: Lemnos
by_whom: Greek Navy (Pavlos Kountouriotis)
basis: Greek naval occupation, First Balkan War
event: Greek forces landed on Lemnos; Moudros became the fleet's anchorage.
date_note: Fleet sailed 18 October [O.S. 5 October]; arrived off Myrina 19 October; landing at Moudros Bay 21 October [O.S. 8 October]; flag raised over the capital 22 October [O.S. 9 October]. en.wikipedia First Balkan War says fighting went on until 27 October.
sources: en.wikipedia Capture of Lemnos; en.wikipedia First Balkan War; Hellenic Navy averof.hellenicnavy.gr/?p=8034 (6-8 October Julian); sansimera.gr articles/840 (8 October)
note: (Julian 8 October 1912).

name: Thasos
by_whom: Greek Navy
basis: Greek naval occupation, First Balkan War
event: Thasos taken.
date_note: Hellenic Navy: 18 October 1912 (Julian) = 31 October. sansimera/in.gr give 8 October (Julian) = 21 October, probably copying the Lemnos date. The navy date is used.
sources: Hellenic Navy averof.hellenicnavy.gr/?p=8034; sansimera.gr articles/840; en.wikipedia First Balkan War (among islands seized by mid-November 1912)
note: (Julian 18 October 1912). Sources disagree (8 vs 18 October Julian).

name: Agios Efstratios
by_whom: Greek Navy
basis: Greek naval occupation, First Balkan War
event: Agios Efstratios taken.
date_note: 18 October 1912 Julian = 31 October Gregorian (Hellenic Navy and sansimera agree).
sources: Hellenic Navy averof.hellenicnavy.gr/?p=8034; sansimera.gr articles/840
note: (Julian 18 October 1912).

name: Imbros
by_whom: Greek Navy
basis: Greek naval occupation, First Balkan War; assigned back to the Ottoman Empire by the Great Powers on 13 February 1914, never carried out
event: Imbros taken by the Greek Navy; it stayed under Greek naval administration despite the 1914 decision.
date_note: Start 18 October 1912 Julian (Hellenic Navy, sansimera) = 31 October. The end date is from a later research batch: en.wikipedia Imbros: 'Between November 1912 and September 1923, Imbros, together with Tenedos, were under the administration of the Greek navy.' The Greek administration did NOT leave after the Great Powers' decision of February 1914, because the Ottomans did not accept that decision and the question stayed open into the First World War.
sources: Hellenic Navy averof.hellenicnavy.gr/?p=8034; en.wikipedia Imbros; en.wikipedia Territorial evolution of Greece ('Imbros, Tenedos, and Kastellorizo are returned to the Ottoman Empire', 13 February 1914); en.wikipedia Treaty of Athens
note: (Julian 18 October 1912). From 1915 the island was also an Allied (British, French, ANZAC) base for the Gallipoli campaign, with a British airstrip; whether the Greek government consented is not stated (Greece was neutral). Later batches: Sèvres awarded it to Greece (1920); Lausanne made it Turkish.
editorial: Handed over with Tenedos in September 1923 (Lausanne, Protocol XV).

name: Samothrace
by_whom: Greek Navy
basis: Greek naval occupation, First Balkan War
event: Samothrace taken.
date_note: 19 October 1912 Julian = 1 November Gregorian (Hellenic Navy and sansimera agree).
sources: Hellenic Navy averof.hellenicnavy.gr/?p=8034; sansimera.gr articles/840
note: (Julian 19 October 1912).

name: Psara and Antipsara
by_whom: Greek Navy
basis: Greek naval occupation, First Balkan War
event: Psara taken.
date_note: Hellenic Navy: 21 October 1912 Julian (= 3 November); sansimera: 22 October Julian (= 4 November).
sources: Hellenic Navy averof.hellenicnavy.gr/?p=8034; sansimera.gr articles/840
note: (Julian 21/22 October 1912). One-day disagreement.

name: Tenedos
by_whom: Greek Navy
basis: Greek naval occupation, First Balkan War; assigned back to the Ottoman Empire by the Great Powers on 13 February 1914, never carried out
event: Tenedos taken by the Greek Navy; it stayed under Greek administration despite the 1914 decision.
date_note: Start disputed: Hellenic Navy 24 October 1912 (Julian) = 6 November; sansimera 18 October (Julian) = 31 October; en.wikipedia Tenedos 'on 20 October 1912, Tenedos was the first island of the north Aegean that came under the control of the Greek Navy' (inconsistent with Lemnos, 21 October). The end date (from a later research batch) is disputed: en.wikipedia Tenedos 'Greek administration of the island lasted until 12 November 1922'; en.wikipedia Imbros gives November 1912 – September 1923 for both islands.
sources: Hellenic Navy averof.hellenicnavy.gr/?p=8034; sansimera.gr articles/840; en.wikipedia Tenedos; en.wikipedia Imbros; en.wikipedia Territorial evolution of Greece
note: (Julian 24 October 1912, navy). British supply base and airstrip in the First World War.
editorial: Greek administration lasted until the island was handed over under the Lausanne settlement (Protocol XV), September 1923; GB3's 12 Nov 1922 is the Mudanya period, not the handover.

name: Lesbos
by_whom: Greek Navy and army
basis: Greek naval and military occupation, First Balkan War
event: Mytilene taken on 21 November 1912; the interior fully controlled after the Ottoman surrender of 21/22 December.
date_note: Landing at Mytilene 07:00, 21 November [O.S. 8 November] 1912, town occupied the same day; Ottoman garrison surrendered 21/22 December 1912 (infobox 21 December; en.wikipedia First Balkan War 22 December). sansimera '7 December' (Julian = 20 December) refers to the end of resistance.
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Lesbos (1912); en.wikipedia First Balkan War; Hellenic Navy averof.hellenicnavy.gr/?p=8034; sansimera.gr articles/840
note: (Julian 8 November – 8/9 December 1912).

name: Chios and Oinousses
by_whom: Greek Navy and army
basis: Greek naval and military occupation, First Balkan War
event: Chios town taken on 25 November 1912; the whole island after the surrender at Pityous on 3 January 1913.
date_note: Landing at Kontari 24 November [O.S. 11 November] 1912; Chios town entered 08:00, 25 November [O.S. 12 November]; last Ottoman forces surrendered 3 January 1913 [O.S. 21 December 1912]. en.wikipedia First Balkan War says landing 27 November (disagrees).
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Chios (1912); en.wikipedia First Balkan War; Hellenic Navy averof.hellenicnavy.gr/?p=8034 (landing 10 November, garrison captured 20 December, Julian); sansimera.gr articles/840 (21 December)
note: (Julian 11 November – 21 December 1912). Kontari coordinates approx.

name: Northern and eastern Aegean islands (1914 award)
basis: Decision of the Great Powers of 13 February 1914, under Art. 5 of the Treaty of London (1913) and the Treaty of Athens (1913), which left the islands' fate to the Powers. All Greek-occupied islands to Greece except Imbros, Tenedos and Kastellorizo; linked to the Greek evacuation of Northern Epirus
event: The Great Powers assigned the occupied islands to Greece; the Ottomans did not accept this, which led to a naval race until the First World War.
in_force: 1914-02-13 (Great-Power decision; the Ottoman Empire refused it)
date_note: Decision of the six Great Powers communicated 13 February 1914 (Julian 31 January). Thasos and Samothrace are assumed to be included (they were Greek-occupied and are not among the exceptions).
sources: en.wikipedia Territorial evolution of Greece ('Protocol of Florence (13 February 1914): The Great Powers assign the islands of the eastern Aegean (apart from the Italian-occupied Dodecanese) to Greece. Imbros, Tenedos, and Kastellorizo are returned to the Ottoman Empire'); en.wikipedia Treaty of Athens (in February 1914 the Powers awarded all except Imbros and Tenedos; the Ottomans refused); en.wikipedia Capture of Lemnos
note: De jure in the brief's sense (recognized by the Great Powers), but Ottoman recognition came only at Lausanne (1923). Lemnos (Moudros) was used as an Allied base from 1915 with the consent of the Venizelos government (not an occupation).

name: Kastellorizo
by_whom: Greek provisional governor sent from Samos
basis: Local revolt and Greek provisional governor; assigned back to the Ottoman Empire by the Great Powers (February 1914)
event: Kastellorizo under a Greek-appointed provisional governor.
date_note: On 14 March 1913 the inhabitants imprisoned the Ottoman governor and proclaimed a provisional government; in August 1913 the Greek government sent from Samos a provisional governor with gendarmes (day not given). It is not clear whether Greek administration continued after the Great Powers decided in early 1914 to return the island to the Ottomans; the French takeover of 28 December 1915 is used as the end.
sources: en.wikipedia Kastellorizo; en.wikipedia Territorial evolution of Greece
note: Extent of Greek control 1914-15 uncertain.

name: Greek-held Macedonia on the eve of the Second Balkan War (line of contact, June 1913)
line: Bulgarian 2nd Army line on 16/29 June 1913 ran from Lake Dojran south-east through Kilkis, Lachanas and Serres to the Pangaion hills and the Aegean; the Greek line faced it from the Gulf of Orfanos (Strymonian Gulf) to the Gevgeli area. Greek–Bulgarian clashes at Nigrita (19 February 1913 Julian) and Pangaion (10-17 May 1913 Julian) preceded the war.
by_whom: Greek Army
basis: Front line
event: Line of contact between the Greek and Bulgarian armies when the Second Balkan War began.
date_note: Snapshot at the Bulgarian surprise attack of the night 16/17 June 1913 Julian (29/30 June Gregorian); the Greek general counter-attack began 19 June Julian (2 July Gregorian).
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Kilkis–Lachanas (Bulgarian line of 16 June; Greek line from the Gulf of Orphanos to the Gevgeli area); stratistoria.wordpress.com 'Β΄ Βαλκανικός πόλεμος' (Nigrita 19 February, Pangaion 10-17 May 1913)
note: Front line snapshot; course between the named points approximate. Dates in en.wikipedia Battle of Kilkis–Lachanas are Julian (O.S.).

name: Kilkis and Lachanas
by_whom: Greek Army (King Constantine)
basis: Military occupation, Second Balkan War
event: Greek victory over the Bulgarian 2nd Army.
date_note: Battle 19-21 June 1913 Julian = 2-4 July Gregorian; Kilkis fell on the morning of 21 June (Julian), Lachanas broken through by 16:00 the same day.
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Kilkis–Lachanas; en.wikipedia Second Balkan War; stratistoria.wordpress.com 'Μάχη του Κιλκίς (20 – 21 Ιουν 1913)'
note: (Julian 19-21 June 1913).

name: Nigrita (Visaltia)
by_whom: Greek 7th Division
basis: Military occupation, Second Balkan War
event: The Greek 7th Division took Nigrita, which the Bulgarians destroyed before leaving.
date_note: 20 June 1913 Julian = 3 July Gregorian.
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Kilkis–Lachanas; sansimera.gr articles/639 (Serres; Nigrita 20 June 1913)
note: (Julian 20 June 1913).

name: Gevgeli (now North Macedonia)
by_whom: Greek Army
basis: Military occupation, Second Balkan War (the Bulgarians had evicted the Serbs)
event: Greek forces retook Gevgeli from the Bulgarians; it was Serbian under the Greek–Serbian line.
date_note: Captured 20 June 1913 Julian (= 3 July); the town was left to Serbia under the Greek–Serbian agreement (end day not found).
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Kilkis–Lachanas ('Gevgelija captured' 20 June)
note: (Julian 20 June 1913). End date not found.

name: Doiran (south shore and Dojran town)
by_whom: Greek Army
basis: Military occupation, Second Balkan War
event: Greek forces took Doiran but could not cut off the Bulgarian retreat through the Strymon pass.
date_note: Battle of Doiran 23 June 1913 Julian = 6 July Gregorian; en.wikipedia Second Balkan War text says the Greeks captured Dojran on 5 July (calendar not stated). The town of Dojran passed to Serbia (day not found); the Greek part became de jure with Bucharest.
sources: en.wikipedia Second Balkan War; en.wikipedia Battle of Kilkis–Lachanas (Dojran 5 July); stratistoria.wordpress.com 'Β΄ Βαλκανικός πόλεμος' ('μάχες της Δοϊράνης (23 Ιουνίου)')
note: (Julian 23 June 1913). Sources disagree by one day; the Dojran (North Macedonia) part ended when handed to Serbia (date unknown).

name: Sidirokastro (Demir Hisar)
by_whom: Greek Army
basis: Military occupation, Second Balkan War
event: Greek forces took Sidirokastro after the Bulgarians burned it and massacred inhabitants.
date_note: Battle of 26-27 June 1913 Julian = 9-10 July Gregorian.
sources: sansimera.gr articles/639; stratistoria.wordpress.com 'Β΄ Βαλκανικός πόλεμος' (Sidirokastro 26 June); en.wikipedia Second Balkan War (Demir Hisar burned)
note: (Julian 26-27 June 1913). Rupel coordinates approx.

name: Serres
by_whom: Greek 7th Division / cavalry
basis: Military occupation, Second Balkan War
event: Greek forces entered Serres after the retreating Bulgarians had burned it.
date_note: Bulgarians burned the town center on 28 June 1913 (Julian) = 11 July; official liberation 29 June Julian = 12 July Gregorian.
sources: sansimera.gr articles/639 'Η Απελευθέρωση των Σερρών' (29 June; burning 28 June); en.wikipedia Second Balkan War ('On 28 June ... burned down the major city of Serres'); stratistoria 1913-drama (7th Division ordered on 28 June to free Serres, Drama, Sidirokastro)
note: (Julian 29 June 1913). sansimera also prints '31 October 1913' for the cavalry entry, evidently a typo.

name: Kavala (mainland)
line: East limit: the Nestos river.
by_whom: Greek Navy, then Greek Army
basis: Military occupation, Second Balkan War
event: Greek Navy took Kavala; the army landed there and advanced into Western Thrace.
date_note: Three Greek warships landed detachments at Kavala on 26 June 1913 Julian = 9 July Gregorian; a division landed there on 6 July Julian = 19 July.
sources: sansimera.gr articles/636 'Η Απελευθέρωση της Καβάλας' ('Στις 26 Ιουνίου 1913 τρία πλοία του ελληνικού στόλου αποβίβασαν αγήματα στην Καβάλα'); stratistoria 'Β΄ Βαλκανικός πόλεμος' (26 June; landing 6 July); en.wikipedia Second Balkan War
note: (Julian 26 June 1913). Kavala had been Bulgarian-held since October/November 1912.

name: Drama
by_whom: Greek 7th Division
basis: Military occupation, Second Balkan War
event: Greek units entered Drama the day after the Bulgarian massacre at Doxato.
date_note: 1 July 1913 Julian = 14 July Gregorian.
sources: stratistoria.wordpress.com 'Απελευθέρωση της Δράμας (1 Ιουλ 1913)'; several local sources in search results ('1η Ιουλίου 1913: Η απελευθέρωση της Δράμας')
note: (Julian 1 July 1913).

name: Nevrokop area, now Bulgaria
by_whom: Greek Army
basis: Military occupation, Second Balkan War; left to Bulgaria by the Treaty of Bucharest
event: Greek forces took Nevrokop.
date_note: en.wikipedia Second Balkan War: 'On 19 July, the Greeks captured Nevrokop' (calendar not stated; taken as Gregorian, = 6 July Julian; the 7th Division was ordered towards Nevrokop on 29 June Julian). End: Greek withdrawal to the Bucharest line in August 1913 (day not found).
sources: en.wikipedia Second Balkan War; stratistoria.wordpress.com 1913-drama (order of 29 June)
note: Extent beyond the town approximate.

name: Upper Strymon valley (Petrich, Melnik, Sveti Vrach), now Bulgaria
by_whom: Greek Army
basis: Military occupation, Second Balkan War; left to Bulgaria by the Treaty of Bucharest
event: Greek advance up the Strymon into present-day Bulgaria.
date_note: Month only: after Sidirokastro (9-10 July) the Greeks made contact with the Serbs on 11 July and pushed up the Strymon; they reached the Kresna gorge about 21-24 July (Battle of Kresna Gorge 21-31 July [O.S. 8-18 July]). End: withdrawal after Bucharest (August 1913; day not found).
sources: en.wikipedia Second Balkan War (11 July, Strymon); en.wikipedia Battle of Kilkis–Lachanas (Greeks reached Kresna Gorge 24 July, calendar unclear); en.wikipedia Battle of Kresna Gorge
note: Days not found; the Greek–Serbian junction and western extent (Strumica valley, now North Macedonia) not established.

name: Kresna gorge north to Simitli and the approaches of Gorna Dzhumaya, now Bulgaria
by_whom: Greek Army
basis: Military occupation, Second Balkan War
event: Greek breakthrough of the Kresna pass to Simitli; the advance was stopped before Gorna Dzhumaya.
date_note: Krupnik captured 25 July, Simitli 26 July (Gregorian: these fall before the armistice of 31 July = 18 July Julian). In the night of 27-28 July the Bulgarians were pushed back to Gorna Dzhumaya; on 28 July the Greeks took the line Cherovo – Hill 1378 and the Bulgarians began to abandon the town in the evening, but the Greeks never entered it. End: withdrawal after Bucharest (August 1913; day not found).
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Kresna Gorge; en.wikipedia Second Balkan War ('On 28 July, the Bulgarian army ... was forced to abandon Gorna Dzhumaya')
note: en.wikipedia sources disagree on whether Gorna Dzhumaya was abandoned (Second Balkan War) or held to the end (Kresna Gorge: 'remained under Bulgarian control at the end of the war'). Treat the town as not Greek-held.

name: Dedeağaç (Alexandroupoli) and the lower Evros to Kornofolia
by_whom: Greek Navy (Kountouriotis) landing parties
basis: Military occupation, Second Balkan War; left to Bulgaria by the Treaty of Bucharest
event: The landing at Dedeağaç cut Bulgaria off from the Aegean.
date_note: en.wikipedia: amphibious landing took Dedeağaç on 25 July 1913; Greek local sources put the naval force at Kornofolia by 12 or 14 July Julian (= 25 or 27 July). End: Greek withdrawal from Western Thrace, due on 5 August Julian (= 18 August) under the Bucharest settlement, with a Bulgarian request to prolong the Greek presence to 18 August Julian (= 31 August); day of departure not found.
sources: en.wikipedia Second Balkan War; sitalkisking.blogspot.com 2018/02 and 2020/09 (Kornofolia 12/14 July; handover due 5 August, extension to 18 August)
note: (Julian c. 11-12 July 1913). Soufli itself passed to Bulgaria under the Bulgarian–Ottoman settlement.
editorial: m:Alexandroupolis;[m:Soufliou;&box:25,40.5,27,41.14]

name: Xanthi (lowland) and Porto Lagos
line: West limit: the Nestos river.
by_whom: Greek 13th Division (crossed the Nestos)
basis: Military occupation, Second Balkan War
event: The Greek Army crossed the Nestos and took Xanthi and Porto Lagos without a fight.
date_note: en.wikipedia: entered Xanthi 26 July 1913 (Gregorian; = 13 July Julian, as in sansimera); stratistoria gives 12 July Julian (= 25 July). End: Greek withdrawal from Western Thrace in August 1913 (see 1913-dedeagatch); Ottoman-backed irregulars reached Xanthi and Komotini on 31 August 1913 (reader comment on a Greek history blog, unverified).
sources: en.wikipedia Second Balkan War; en.wikipedia Battle of Kresna Gorge; sansimera.gr articles/1350 ('ο ελληνικός στρατός κατέλαβε την πόλη στις 13 Ιουλίου 1913'); stratistoria 'Β΄ Βαλκανικός πόλεμος' (12 July); sitalkisking.blogspot.com 2018/02
note: (Julian 12/13 July 1913).
editorial: See 1913-dedeagatch.

name: Komotini and the Rhodope lowland
by_whom: Greek Army
basis: Military occupation, Second Balkan War
event: Greek forces entered Komotini without Bulgarian opposition.
date_note: 27 July 1913 Gregorian (en.wikipedia: 'the next day Komotini' after Xanthi) = 14 July Julian (Greek sources). End: August 1913 (see 1913-dedeagatch).
sources: en.wikipedia Second Balkan War; en.wikipedia Battle of Kresna Gorge; stratistoria and sitalkisking.blogspot.com (14 July Julian)
note: (Julian 14 July 1913). After the Greek withdrawal the area passed to the Muslim 'Provisional Government of Western Thrace' (Ottoman-backed, Aug/Sept – Oct 1913) and then to Bulgaria (October 1913): not Greek, not recorded as an event.
editorial: See 1913-dedeagatch.

name: Greek front at the armistice of 31 July 1913
line: From west to east: Greek–Serbian junction in the Pehčevo/Berovo sector (now North Macedonia) – Cherovo – Hill 1378 – south of Gorna Dzhumaya (Bulgarian-held) – Predela pass and the Mehomia sector (Greek attacks; Mehomia not taken) – Nevrokop (Greek) – Nestos – then in Western Thrace a line of posts north of Xanthi and Komotini to Kornofolia on the Evros, with Dedeağaç held from the sea.
by_whom: Greek Army
basis: Front line at the armistice
event: On 29 July the Bulgarians cut the Greek line of retreat through Berovo and Strumica; by 30 July their attacks subsided and the Greeks held their positions at Pehčevo and Mehomia; the armistice froze the front.
date_note: Five-day armistice agreed at Bucharest on 30 July, in force 31 July 1913 (Julian 18 July); Treaty of Bucharest 10 August (Julian 28 July). en.wikipedia Battle of Kresna Gorge wrongly calls the 31 July event the signing of the treaty.
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Kresna Gorge; en.wikipedia Second Balkan War; stratistoria 'Β΄ Βαλκανικός πόλεμος' (armistice 18 July Julian)
note: Front line snapshot. The positions of Cherovo and Hill 1378 could not be located; Greek presence in the Strumica–Berovo–Pehčevo area (now North Macedonia) is implied but its extent is not established.
editorial: Status changed from 'de_facto' to 'note'.

name: Western and Central Macedonia (1913 Greek–Serbian line)
line: Northern line = present Greece–North Macedonia border from the tripoint with Albania in Lake Prespa east over Kaimaktsalan (Voras), Tzena, across the Vardar between Evzonoi and Bogorodica (Gevgeli to Serbia), through Lake Doiran (Dojran town to Serbia), to the western Beles, where the 1913 Serbian–Bulgarian line (Vardar–Strymon watershed) met the Greek border. The rest of the present Greece–North Macedonia border along Beles east to Tumba was Greek–Bulgarian in 1913-1919 (Strumica valley Bulgarian). The Greek–Serbian line was agreed in the Greek–Serbian treaty of alliance (1 June 1913, Julian 19 May) and confirmed at Bucharest.
basis: Treaty of London (30 May 1913); Greek–Serbian treaty (1 June 1913); Treaty of Bucharest (10 August 1913); Treaty of Athens (14 November 1913)
event: The Macedonian conquests became Greek under the Balkan peace settlement; the Ottoman Empire recognized them in the Treaty of Athens.
date_note: Start = exchange of ratifications of the Treaty of Bucharest (30 August 1913). Alternatives: Treaty of London (30 May 1913, Ottoman cession west of the Enos–Midia line to the allies jointly; ratification not found) or Treaty of Athens (14 November 1913, Ottoman recognition of the cession to Greece).
sources: en.wikipedia Treaty of Bucharest (1913) (signed 'July 28/August 10, 1913', ratifications exchanged 30 August 1913); en.wikipedia Territorial evolution of Greece (Greek–Serbian treaty 1 June 1913, border now Greece–North Macedonia); en.wikipedia Treaty of Athens; en.wikipedia Treaty of London (1913)
note: Later minor rectifications of the Greek–Yugoslav border not checked. The Lake Prespa tripoint and the Beles junction coordinates are approximate.

name: Eastern Macedonia to the Nestos (Bucharest line)
line: Treaty of Bucharest: the Greek–Bulgarian frontier was 'drawn from the crest of Belasica to the mouth of the Mesta (Nestos), on the Aegean Sea'. Course: Beles crest from the 1913 Serbo-Bulgarian junction (west of the present tripoint) east to Tumba; then the present Greece–Bulgaria border across the Strymon at the Rupel/Kulata gorge, along Orvilos (Ali Botush) and the Rhodope crest north of Kato Nevrokopi to the Nestos; then down the Nestos to its mouth. West of the Nestos Greek, east of it (Xanthi, Rhodope, Evros) Bulgarian.
basis: Treaty of Bucharest (10 August 1913; Julian 28 July), Greek–Bulgarian frontier; France and Germany secured Kavala for Greece
event: Bulgaria recognized Greek sovereignty over Serres, Drama and Kavala.
date_note: Start = exchange of ratifications of the Treaty of Bucharest (30 August 1913).
sources: en.wikipedia Treaty of Bucharest (1913); fhw.gr chronos 13 'Treaty of Bucharest' ('The Greco-Bulgarian border was fixed on the Serbian-Bulgarian borders in Beles mountain ... at the mouth of River Nestos'); en.wikipedia Second Balkan War
note: The treaty text (Art. V) could not be read (oocities.org copy failed). Whether the 1913 line followed the Nestos over its whole Greek course (so that any part of Drama regional unit east of the river, in Paranesti municipality, was Bulgarian) is not verified. The Beles section between the 1913 Serbo-Bulgarian junction and Tumba is now the Greece–North Macedonia border.

name: Southern Epirus (Protocol of Florence line)
line: Northern line = the Protocol of Florence (17 December 1913) Greek–Albanian frontier, essentially the present Greece–Albania border: from the Ionian coast at Cape Stylos opposite Corfu (Konispoli to Albania, Filiates and Sagiada to Greece), over the Mourgana range, leaving the Drinos valley (Dropoli, Argyrokastro) to Albania and Pogoni to Greece (Kakavia), over Nemercka, crossing the Aoos below Leskoviki (Leskoviki and Kolonia to Albania, Konitsa to Greece), along the Grammos crest, leaving Bilishti/Kapeshtitsa (Devoll) to Albania and the Kastoria and Florina villages to Greece, to Lake Prespa.
basis: Treaty of London (30 May 1913); Treaty of Athens (14 November 1913); Protocol of Florence (17 December 1913, Great Powers' commission)
event: Ioannina, Preveza and Thesprotia became Greek; the Powers drew the Greek–Albanian line at Florence and assigned Northern Epirus to Albania.
date_note: Start = Treaty of Athens (14 November 1913, Julian 1 November; ratification date not found), the Ottoman cession of Epirus to Greece. The northern line was fixed by the Great Powers only on 17 December 1913 and accepted by Greece in February 1914 (evacuation of the north completed 28 April 1914).
sources: en.wikipedia Treaty of Athens; en.wikipedia Territorial evolution of Greece ('Treaty of Florence (17 December 1913): The Great Powers assign Northern Epirus to Albania, and order Greek troops to leave'); en.wikipedia Autonomous Republic of Northern Epirus
note: The en.wikipedia 'Protocol of Florence' page was not found, so the protocol text was not read; the line description is the present border, which the final delimitation of 1922-1925 fixed with minor local changes. Confidence 'good', not 'exact'.

name: Autonomous Republic of Northern Epirus
line: Southern limit: the Protocol of Florence line. Northern limit roughly the 1913 Greek-held limit (Chimarra – Tepeleni – Premeti), with Korytsa contested.
by_whom: Provisional Government of Northern Epirus
battle: Fighting at Cepo (c. 7 March 1914), Korytsa (22-27 March 1914); armistice 7 May 1914
basis: Declaration of autonomy by the Panepirotic Council (Georgios Christakis-Zografos); Protocol of Corfu (17 May 1914): autonomy of the provinces of Korytsa and Argyrokastro under nominal Albanian sovereignty (Prince Wied), Greek co-official, Chimarra's privileges renewed, guaranteed by the Great Powers (International Control Commission)
event: Greek-populated Northern Epirus resisted incorporation into Albania and won autonomy at Corfu; the Protocol was never fully applied after Wied left on 3 September 1914 and was annulled in 1921.
in_force: Protocol approved by the Great Powers on 1 June (Protocol of Corfu article) or 18 June 1914 in Athens (Autonomous Republic article); by the Albanian government on 23 June 1914
date_note: Declared 28 February 1914 at Argyrokastro (en.wikipedia Autonomous Republic); a Greek source (himara.gr) gives 17 February 1914 (Julian = 2 March); en.wikipedia Northern Epirus says 'March 1914'. End: Greek Army re-entry on 27 October 1914 (Julian 14 October), after which the provisional government ceased to exist.
sources: en.wikipedia Autonomous Republic of Northern Epirus; en.wikipedia Protocol of Corfu; en.wikipedia Northern Epirus; himara.gr 'The three liberations of Northern Epirus' ('κήρυξαν στίς 17 Φεβρουαρίου 1914, στό Ἀργυροκάστρο, τήν Αὐτονομία')
note: Sources disagree on the declaration date (28 Feb vs 17 Feb Julian = 2 Mar vs 'March') and on the Great Powers' approval (1 vs 18 June). Show faintly.

name: Northern Epirus: prefecture of Argyrokastro (1914-16)
by_whom: Greek Army (V Army Corps); royal government
basis: Greek re-occupation with Allied consent (agreement among the Allies of October 1914); union with Greece declared March 1916, revoked under Great-Power pressure
event: Greek administration of Northern Epirus: Northern Epirus elected 16 deputies to the Greek parliament in the December 1915 elections; in March 1916 Greece declared union and set up the prefectures of Argyrokastro and Korytsa; Italy took over in August–October 1916.
date_note: Start: V Army Corps entered on 27 October 1914 (Julian 14 October, himara.gr). End, in stages: Italian occupation began 23 August 1916 (en.wikipedia Balkan Front); Italians took Tepeleni on 30 August 1916 and landed at Agioi Saranta on 2 October 1916 (en.wikipedia Greece during WWI); Italians entered Argyrokastro in September 1916 (en.wikipedia Autonomous Republic); Greek Army left Northern Epirus on 10 October 1916 (himara.gr; probably Julian = 23 October). dcstamps gives 10 August 1916, probably wrong.
sources: en.wikipedia Autonomous Republic of Northern Epirus; en.wikipedia Protocol of Corfu; en.wikipedia Northern Epirus (occupation 'from October 1914'; annexation March 1916; Italy 1916-17); en.wikipedia Greece during World War I; en.wikipedia Balkan Front (WWI); himara.gr; dcstamps.com
note: The brief mentions '1916 elections': the sources read give the December 1915 general election. Tepeleni area ends 1916-08-30. Possible Italian move into Greek Epirus (Ioannina) in June 1917 not verified, not recorded.

name: Northern Epirus: prefecture of Korytsa (1914-16)
by_whom: Greek Army; royal government
basis: Greek re-occupation with Allied consent; union declared March 1916
event: Greek administration of the Korytsa district until the Bulgarian advance of August 1916.
date_note: Start: 'On October 27, 1914, the Greek army re-entered the area' (Autonomous Province of Korytsa article). End: on 18 August 1916 the Bulgarian army occupied Korytsa and ejected the Greek garrison.
sources: en.wikipedia Autonomous Albanian Republic of Korçë / Autonomous Province of Korçë; en.wikipedia Autonomous Republic of Northern Epirus
note: Whether Kolonia (Erseka, Leskoviki) was lost at the same time is not stated.

name: Northern Epirus: Argyrokastro prefecture under Italy
basis: Italian military occupation with the permission of the Allied command, against the will of the Greek (royal) government
event: Italian troops evicted the Greek Army from Northern Epirus (Argyrokastro prefecture).
date_note: Start 23 August 1916 (en.wikipedia Balkan Front); completed by October 1916 (Tepeleni 30 August, Agioi Saranta landing 2 October, Greek Army out by 10/23 October 1916). End outside this batch: the Italians left southern Albania in 1920 (later batch).
sources: en.wikipedia Balkan Front (World War I) ('Italy, with the permission of Allied command, occupied Northern Epirus on August 23, 1916'); en.wikipedia Greece during World War I; en.wikipedia Protocol of Corfu ('Italian troops evicted the Greek army from the area' in the second half of 1916); en.wikipedia National Schism; en.wikipedia Northern Epirus ('In 1917, Greece lost control of the rest of Northern Epirus to Italy')
note: Territory held de facto by Greece, not sovereign. Sources disagree on dates (August vs September vs October 1916; en.wikipedia Northern Epirus even says 1917).
editorial: Status changed from 'occupied' to 'note'.

name: Korytsa under Bulgarian occupation
basis: Bulgarian military occupation (Central Powers' offensive of August 1916)
event: The Bulgarians took Korytsa from its Greek garrison.
date_note: Bulgarian army occupied Korytsa and ejected the Greek garrison on 18 August 1916; French troops entered on 29 November 1916.
sources: en.wikipedia Autonomous Province of Korçë
note: Territory held de facto by Greece, not sovereign.
editorial: Status changed from 'occupied' to 'note'.

name: Korytsa under French occupation (Autonomous Albanian Republic of Korytsa)
basis: French military occupation; Greek administration not restored
event: France replaced the Bulgarians in Korytsa and set up an Albanian autonomous province under French protection.
date_note: French troops entered Korytsa on 29 November 1916; Colonel Descoins proclaimed the autonomous republic on 10 December 1916 for Korytsa, Bilishti, Kolonia, Opar and Gora; the French army left on 15 June 1920 (outside this batch).
sources: en.wikipedia Autonomous Province of Korçë; en.wikipedia Northern Epirus ('the French Army occupied the area around Korçë in 1916, and established the Republic of Korçë')
note: Not against a Greek garrison (it had already been ejected) but it prevented the return of Greek administration; occupier recorded for the map.
editorial: Status changed from 'occupied' to 'note'.

name: Entente zone in Macedonia (Salonika front, rear)
line: Grew from the fortified camp of Thessaloniki and the Axios railway (October–December 1915) to all Greek Macedonia west of the Strymon behind the Allied front by 1916.
occupier: Entente (France, Britain; later Serbia, Italy, Russia)
basis: Allied (Armée d'Orient, British Salonika Army; later Serbian, Italian, Russian) presence invited by Venizelos but formally protested by the Greek government
event: The Entente landed at Thessaloniki to support Serbia and kept the city as the base of the Macedonian front.
date_note: Allied ships arrived 30 September; Venizelos gave the green light and landing began (en.wikipedia Greece during WWI: 2 October; en.wikipedia Macedonian front: first troops landed 5 October 1915). End: the unified Venizelos government (late June 1917, after Constantine's abdication on 11/12 June) consented; Greece declared war on 30 June 1917.
sources: en.wikipedia Greece during World War I ('the Greek government replied with a protest but no further actions'); en.wikipedia Macedonian front
note: BORDERLINE CASE for the brief: consent by the prime minister, formal protest by the government; after August/October 1916 the National Defense government consented (see 1916-national-defense-macedonia). Show as Allied presence rather than enemy occupation. Greek civil administration continued.
editorial: Status changed from 'occupied' to 'note'.

name: Milos (Allied naval base)
basis: Allied seizure to pressure the neutral royal government
event: The Allies occupied Milos.
date_note: Allies occupied Milos on 21 November 1915. End: consent of the unified Greek government, late June 1917 (approx).
sources: en.wikipedia Greece during World War I ('on 21 November the Allies occupied Milos')
note: Extent (whole island or the bay) not stated; Greek civil administration presumably continued.
editorial: Status changed from 'occupied' to 'note'.

name: Lesbos (Allied base)
basis: Allied seizure without the consent of the royal government
event: The Allies seized Lesbos as a base.
date_note: Allies seized Lesbos on 28 December 1915 'for use as a base of operations'. From September–October 1916 the island adhered to the National Defense government, which consented to the Allied presence; end set at the unification of June 1917 (approx).
sources: en.wikipedia Greece during World War I
note: Greek civil administration continued; may be shown as a note rather than an occupation.
editorial: Status changed from 'occupied' to 'note'.

name: Kastellorizo (French occupation)
basis: French occupation at the request of the inhabitants; a Greek Evzone landing attempted the same day was blocked by the French
event: France occupied Kastellorizo and blocked a Greek landing the same day; Ottoman batteries shelled the island in 1917.
date_note: French occupation 28 December 1915; Italian navy took over from the French on 1 March 1921 (outside this batch).
sources: en.wikipedia Kastellorizo
note: Kastellorizo was not Greek sovereign territory (assigned to the Ottomans in February 1914); recorded as occupied because Greece held it de facto in 1913 and tried to land troops. Sèvres later assigned it to Italy.
editorial: Status changed from 'occupied' to 'note'.

name: Corfu (French occupation)
occupier: France (Entente); Serbian army and government in exile on the island
basis: French seizure, against the protests of the royal government, to shelter the evacuated Serbian army and government
event: French troops took over Corfu as a refuge for the Serbian army.
date_note: Seized by French troops on 11 January 1916 (the day after the Allied decision of 10 January). End: consent of the unified Greek government, late June 1917 (approx); Allied and Serbian presence continued to 1918-19 with consent.
sources: en.wikipedia Greece during World War I ('the Greek island of Corfu, which was seized by French troops on the next day'); en.wikipedia Movement of National Defence says 'In December 1915 the French, with the permission of Venizelos, occupied Corfu' (disagrees on date and consent)
note: Sources disagree on date (December 1915 vs 11 January 1916) and on consent (Venizelos was then out of office).
editorial: Status changed from 'occupied' to 'note'.

name: Rupel pass and Fort Rupel
basis: German–Bulgarian occupation, surrendered on the orders of the royal government without resistance
event: The royal government in Athens permitted the surrender of Fort Rupel to German–Bulgarian forces.
date_note: Surrender date disputed: 23 May 1916 (en.wikipedia Fort Rupel), 25 May (en.wikipedia National Schism), 26 May (slpress.gr), 27 May 'surrendered and the garrison withdrew' (en.wikipedia Greece during WWI). End: Bulgarian armistice signed 29 September, in force at noon 30 September 1918; actual evacuation date not found.
sources: en.wikipedia Fort Rupel; en.wikipedia Greece during World War I; en.wikipedia National Schism; slpress.gr 'Η παράδοση του Ρούπελ'
note: Against the will of the Greek state? The royal government ordered the surrender but Greece did not invite the occupation; treated as occupied. Coordinates approx.

name: Eastern Macedonia east of the Strymon (Bulgarian occupation 1916-18)
line: West limit: the Strymon (Strymonas) from the Rupel gorge to the sea, which was the front; small British bridgeheads on the east bank from autumn 1916 not mapped. East limit: the Nestos (the 1913 border). Thasos was NOT occupied (Greek troops from Kavala escaped there).
battle: Bulgarian Strymon offensive (August 1916); Vardar offensive / Dobro Pole (15 September 1918)
basis: Bulgarian (with German units) military occupation; the Greek Army had been ordered not to resist
event: The Bulgarians occupied Greek territory between the Strymon and the Nestos (the 'second Bulgarian occupation') until the armistice of 1918.
date_note: The Bulgarian offensive began on 17 August 1916; 'By 22 August, eastern Macedonia was effectively under Bulgarian occupation', though the Greek 5th Division stayed in Drama and the 16th Regiment in Serres for some weeks. End: Armistice of Salonica, signed 29 September 1918 (Julian 16 September), ceasefire noon 30 September; Bulgaria then evacuated the area in early October 1918 (days of the Greek re-entry into Serres, Drama and Kavala not found).
sources: en.wikipedia Macedonian front ('they easily conquered all Greek territory east of the river Struma'; armistice 29 September; ceasefire noon 30 September 1918); en.wikipedia Greece during World War I; ergasia-press.gr ('μεταξύ των ποταμών Στρυμώνα και Νέστου (Νομοί Σερρών, Δράμας, Καβάλας)', August 1916 – September 1918, 16/29 September 1918); kavalapost.gr (August 1916 – September 1918)
note: No Greek occupation of Bulgarian or Serbian territory after the September 1918 breakthrough was found in the sources read; one Greek division went through Bulgaria by rail with the Allied Army of the Danube (October–November 1918), which was transit, not occupation.

name: Kavala town and forts
basis: Bulgarian–German occupation
event: Kavala fell after the surrender of the Greek IV Army Corps, interned at Görlitz until the end of the war; part of the garrison escaped to Thasos.
date_note: Month only. Allies blockaded Kavala harbor from 23 August 1916; the Greek 6th Division reached Kavala on 4 September; the Bulgarians then encircled the town and took the ring of forts; the Greek IV Army Corps (Hatzopoulos) surrendered and was taken by train to Görlitz in Germany (mid-September 1916; exact day not found). End: early October 1918 (day not found).
sources: en.wikipedia Greece during World War I; en.wikipedia Ioannis Hatzopoulos
note: Days not found.

name: Florina area (Bulgarian offensive of August 1916)
line: Bulgarian advance stopped near Lake Ostrovo (Vegoritida) and on the Voras/Kaimaktsalan massif.
battle: Florina (Chegan) offensive; Kaimaktsalan; Allied counter-offensive of September 1916
basis: Bulgarian military occupation
event: Short Bulgarian occupation of the Florina area.
date_note: Bulgarian offensive began 17 August 1916 (en.wikipedia Macedonian front); Florina fell in its first days (day not verified). The Allies counter-attacked from 12 September 1916 and retook Florina later that month (day not verified).
sources: en.wikipedia Macedonian front (offensive of 17 August; counter-attack from 12 September 1916); slpress.gr (Florina among occupied areas)
note: Dates and extent approximate; the front then ran just north of the Greek–Serbian border towards Monastir (taken by the Allies on 19 November 1916).
