name: Skra salient (Kilkis regional unit)
basis: Bulgarian (Central Powers) front positions inside Greek territory
event: Greek (and French) forces took the heavily fortified Skra salient on 30 May 1918.
date_note: Start not established (Bulgarian front positions on Greek soil from 1916). End: Battle of Skra-di-Legen, 30 May 1918.
sources: en.wikipedia Macedonian front ('On 30 May 1918, the Allies launched an offensive on the heavily fortified Skra salient'); en.wikipedia Greece during World War I
note: Small area; start date and extent approximate. Coordinates approx.
editorial: The research gives only the year of the start (1916); drawn from the Bulgarian offensive of 17 Aug 1916 (approximate).

name: Macedonia under the National Defense government (Thessaloniki)
line: South limit: an Allied-imposed neutral zone between the Venizelist north and royalist Thessaly (from about December 1916); its course was not found in the sources read.
by_whom: Provisional Government of National Defense
basis: Greek sovereignty unchanged; a rival Greek government (Provisional Government of National Defense: Venizelos, Danglis, Kountouriotis), recognized by France and Britain at the end of 1916
event: Two Greek governments: the Venizelist government in Thessaloniki controlled Greek Macedonia under Allied protection, the royal government the south.
date_note: Coup in Thessaloniki 30 August 1916 (Julian 17 August); Venizelos arrived 9 October 1916 (en.wikipedia Greece during WWI) or 24 September/7 October (Movement of National Defense article); provisional government formed 28 September/11 October 1916. End: Constantine abdicated 11 June 1917 (National Schism; 29 May Julian) and Venizelos took over in Athens in late June 1917 (day not in the sources read).
sources: en.wikipedia Movement of National Defence; en.wikipedia National Schism ('the National Defence Army attacked the Royalist Army at Katerini aiming to capture Thessaly', November 1916); en.wikipedia Greece during World War I
note: two Greek governments. Not a change of sovereignty; for the map, a hatch or tint for 'National Defence' areas. Eastern Macedonia east of the Strymon was Bulgarian-occupied in the same period.
editorial: Status changed from 'de_jure' to 'note'.

name: Aegean islands under the National Defense government
by_whom: Provisional Government of National Defense
basis: Greek sovereignty unchanged; adherence to the Provisional Government of National Defense
event: Two Greek governments: Crete and the eastern Aegean islands joined the Thessaloniki government.
date_note: Month only: uprisings at Chania, Heraklion and Samos within a few days of Venizelos leaving Athens (late September 1916); Crete, Samos, Mytilene and Chios 'promptly declared their support'; 'soon the revolutionary government had control of all the islands in the Aegean Sea except for the Cyclades'.
sources: en.wikipedia Greece during World War I; en.wikipedia National Schism; en.wikipedia Movement of National Defence
note: two Greek governments. Which smaller islands joined and when is not established.
editorial: Status changed from 'de_jure' to 'note'.

name: Thessaly and the Isthmus of Corinth (June 1917)
basis: Allied (French) military occupation against the royal government, to force Constantine's abdication (and secure the harvest)
event: French troops occupied Thessaly and the Isthmus; King Constantine abdicated and Venizelos took over the whole country.
date_note: Month only: 'In June 1917 the French captured Thessaly'; 'the Venizelists and the Allies occupied Thessaly and Isthmus of Corinth, dividing the country'; this preceded the abdication of 11/12 June 1917. End: consent of the unified Venizelos government in late June 1917.
sources: en.wikipedia National Schism ('In June 1917, the French captured Thessaly'); en.wikipedia Macedonian front; en.wikipedia Balkan Front (WWI); en.wikipedia Movement of National Defence says the Venizelist state took Thessaly 'early in 1917' (disagrees)
note: Very short. The Allied landing at Piraeus/Athens of 1 December 1916 (Noemvriana), repulsed the same day, and the Allied blockade (from 6 June 1916 partial; 106 days from December 1916) are not territorial changes and are not recorded.
editorial: Status changed from 'occupied' to 'note'.

name: Odessa (Allied-held city)
joint_with: France (Army of the Danube / Armee d'Orient), Russian Volunteer Army (c. 4,000 at Odessa), Polish (c. 3,000) and Romanian (c. 2,500) contingents; German 7th Division awaiting repatriation
by_whom: Greek I Army Corps (Lt-Gen. Konstantinos Nider): 2nd and XIII Divisions, under French command (Gen. d'Anselme, Odessa; C-in-C Franchet d'Esperey)
basis: Allied (French-led) intervention in southern Russia after the Armistice of 1918; Greek participation agreed with France
event: Greek troops landed at Odessa from 20 January 1919 and formed almost half of the Allied garrison (the French about a third); the Allies evacuated the city 3-7 April 1919, Greek XIII Division units covering the retreat west to the Dniester.
date_note: Start = arrival of the first Greek ground units (3,600 men of the 34th Regiment, XIII Division) at Odessa on 20 January 1919 (Stefanidis); newgreektv gives 7 January, the Julian date. French troops had landed in late December 1918. End: Paris ordered the withdrawal on 1 April; the Allied evacuation ran 3-7 April 1919 (en.wikipedia); the Greek XIII Division regiments reached Odessa from the front on 6 April and crossed the Dniester into Bessarabia about 11 April (Stefanidis). (Julian 7 January - 24 March 1919.)
sources: Stefanidis, 'Greece and the Allied intervention in southern Russia' (Balkan Studies, imxa.gr/files/bsfiles/55/4_Ioannis Stefanidis.pdf; Gregorian dates, citing the Hellenic Army General Staff history); en.wikipedia Southern Russia intervention; newgreektv.com 'When Greeks fought in the Ukraine' (dates evidently Julian); en.wikipedia I Army Corps (Greece)
note: After Odessa the Greek units held positions on the west bank of the Dniester in Bessarabia (then held by Romania, with its consent) until relieved by Romanian units; the evacuation of the expeditionary force was completed by 17 July 1919 (Stefanidis, footnote citing the General Staff history; fhw.gr says 'summer of 1919'); much of it went on to Smyrna. That stay is not Greek control and is not recorded as an event. Total Greek strength in Ukraine c. 23,351 men (Stefanidis). (Julian 7 January - 24 March 1919.)
editorial: Kept as information about the Greek forces' operations, not drawn on the map: Greek troops served under French command in the Allied intervention of 1919, and Greece held no land of its own there. Status changed from 'de_facto' to 'note'.

name: Allied perimeter north-east of Odessa (Berezovka - Serbka front)
line: Allied front of March 1919 covering Odessa from the north-east: forward at Berezovka (c. 60 km NE of Odessa, lost 16 or 18 March), then the Serbka line (village of Serbka, between Berezovka and Odessa; coordinates not established), abandoned on 31 March. The wider Allied perimeter of January-February 1919 included Tiraspol (now Moldova) and a strip reaching the Dnieper (Kherson, Nikolaev).
joint_with: France (incl. French artillery and tanks at Berezovka), Russian Volunteer Army
by_whom: Greek I Army Corps (Lt-Gen. Konstantinos Nider): 2nd and XIII Divisions, under French command (Gen. d'Anselme, Odessa; C-in-C Franchet d'Esperey)
basis: Allied intervention in southern Russia
event: Greek and French troops held the front north-east of Odessa in March 1919; Berezovka was lost in mid-March and the Serbka line abandoned on 31 March, after which the Allies fell back on Odessa.
date_note: Month only for the start: Greek units were on the Berezovka front before it broke on the evening of 18 March (Stefanidis; en.wikipedia dates the fall of Berezovka to 16 March). The 3rd Regiment arrived at Odessa on 12 March and went to the front; Serbka was lost on 26 March, retaken on 27 March, the 5/42 Evzone Regiment (Plastiras) relieved the 3rd Regiment on 28 March, and the Serbka line was abandoned on 31 March 1919 (Stefanidis).
sources: Stefanidis, 'Greece and the Allied intervention in southern Russia' (Balkan Studies, imxa.gr/files/bsfiles/55/4_Ioannis Stefanidis.pdf; Gregorian dates, citing the Hellenic Army General Staff history); en.wikipedia Southern Russia intervention
note: Draw faintly as a sector of the Odessa perimeter; dates of the perimeter's extension (talks with Petliura's delegates, January-February 1919) are not given in the sources.
editorial: Kept as information about the Greek forces' operations, not drawn on the map: Greek troops served under French command in the Allied intervention of 1919, and Greece held no land of its own there. Status changed from 'de_facto' to 'note'.

name: Kherson (Allied garrison)
joint_with: France (c. 150 French soldiers, French naval guns), some Russian officers
by_whom: Greek I Army Corps (Lt-Gen. Konstantinos Nider): 2nd and XIII Divisions, under French command (Gen. d'Anselme, Odessa; C-in-C Franchet d'Esperey); c. 700 men of the 7th Regiment at the time of the attack
battle: end: Grigoriev's attack on Kherson (7-10 March 1919)
basis: Allied intervention in southern Russia; town ceded by agreement with the Ukrainian Directorate's delegates
event: Greek troops formed most of the Allied garrison of Kherson (c. 700 Greeks, c. 150 French); after the attack of 7 March they withdrew into the old citadel and the town was evacuated by sea on 10 March 1919.
date_note: Month only for the start: Kherson and Nikolaev were handed over peacefully by Petliura's delegates to Gen. d'Anselme in early 1919 (en.wikipedia, no date). Greek troops were in Kherson by 1 March 1919 (Stefanidis: Lt Matthios at the Kherson railway station on 1 March); the 34th Regiment was the only Greek unit in the region for 38 days after 20 January, so other Greek units (2nd Division) arrived from about late February. End: Grigoriev attacked on 7 March; the Greek defenders decided on 9 March to evacuate and the Allied force left by sea in the early hours of 10 March 1919 (Stefanidis; en.wikipedia). (Julian 25 February.)
sources: Stefanidis, 'Greece and the Allied intervention in southern Russia' (Balkan Studies, imxa.gr/files/bsfiles/55/4_Ioannis Stefanidis.pdf; Gregorian dates, citing the Hellenic Army General Staff history); en.wikipedia Southern Russia intervention; newgreektv.com 'When Greeks fought in the Ukraine' (dates evidently Julian)
note: newgreektv dates the relief of the Kherson garrison by the 1st Regiment to '25 February', probably Julian (= 10 March Gregorian) or confused; not used for the start. (Julian 25 February.)
editorial: Kept as information about the Greek forces' operations, not drawn on the map: Greek troops served under French command in the Allied intervention of 1919, and Greece held no land of its own there. Status changed from 'de_facto' to 'note'.

name: Nikolaev (Allied garrison)
joint_with: France (two weak French companies); the German 15th Division (c. 12,000 men awaiting repatriation, of doubtful loyalty) was also in the city
by_whom: Greek I Army Corps (Lt-Gen. Konstantinos Nider): 2nd and XIII Divisions, under French command (Gen. d'Anselme, Odessa; C-in-C Franchet d'Esperey)
basis: Allied intervention in southern Russia; city ceded by agreement with the Ukrainian Directorate's delegates
event: Nikolaev was held by about 500 Greeks and two French companies; it was evacuated 14-16 March 1919.
date_note: Month only for the start: a Greek garrison (c. 500 men) was in the city by early March (en.wikipedia, Grigoriev's attack after 7 March); arrival not dated in the sources, possibly late February. End: lost on 14 March 1919 (Stefanidis); en.wikipedia says the evacuation took place 14-16 March without incident. (Julian 1 March.)
sources: Stefanidis, 'Greece and the Allied intervention in southern Russia' (Balkan Studies, imxa.gr/files/bsfiles/55/4_Ioannis Stefanidis.pdf; Gregorian dates, citing the Hellenic Army General Staff history); en.wikipedia Southern Russia intervention
note: (Julian 1 March.)
editorial: Kept as information about the Greek forces' operations, not drawn on the map: Greek troops served under French command in the Allied intervention of 1919, and Greece held no land of its own there. Status changed from 'de_facto' to 'note'.

name: Sevastopol (Allied garrison)
joint_with: France (French navy and troops), Britain (Royal Navy battleships from 21 April), Russian Volunteer Army
by_whom: Greek I Army Corps (Lt-Gen. Konstantinos Nider): 2nd and XIII Divisions, under French command (Gen. d'Anselme, Odessa; C-in-C Franchet d'Esperey)
basis: Allied intervention in southern Russia
event: Greek infantry of the XIII Division helped hold Sevastopol with the French until the Allied evacuation of 23-29 April 1919.
date_note: Month only for the start: Greek units of the 2nd Regiment, XIII Division, were based in Sevastopol in early April 1919 (Stefanidis); by mid-April about 2,000 Greek and 2,400 French troops were in the city. The Bolsheviks reached the city on 14 April; truce 17-25 April; evacuation ordered 21 April, embarkation from 23 April, ended 28 April (en.wikipedia); the city was handed over on 29 April 1919 (Stefanidis). newgreektv: the 2nd Regiment 'remained in the Crimea until 14 April 1919' (Julian = 27 April). (Julian 16 April for the end.)
sources: Stefanidis, 'Greece and the Allied intervention in southern Russia' (Balkan Studies, imxa.gr/files/bsfiles/55/4_Ioannis Stefanidis.pdf; Gregorian dates, citing the Hellenic Army General Staff history); en.wikipedia Southern Russia intervention; newgreektv.com 'When Greeks fought in the Ukraine' (dates evidently Julian)
note: Naval only before this: the Greek destroyer Panther was at Sevastopol from 26 November 1918 to 8 March 1919 (Stefanidis). Greek warships (battleship Limnos) also lay off Feodosia in April 1919; no Greek ground control there is documented. (Julian = 27 April) (Julian 16 April for the end.)
editorial: Kept as information about the Greek forces' operations, not drawn on the map: Greek troops served under French command in the Allied intervention of 1919, and Greece held no land of its own there. Status changed from 'de_facto' to 'note'.

name: Smyrna
by_whom: Greek Army (Army of Occupation, from late 1919 Army of Asia Minor)
battle: start: landing at Smyrna; end: Battle of Dumlupınar and the Greek retreat, 26 Aug - 18 Sept 1922
basis: Greek military occupation of western Asia Minor: landing at Smyrna authorized by the Allied Supreme Council (6 May 1919), zone extended by the Greek Army; Greek High Commission of Smyrna (Stergiadis) as administration; no sovereignty (Sèvres never in force)
event: About 13,000-20,000 Greek troops (1st Division, Col. Nikolaos Zafeiriou) landed under Allied naval cover on 15 May 1919 and took the city. On 14 May Allied detachments had taken posts nearby (British: Karaburun and Uzunada; French: Vourla and Phocaea; Greek: Yenikale fort). Greek troops left on 9 September 1922, when the Turkish army entered.
date_note: Landing 15 May 1919 (Julian 2 May). Greek civil administration under High Commissioner Aristeidis Stergiadis from 19/21 May 1919 (en.wikipedia Occupation of Smyrna: four days after the landing; Treaty of Sèvres article: 21 May). End: the Greek headquarters and authorities left on 8-9 September 1922 and Turkish cavalry entered on the morning of 9 September (c. 10:00, timeturk); en.wikipedia Greco-Turkish War also says the Greek authorities left 'two days before', which conflicts. (Julian 27 August 1922.)
sources: en.wikipedia Greek landing at Smyrna; en.wikipedia Occupation of Smyrna; en.wikipedia Greco-Turkish War (1919-1922); T.C. Kultur ve Turizm Bakanligi, 'Kuva-yi Milliye Kronolojisi' (yakegm.ktb.gov.tr/Eklenti/1009); Yucel Guclu, TTK article on the Greek occupation of Western Anatolia (ttk.gov.tr/wp-content/uploads/2024/05/13-Yucel-Turkce.pdf); timeturk.com '9 Eylul ve Izmir'in kurtulusu'; en.wikipedia Treaty of Sevres
note: Smyrna stayed the seat of the Greek High Commission throughout. On 30 July 1922 the Greek government proclaimed a protectorate/autonomous administration for the zone (Treaty of Sèvres article infobox). A small British force entered after the Greek departure (Occupation of Smyrna). (Julian 2 May) (Julian 27 August 1922.)

name: Greek-held zone, June 1919 (before the setbacks at Nazilli and Aydın)
line: Front line, north to south (outer Greek posts): Aegean coast north of Kydonies (39.32 N 26.69 E) - Pergamon (39.121, 27.180; held 12-15 June and again from 20 June) - east of Menemen and Magnesia (38.614, 27.429) - Kasaba (38.495, 27.700) - Ahmetli (38.519, 27.938) - Ödemiş (38.228, 27.970) - Nazilli (37.913, 28.320; the eastern point, along the Smyrna-Aydın railway) - back west along the Maeander valley (north bank) to Aydın (37.848, 27.845) - Germencik - Aegean coast between Ayasoluk (Greek) and Scala Nova (Italian). South of the Maeander and at Scala Nova and Sokia lay the Italian occupation zone.
by_whom: Greek Army (Army of Occupation, from late 1919 Army of Asia Minor)
battle: start: landing at Smyrna and occupation of the hinterland; end: Nazilli, Pergamon, Aydın (June 1919)
basis: Greek military occupation of western Asia Minor: landing at Smyrna authorized by the Allied Supreme Council (6 May 1919), zone extended by the Greek Army; Greek High Commission of Smyrna (Stergiadis) as administration; no sovereignty (Sèvres never in force)
event: Within three weeks of the landing the Greek Army held the coast from Kydonies to Ayasoluk and the railway valleys inland to Magnesia, Kasaba, Ödemiş, Aydın and Nazilli.
date_note: Snapshot: 4 June 1919 (Nazilli and Ahmetli taken) to 20 June 1919 (Nazilli lost). Within this window Pergamon was taken on 12 June, lost on 15 June and retaken on 20 June; Aydın was lost on 30 June and regained in early July. See the town events for exact days.

IX, doc. 6 (Council of Heads of Delegations, 12 Nov. 1919)

name: Greek zone within the Milne line (1919-1920)
line: Milne line as given in ATBD 115 (preface, p. VII; Turkish text translated): starting from a point on the sea coast ['seven miles north-east of Aidin', as printed: the place name is evidently garbled: the first named points lie north and north-east of Kydonies and Pergamon, so the start must be on the Gulf of Adramyttion coast north-east of Kydonies, south of Burhaniye] - Hacı Osman - Yaylacık Dağı - Madra Dağı - Kesnaten Dağı - summit of Akmaz Dağı - Döşeme village - the ridges between the Ürgüt and Menteşe streams - the junction of the Kaikos and the Cumalı stream - west of Tuğlacık - the Sarıtaş peaks - Özpekkaya - Karasilli - Yenice - Tepecik - Tatarköy - Yeni Çiftlik - Papazlı - south-east of Belen Dağı - Kestelli - Yarışlı - Sart (38.488, 28.040) - Bucak - Çaylı - Bademiye, to the southern boundary of the sanjak of Smyrna. South of that the source gives no course; the Greek line continued to the Maeander near Aydın and ran 'along the north bank of the river', leaving 'a triangle between the river, the railroad and the Greek line, which included Aidin' (FRUS, 12 Nov. 1919); the Greek-Italian line south of it had been 'fixed by agreement between M. Venizelos and the Italian Government' (FRUS). Most villages on the line are not located here (coordinates not established); the points list gives towns on each side.
by_whom: Greek Army (Army of Occupation, from late 1919 Army of Asia Minor)
battle: end: Greek summer offensive of 1920 (from 22 June 1920)
basis: Demarcation line fixed by the Allied Supreme Council on the report of Gen. G. Milne (autumn 1919) between the Greek occupation zone and Ottoman territory; Greek-Italian line by Venizelos-Italian agreement
event: From summer 1919 to June 1920 the Greek Army stayed behind a demarcation line confirmed by the Allies (the Milne line), with fighting along it (e.g. Turkish repulse of Greek attacks on the Soma and Salihli fronts, 18 January 1920, KTB).
date_note: Start month only: the Greek zone reached roughly this extent in the operations of July 1919 (en.wikipedia Army of Asia Minor: the line reached then 'formed the boundary of the Greek-controlled Smyrna Zone until June 1920'). The line was drawn by Gen. George Milne for the Supreme Council and notified to the Ottoman War Minister Cemal Paşa on 3 November 1919 (KTB); on 15 November 1919 the Ottoman government had not yet accepted it (ATBD 115, doc. 4242); on 12 November 1919 the Council of Heads of Delegations agreed that the Greeks would stay at Aydın but not advance further (FRUS). Greek troops were not to cross it except in pursuit, and then not more than 3 km (en.wikipedia Occupation of Smyrna). End: the Greek general offensive from the Milne line began on 22 June 1920 (KTB; Metin); en.wikipedia Occupation of Smyrna says the Greek divisions crossed it on 22 July 1920, which conflicts with the dated captures of 22-24 June 1920.
sources: Askeri Tarih Belgeleri Dergisi 115 (MSB, Milne line documents; preface p. VII; docs 4236-4242); T.C. Kultur ve Turizm Bakanligi, 'Kuva-yi Milliye Kronolojisi' (yakegm.ktb.gov.tr/Eklenti/1009); FRUS 1919, Paris Peace Conference vol. IX, doc. 6 (Council of Heads of Delegations, 12 Nov. 1919); en.wikipedia Army of Asia Minor (some dates Julian); en.wikipedia Occupation of Smyrna; Omer Metin, chapter on Philadelphia, 1920-22, in Milli Mucadelede Manisa (Manisa Buyuksehir Bel. 2020), makale.isam.org.tr bitstream 14127483; Ataturk Ansiklopedisi, 'Milli Mucadelede Bati Cephesi' (ataturkansiklopedisi.gov.tr)
note: Places on the line identified with present villages only where certain. ATBD 115 also records Greek posts near Salihli abandoned on 20 October 1919 (doc. 4239), Greek troops pushed back to the ridges north of Küçükören (15 Oct. 1919, doc. 4237) and Güre as a place Milne allowed the Greeks to occupy (doc. 4236). Atatürk Ansiklopedisi says by mid-1920 the occupation reached a line from Prusa through Uşak to Denizli (i.e. after the summer offensive).

name: Smyrna zone (Sèvres Art. 66)
line: Treaty of Sèvres, Article 66 (text as transcribed in consecutive extracts from the treaty PDF; check against the official text): 'The geographical limits of the territory adjacent to the city of Smyrna will be laid down as follows: From the mouth of the river which flows into the Aegean Sea about 5 kilometres north of Skalanova, eastwards, the course of this river upstream; then south-eastwards, the course of the southern branch of this river; then south-eastwards, to the western point of the crest of the Gumush Dagh; A line to be fixed on the ground passing west of Chinar K, and east of Akche Ova; thence north-eastwards, this crest line; thence northwards to a point to be chosen on the railway from Ayasoluk to Deirmendik about 1 kilometre west of Balachik station, a line to be fixed on the ground leaving the road and railway from Sokia to Balachik station entirely in Turkish territory; thence northwards to a point to be chosen on the southern boundary of the Sandjak of Smyrna, a line to be fixed on the ground; thence to a point to be chosen in the neighbourhood of Bos Dagh situated about 15 kilometres north-east of Odemish, the southern and eastern boundary of the Sandjak of Smyrna; thence northwards to a point to be chosen on the railway from Manisa to Alashehr about 6 kilometres west of Salihli, a line to be fixed on the ground; thence northwards to Geurenez Dagh, a line to be fixed on the ground passing east of Mermer Geul [and] west of Kemer, crossing the Kum Chai approximately south of Akshalan, and then following the watershed west of Kavakalan; thence north-westwards to a point to be chosen on the boundary between the Cazas of Kirkagach and Ak Hissar about 18 kilometres east of Kirkagach and 20 kilometres north of Ak Hissar, a line to be fixed on the ground; thence westwards to its junction with the boundary of the Caza of Soma, the southern boundary of the Caza of Kirkagach, thence westwards to its junction with the boundary of the Sandjak of Smyrna, the southern boundary of the Caza of Soma; thence northwards to its junction with the boundary of the vilayet of Smyrna, the north-eastern boundary of the Sandjak of Smyrna; thence westwards to a point to be chosen in the neighbourhood of Charpajik (Tepe), the northern boundary of the vilayet of Smyrna; thence northwards to a point to be chosen on the ground about 4 kilometres southwest of Keuiluje, a line to be fixed on the ground; thence westwards to a point to be selected on the ground between Cape Dahlina and Kemer Iskele, a line to be fixed on the ground passing south of Kemer and Kemer Iskele together with the road joining these places.' Reading on present maps: the southern limit starts on the coast a few km north of Scala Nova (Scala Nova, left outside) and runs roughly along the southern edge of present Ayasoluk district (Ayasoluk inside) to the Smyrna-Aydın railway just west of Balachik station (probably Ortaklar, Germencik; the Sokia branch left to Turkey); then north to the old Smyrna-Aydın sanjak boundary (roughly the present Smyrna-Aydın provincial boundary) and along it east and north to the Boz Dağ range c. 15 km NE of Ödemiş; then north to the Magnesia-Philadelphia railway c. 6 km west of Salihli (near Sart; Salihli outside); then north passing east of Lake Marmara (Mermer Geul; Gölmarmara inside) to a point c. 18 km east of Kırkağaç and 20 km north of Akhisar (Akhisar inside); then west along the southern boundaries of the old kazas of Kırkağaç and Soma (both outside) to the Smyrna sanjak boundary, north along it (Pergamon inside) to the vilayet boundary, west along the vilayet boundary to Charpajik Tepe, north to a point 4 km SW of Keuiluje and west to the Gulf of Adramyttion coast between Cape Dahlina and Kemer Iskele, leaving Kemer (probably Burhaniye, formerly Kemer) and its landing-place outside: Kydonies inside, Burhaniye outside. Gumush Dagh, Chinar K., Akche Ova, Deirmendik, Geurenez Dagh, Kemer (near Lake Marmara), Akshalan, Kavakalan, Charpajik Tepe, Keuiluje and Cape Dahlina are not identified here.
by_whom: Greece (administration under Arts. 69-70); sovereignty formally Turkish
basis: Treaty of Sèvres (Treaty of Peace with Turkey), Part III, Section IV 'Smyrna', Arts. 65-83: Art. 66 boundary; Art. 67 boundary commission (Britain, France, Italy, Greece, Turkey) to fix the line on the ground; Art. 69 Turkish sovereignty retained but its exercise transferred to Greece, Turkish flag on an outer fort; Art. 70 Greek administration; Art. 72 local parliament; Art. 83 after five years the local parliament could ask the League of Nations Council for definitive incorporation into Greece (plebiscite possible)
event: The Treaty of Sèvres placed Smyrna and a defined hinterland under Greek administration, with possible incorporation into Greece after five years; the zone was smaller than the area the Greek Army actually held after the summer 1920 offensive.
date_note: Awarded from signature (10 August 1920). The treaty was never ratified by Greece, the Ottoman Empire or the four principal Allied Powers (en.wikipedia), so the award never came into force. End: superseded by the Treaty of Lausanne, signed 24 July 1923 (in force 6 August 1924), which left the whole area to Turkey. (Julian 28 July 1920.)
sources: Treaty of Peace with Turkey, Sevres 10 Aug. 1920, Part III Section IV (Smyrna), Arts. 65-83 (text PDF fransamaltingvongeusau.com/documents/dl1/h1/1.1.18.pdf; Wikisource page could not be fetched); en.wikipedia Treaty of Sevres; en.wikipedia Occupation of Smyrna
note: Draw as an awarded outline over the de_facto zone. The area was held de facto by the Greek Army until 9-16 September 1922 (see the de_facto events). The boundary commission of Art. 67 never fixed the line on the ground, so the 'line to be fixed on the ground' stretches are approximate; confidence 'good' refers to the defined course, not to field demarcation. (Julian 28 July 1920.)

line: Front, north to south: Sea of Marmara east of Yalova (40.655, 29.276) and the Armutlu peninsula (the Nicomedia peninsula to the north-east was under British occupation from 6 July 1920, KTB) - west shore of the lake of Nicaea, east of Pazarköy and Kios (Nicaea itself Turkish) - Yenişehir (40.264, 29.653) - İnegöl (40.078, 29.510), c. 40 km short of Bilecik - south through the uplands east of Adranos (39.903, 28.987), west of Tavşanlı - Simav (39.088, 28.979) - west of Gediz (39.003, 29.414) - east of Uşak (38.682, 29.408) - south via Eşme (38.400, 28.970) to Buldan (38.045, 28.830) - the Maeander at Nazilli (37.913, 28.320) - west along the north bank of the Maeander past Aydın (37.848, 27.845) to the coast north of Scala Nova. The Biga peninsula and the Marmara coast from Panormos to Mudanya were Greek-held behind the front. The Turkish side: Nicaea, Bilecik, Tavşanlı, Kütahya, Gediz, Denizli.
by_whom: Greek Army (Army of Occupation, from late 1919 Army of Asia Minor)
battle: start: Greek summer offensive 1920, Battle of Gediz (Oct. 1920); end: First Battle of İnönü (Jan. 1921)

event: The summer offensive of June-August 1920 extended Greek control over all of western and most of north-western Anatolia, from the Marmara and the Biga peninsula to Uşak and the Maeander.

Gediz changed hands on 24 October and Simav on 3 November 1920. Atatürk Ansiklopedisi summarizes the 1920 result as a line from Prusa through Uşak to Denizli (Denizli itself was not taken).

note: In late December 1920 (Julian) a gap of about 160 km separated the Greek I Corps in the south (Uşak) from III Corps near Prusa (en.wikipedia Army of Asia Minor), so the front between Adranos and Simav was a thin screen.

by_whom: Greek Army (Army of Occupation, from late 1919 Army of Asia Minor)
basis: Greek military occupation of western Asia Minor: landing at Smyrna authorized by the Allied Supreme Council (6 May 1919), zone extended by the Greek Army; Greek High Commission of Smyrna (Stergiadis) as administration; no sovereignty (Sèvres never in force)
date_note: The Greek Army advanced on 6 January 1921 from Prusa and Uşak; Bilecik and Bozüyük were occupied on 9 January (KTB); the Greeks reached İnönü on 9 January, attacked on 10 January and began withdrawing on 11 January (Ataturk Ansiklopedisi; KTB). End = start of the withdrawal; the exact day each town was left is not given. (Julian 27-29 December 1920.)
sources: T.C. Kultur ve Turizm Bakanligi, 'Kuva-yi Milliye Kronolojisi' (yakegm.ktb.gov.tr/Eklenti/1009); Ataturk Ansiklopedisi, 'Milli Mucadelede Bati Cephesi' (ataturkansiklopedisi.gov.tr); en.wikipedia Greco-Turkish War (1919-1922)
note: (Julian 27-29 December 1920.)

name: Bilecik, Bozüyük, Söğüt and Pazaryeri (Second İnönü advance)
by_whom: Greek Army (Army of Occupation, from late 1919 Army of Asia Minor)
battle: Second Battle of İnönü (23 March - 1 April 1921)
basis: Greek military occupation of western Asia Minor: landing at Smyrna authorized by the Allied Supreme Council (6 May 1919), zone extended by the Greek Army; Greek High Commission of Smyrna (Stergiadis) as administration; no sovereignty (Sèvres never in force)
date_note: The Greek offensive from Prusa and Uşak began on 23 March 1921; Söğüt was occupied on 26 March (KTB) and by 30 March the Greeks held Yenişehir, Pazarcık, Bozüyük, Bilecik and Dumlupınar (Ataturk Ansiklopedisi). After the Turkish counter-attack of 31 March they withdrew in the night of 31 March / 1 April to their original positions (Ataturk Ansiklopedisi; en.wikipedia Army of Asia Minor dates the start '10 March', the Julian date).
sources: T.C. Kultur ve Turizm Bakanligi, 'Kuva-yi Milliye Kronolojisi' (yakegm.ktb.gov.tr/Eklenti/1009); Ataturk Ansiklopedisi, 'Milli Mucadelede Bati Cephesi' (ataturkansiklopedisi.gov.tr); en.wikipedia Army of Asia Minor (some dates Julian); en.wikipedia Greco-Turkish War (1919-1922)

name: Adapazarı (March 1921)
by_whom: Greek Army (Army of Occupation, from late 1919 Army of Asia Minor)
basis: Greek military occupation of western Asia Minor: landing at Smyrna authorized by the Allied Supreme Council (6 May 1919), zone extended by the Greek Army; Greek High Commission of Smyrna (Stergiadis) as administration; no sovereignty (Sèvres never in force)
date_note: KTB records the occupation of 'Adapazarı and Söğüt' by the Greeks on 26 March 1921. End month only and uncertain: not recorded; probably given up in the general withdrawal after Second İnönü (from 1 April 1921), at the latest with the evacuation of Nicomedia (28 June 1921).
sources: T.C. Kultur ve Turizm Bakanligi, 'Kuva-yi Milliye Kronolojisi' (yakegm.ktb.gov.tr/Eklenti/1009)
note: Single source; the route of the force that reached Adapazarı is not given. Treat as uncertain.

name: Afyon Karahisar (first occupation)
by_whom: Greek Army (Army of Occupation, from late 1919 Army of Asia Minor)
battle: Second Battle of İnönü / Battle of Aslıhanlar-Dumlupınar (March-April 1921)
basis: Greek military occupation of western Asia Minor: landing at Smyrna authorized by the Allied Supreme Council (6 May 1919), zone extended by the Greek Army; Greek High Commission of Smyrna (Stergiadis) as administration; no sovereignty (Sèvres never in force)
date_note: Occupied 27 March 1921 (KTB; en.wikipedia Battle of Kütahya-Eskişehir: 'in March'). After Second İnönü the Greek southern group took Dumlupınar and Afyon Karahisar and reached the Çay-Bolvadin line, and a Turkish attack at Aslıhanlar failed (Ataturk Ansiklopedisi). End month only and uncertain: the date the Greeks left Afyon Karahisar is not given; KTB records a 'second' occupation on 13 July 1921, so the town was given up in between, probably in April 1921.
sources: T.C. Kultur ve Turizm Bakanligi, 'Kuva-yi Milliye Kronolojisi' (yakegm.ktb.gov.tr/Eklenti/1009); en.wikipedia Battle of Kutahya-Eskisehir; Ataturk Ansiklopedisi, 'Milli Mucadelede Bati Cephesi' (ataturkansiklopedisi.gov.tr)

name: Afyon Karahisar (1921-1922)
by_whom: Greek Army (Army of Occupation, from late 1919 Army of Asia Minor)
battle: start: Battle of Kütahya-Eskişehir (10-24 July 1921); end: Battle of Dumlupınar and the Greek retreat, 26 Aug - 18 Sept 1922

sources: T.C. Kultur ve Turizm Bakanligi, 'Kuva-yi Milliye Kronolojisi' (yakegm.ktb.gov.tr/Eklenti/1009); en.wikipedia Battle of Dumlupinar; Afyon Kocatepe Univ. note: In 1922 Afyon Karahisar formed the eastern salient of the Greek front (I Corps, Trikoupis), with Dumlupınar on the railway c. 48 km to the west (en.wikipedia Battle of Dumlupınar). (Julian 30 June 1921 - 14 August 1922.)

sources: T.C. Kultur ve Turizm Bakanligi, 'Kuva-yi Milliye Kronolojisi' (yakegm.ktb.gov.tr/Eklenti/1009); Afyon Kocatepe Univ. SBD article (sbd.aku.edu.tr/X2/98109.pdf; Ataturk's Nutuk and Fevzi Cakmak on the 1921-22 front)

name: Sandıklı
by_whom: Greek Army (Army of Occupation, from late 1919 Army of Asia Minor)
basis: Greek military occupation of western Asia Minor: landing at Smyrna authorized by the Allied Supreme Council (6 May 1919), zone extended by the Greek Army; Greek High Commission of Smyrna (Stergiadis) as administration; no sovereignty (Sèvres never in force)
date_note: Occupied 7 August 1921 (KTB). KTB dates its recapture to 12 September 1922, which is doubtful: after the Sakarya the Greek right flank rested on the Kamalar and Ahır mountains south-west of Afyon Karahisar (Fevzi Çakmak in AKÜ SBD), and the Turkish offensive of 26 August 1922 was launched from that sector, so Sandıklı was probably Turkish again from September 1921. End date unresolved.
sources: T.C. Kultur ve Turizm Bakanligi, 'Kuva-yi Milliye Kronolojisi' (yakegm.ktb.gov.tr/Eklenti/1009); Afyon Kocatepe Univ. SBD article (sbd.aku.edu.tr/X2/98109.pdf; Ataturk's Nutuk and Fevzi Cakmak on the 1921-22 front)
editorial: End date unresolved in the research: KTB's 12 Sep 1922 is doubtful, since the Greek right flank rested on the Kamalar and Ahır mountains south-west of Afyon Karahisar after the Sakarya. Drawn until the withdrawal of 24 Sep 1921.

name: Greek-held Asia Minor, late July 1921 (after Kütahya-Eskişehir)
line: Front, north to south: Gulf of Kios (40.432, 29.157; Nicomedia evacuated 28 June and Yalova lost 19 July 1921) - the lake of Nicaea - Bilecik (40.142, 29.979) - Söğüt (40.018, 30.181) - east of Eskişehir (39.777, 30.521) - Seyitgazi (39.445, 30.694) - east of Afyon Karahisar (38.757, 30.538), with forward posts towards Çay and Bolvadin - south-west to the upper Maeander at Çivril (38.301, 29.739) - down the Maeander (north bank) past Buldan (38.045, 28.830), Nazilli (37.913, 28.320) and Aydın (37.848, 27.845) to the coast north of Scala Nova. The Turkish army had withdrawn east of the Sakarya (completed 25 July 1921, KTB).
by_whom: Greek Army of Asia Minor (I, II and III Corps; C-in-C Anastasios Papoulas)
battle: start: Battle of Kütahya-Eskişehir (10-24 July 1921); end: advance to the Sakarya
basis: Greek military occupation of western Asia Minor: landing at Smyrna authorized by the Allied Supreme Council (6 May 1919), zone extended by the Greek Army; Greek High Commission of Smyrna (Stergiadis) as administration; no sovereignty (Sèvres never in force)
event: The July 1921 offensive took Afyon Karahisar (13 July), Kütahya (17 July) and Eskişehir (19 July); the Turks withdrew east of the Sakarya.
date_note: Snapshot from 25 July 1921 (Turkish withdrawal east of the Sakarya completed, KTB) to 13 August 1921 (Greek advance towards the Sakarya, KTB; operations began 1 August Julian = 14 August, en.wikipedia Army of Asia Minor). Sandıklı was taken on 7 August 1921.
sources: T.C. Kultur ve Turizm Bakanligi, 'Kuva-yi Milliye Kronolojisi' (yakegm.ktb.gov.tr/Eklenti/1009); en.wikipedia Battle of Kutahya-Eskisehir; en.wikipedia Army of Asia Minor (some dates Julian); Ataturk Ansiklopedisi, 'Milli Mucadelede Bati Cephesi' (ataturkansiklopedisi.gov.tr); en.wikipedia Greco-Turkish War (1919-1922)
note: The exact course between Afyon Karahisar and Çivril and the status of Nicaea in July 1921 are not established.

name: Greek-held Asia Minor at the furthest advance (Sakarya, late August - mid-September 1921)
line: At the furthest advance the Greek Army held a salient east of the Sakarya: from the Eskişehir front east along the Porsuk/Sakarya valleys to the Sakarya bend, across the river south of the Gök (Ilıca?) stream, and in an arc west and south of Polatlı (39.584, 32.147; Turkish headquarters, not taken) over the heights south of Polatlı including Mount Çal (Çal Dağı, in Greek hands by 2 September; coordinates not established) to west of Haymana (39.433, 32.497; not taken, 40 km south of Ankara); some Greek units came within 50 km of Ankara. Behind the salient: Sivrihisar (39.450, 31.537), and on the southern flank Aziziye (39.020, 31.150), Bolvadin (38.711, 31.049) and Çay (38.592, 31.027). West of Afyon Karahisar the front was as in July 1921 (Sandıklı added).
by_whom: Greek Army of Asia Minor (I Corps Kontoulis, II Corps Prince Andrew, III Corps Polymenakos, southern group Trikoupis)
battle: Battle of the Sakarya (23 Aug. - 13 Sept. 1921)
basis: Greek military occupation of western Asia Minor: landing at Smyrna authorized by the Allied Supreme Council (6 May 1919), zone extended by the Greek Army; Greek High Commission of Smyrna (Stergiadis) as administration; no sovereignty (Sèvres never in force)
event: The Greek Army marched east from the Eskişehir-Afyon Karahisar line, crossed the Sakarya and fought the 21-day Battle of the Sakarya less than 100 km from Ankara; it then withdrew to the line it had held a month earlier.
date_note: Battle 23 August - 13 September 1921 (Julian 10-31 August); first contact on 23 August south of the Gök river, general Greek attack 26 August, Mount Çal taken by 2 September, Turkish counter-attack 8 September; the Greeks broke off on 14 September and withdrew across the Sakarya (en.wikipedia Battle of the Sakarya; KTB: Turkish forces crossed to the west bank on 14 September, Greek forces withdrew towards Eskişehir on 18 September).
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of the Sakarya; en.wikipedia Greco-Turkish War (1919-1922); T.C. Kultur ve Turizm Bakanligi, 'Kuva-yi Milliye Kronolojisi' (yakegm.ktb.gov.tr/Eklenti/1009); en.wikipedia Army of Asia Minor (some dates Julian); Ataturk Ansiklopedisi, 'Milli Mucadelede Bati Cephesi' (ataturkansiklopedisi.gov.tr)
note: The line inside the Sakarya bend is the least certain part of this file; draw it as an approximate salient. Turkish recaptures during the Greek withdrawal: Sivrihisar 20 Sept., Aziziye 22 Sept., Bolvadin and Çay 24 Sept. 1921. (Julian 10-31 August)

name: Greek-held Asia Minor, September 1921 - August 1922 (Eskişehir-Afyon Karahisar line)
line: Front, north to south (c. 700-713 km in all, en.wikipedia Battle of Dumlupınar): the Sea of Marmara near Kios (40.432, 29.157), the Greek left flank lying north and south of the lake of Nicaea (AKÜ SBD) - Nicaea (40.429, 29.721) - Bilecik (40.142, 29.979) - Söğüt (40.018, 30.181) - east of Eskişehir (39.777, 30.521; III Corps at Eskişehir), the left of the main sector on 'Bozdağı' (Fevzi Çakmak; location not identified here) - Seyitgazi (39.445, 30.694) - Döğer (II Corps area, village in İhsaniye district; coordinates not established) - the fortified line of 90-100 km east and south of Afyon Karahisar (38.757, 30.538; I Corps), its right on the Kamalar and Ahır mountains south-west of Afyon Karahisar (Çakmak) - west and south-west to the upper Maeander at Çivril (38.301, 29.739) - along the Maeander past Buldan (38.045, 28.830), Nazilli (37.913, 28.320) and Aydın (37.848, 27.845) - Sokia (37.751, 27.410) and Scala Nova (37.858, 27.261) on the coast after the Italian evacuation (the Greek right flank rested on the Maeander, AKÜ SBD).
by_whom: Greek Army of Asia Minor (C-in-C Papoulas, from May 1922 Hatzianestis; I Corps Trikoupis at Afyon Karahisar, II Corps Digenis, III Corps Soumilas at Eskişehir)
battle: start: Battle of the Sakarya (Greek withdrawal); end: Battle of Dumlupınar (26-30 Aug. 1922)
basis: Greek military occupation of western Asia Minor: landing at Smyrna authorized by the Allied Supreme Council (6 May 1919), zone extended by the Greek Army; Greek High Commission of Smyrna (Stergiadis) as administration; no sovereignty (Sèvres never in force)
event: For eleven months the Greek Army held a long front from the Marmara to the Maeander, with a salient around Eskişehir and Afyon Karahisar.
date_note: From the end of the Greek withdrawal after the Sakarya (last Turkish recaptures 24 September 1921; the Greeks went back to 'the June-July line, around Eskişehir in the north and Afyonkarahisar in the south', en.wikipedia Army of Asia Minor) to the start of the Turkish offensive at 05:00-05:30 on 26 August 1922 (KTB; Ataturk Ansiklopedisi). (Julian 11 September 1921 - 13 August 1922.)
sources: Afyon Kocatepe Univ. SBD article (sbd.aku.edu.tr/X2/98109.pdf; Ataturk's Nutuk and Fevzi Cakmak on the 1921-22 front); en.wikipedia Battle of Dumlupinar; en.wikipedia Army of Asia Minor (some dates Julian); en.wikipedia Battle of the Sakarya; T.C. Kultur ve Turizm Bakanligi, 'Kuva-yi Milliye Kronolojisi' (yakegm.ktb.gov.tr/Eklenti/1009); Ataturk Ansiklopedisi, 'Milli Mucadelede Bati Cephesi' (ataturkansiklopedisi.gov.tr); en.wikipedia Greco-Turkish War (1919-1922)
note: Corps positions per en.wikipedia Battle of Dumlupınar (I Corps Kara Hisar, II Corps 'Gazligöl', III Corps Eskişehir) and AKÜ SBD (4-5 divisions east and south of Afyon Karahisar, 3 at Eskişehir and Seyitgazi, 3 at Döğer, about 2 near Kios and the lake of Nicaea). The course between Afyon Karahisar and Çivril is the least certain stretch. (Julian 11 September 1921 - 13 August 1922.)

name: Greek retreat from Asia Minor (26 August - 18 September 1922)
line: Shrinking area; the town events give each end date. Recapture / evacuation sequence (Gregorian): 26 Aug Nicaea (KTB); 27 Aug Afyon Karahisar; 30 Aug Kütahya (evening; KTB 31 Aug), 31 Aug Çivril; 1 Sept Uşak, Gediz, Seyitgazi; 2 Sept Eskişehir; 3 Sept Ödemiş, Emet, Tavşanlı, Eşme, Sındırgı, Dursunbey, Bigadiç, Selendi; 4 Sept Tire, Bayındır, Buldan, Simav, Kula, Sarıgöl, Bozüyük, Söğüt, Demirci; 5 Sept Nazilli, Philadelphia, Salihli, Gördes, Pazaryeri; 6 Sept Akhisar, Balıkesir, Bilecik, Sokia, Gönen, İnegöl; 7 Sept Aydın, Germencik, Scala Nova, Kasaba; 8 Sept Magnesia, Nif, Ayasoluk, Burhaniye; 9 Sept Smyrna, Menemen, Adramyttion; 10 Sept Prusa, Phocaea, Adranos; 11 Sept Kios and Mudanya; 12 Sept Vourla, Kırkağaç; 13 Sept Soma; 14 Sept Pergamon, Dikili, Mihaliç; 15 Sept Kydonies, Alatsata; 16 Sept Krini (last Greek troops left the Smyrna zone); 17 Sept Panormos; 18 Sept Artaki, the Kyzikos peninsula and Biga (last Greek troops left Anatolia).
by_whom: Greek Army of Asia Minor
battle: Great Offensive (Battle of Dumlupınar, 26-30 Aug. 1922) and pursuit
basis: Greek military occupation of western Asia Minor: landing at Smyrna authorized by the Allied Supreme Council (6 May 1919), zone extended by the Greek Army; Greek High Commission of Smyrna (Stergiadis) as administration; no sovereignty (Sèvres never in force)
event: The Turkish offensive broke the Greek front south and east of Afyon Karahisar on 26-27 August 1922; the Greek Army retreated to the coast and was evacuated from Asia Minor, the last troops leaving Krini on 16 September and Artaki and Biga on 18 September 1922.
date_note: Dates from KTB, Yeni Asır, Sabah, Metin, en.wikipedia (Greco-Turkish War, Battle of Dumlupınar, Great Offensive). Disagreements: Uşak 1 Sept (most) or 2 Sept (timeturk); Tire 4 or 5 Sept; Bilecik 5 (Yeni Asır) or 6 Sept (KTB, en.wikipedia); Prusa 10, 11 or 12 Sept; Kios 10, 11 or 12 Sept; Mudanya 11 or 12 Sept; Kütahya 30 or 31 Aug. (Julian 13 August - 5 September 1922.)
sources: T.C. Kultur ve Turizm Bakanligi, 'Kuva-yi Milliye Kronolojisi' (yakegm.ktb.gov.tr/Eklenti/1009); Yeni Asir, Erkin Usman, 'Ege ve Izmir'in kurtulusu' (9 Sept. 2010) - list of the dates of the Turkish recapture, 1922; Sabah, Erdal Safak, 'Ege'de Eylul' (10 Sept. 2012) - list of the dates of the Turkish recapture, 1922; Omer Metin, chapter on Philadelphia, 1920-22, in Milli Mucadelede Manisa (Manisa Buyuksehir Bel. 2020), makale.isam.org.tr bitstream 14127483; CYDD PDF (cydd.org.tr) on the Great Offensive; en.wikipedia Greco-Turkish War (1919-1922); en.wikipedia Battle of Dumlupinar; en.wikipedia Great Offensive; Ataturk Ansiklopedisi, 'Milli Mucadelede Bati Cephesi' (ataturkansiklopedisi.gov.tr); Afyon Kocatepe Univ. SBD article (sbd.aku.edu.tr/X2/98109.pdf; Ataturk's Nutuk and Fevzi Cakmak on the 1921-22 front)
note: The Armistice of Mudanya (signed 11 October 1922; Greece acceded 14 October; in force 15 October) concerned Eastern Thrace and the Straits and is left to the Thrace batch. Lausanne (24 July 1923) confirmed Turkish sovereignty over the whole area. (Julian 13 August - 5 September 1922.)

name: Inter-Allied Thrace (Western Thrace under French-led Allied administration)
line: Western Thrace as Bulgaria held it 1913/1915-1919: west = the Nestos from the sea up to the Greek-Bulgarian frontier of 1913; north = the Greek-Bulgarian frontier of Neuilly (the present border); east = the Evros from the Bulgarian frontier to the Aegean, including the Karaağaç suburb on the right bank; south = the Aegean. Samothrace (Greek since 1912) is not part of it.
by_whom: France (General Charles Antoine Charpy) for the Allied Powers
basis: Allied decision after the Armistice of Salonica (29 September 1918), under which Bulgaria kept Western Thrace until the Allies ordered its evacuation in autumn 1919; Treaty of Neuilly (27 November 1919) Bulgaria renounced the territory in favor of the Allied Powers.
event: Bulgarian troops and officials evacuated Western Thrace in autumn 1919; Allied (mainly French) troops took over and General Charpy governed it from Komotini until he handed it to the Greek Army in May 1920.
handover: 1920-05-27/06-02 (handover to the Greek Army; Old Style 14-20 May 1920)
date_note: Start: October 1919 (HAGS army.gr: 'October 1919: the French General Charles Antoine Charpy took political and military command of Thrace, based in Komotini'). dcstamps gives 10 October 1919 (Charpy assumes military control at Komotini) and 22 October 1919 (Charpy appointed Governor); the Greek compilation on elisme.gr gives 4 October 1919 for the entry of Entente troops into Xanthi. The calendar of these day dates is not stated (they may be Old Style, i.e. 17 Oct / 23 Oct / 4 Nov Gregorian). End: the Greek takeover, 14-20 May 1920 as given in Greek sources, here read as Old Style = 27 May - 2 June 1920 Gregorian (see 1920-komotini).
sources: army.gr/en/?p=58120 and ?p=44441 (Hellenic Army General Staff, 'Liberation of West Thrace'); dcstamps.com 'Western Thrace, Inter Allied Occupation (1919-1920)'; elisme.gr dossier 'Apeleftherosi Thrakis' (Greek press of May 1920); Gyudurov, ebox.nbu.bg/hist14 (Bulgarian: about 20,000 Bulgarians left in autumn 1919 and 20,000 more under the inter-Allied administration); en.wikipedia Western Thrace ('under temporary management of the Entente led by French General Charles Antoine Charpy').
note: Not a Greek status: recorded so that the map can show Western Thrace as Allied-administered (neutral color) between the Bulgarian departure and the Greek entry. The en.wikipedia page 'Interallied Thrace' named in the task does not exist (url_not_found). Whether Greek units took part in the Allied occupation (e.g. in the Xanthi area) is not stated in the sources found; the HAGS page names a 'Xanthi Division' already in May 1920, which hints at a Greek presence in Xanthi before the takeover, but this is not confirmed. TUBA ch10 mentions a 'French zone' still existing at Karaağaç on 22 July 1920.

name: Western Thrace ceded by Bulgaria to the Allied Powers (Neuilly)
line: Bulgaria's new southern frontier = the present Greek-Bulgarian border from the Nestos to the Evros (and the Bulgarian-Turkish border); everything south of it between the Nestos and the Evros was renounced.
basis: Treaty of Neuilly-sur-Seine (27 November 1919): Bulgaria ceded Western Thrace to the Entente (Principal Allied and Associated Powers), who undertook to ensure Bulgaria's economic outlet to the Aegean; the Entente then gave it to Greece (San Remo, April 1920; Thrace treaty of Sevres, 10 August 1920).
event: Bulgaria renounced Western Thrace in favor of the Allied Powers, losing its direct outlet to the Aegean.
date_note: Signed 27 November 1919. Entry into force 9 August 1920 is the standard date but was not found in the pages fetched (en.wikipedia gives only 'Ratification by Bulgaria and four Principal Allied Powers'). End: the Allied title passed to Greece when the Sevres Thrace treaty came into force with Lausanne (6 August 1924).
sources: en.wikipedia Treaty of Neuilly-sur-Seine (signed 27 November 1919 at the Hotel de Ville of Neuilly; Western Thrace ceded to the Entente, then awarded to Greece at San Remo); en.wikipedia Western Thrace ('ceded to the Entente in December 1919' - disagrees on the month); Gyudurov (Bulgarian): Neuilly placed Western Thrace under Allied administration.
note: Not a Greek status; legal step in the chain Bulgaria -> Allied Powers -> Greece. The article number (Art. 48 in the standard text) was not confirmed in the fetched pages. en.wikipedia Western Thrace says 'ceded to the Entente in December 1919', which disagrees with the signature date.

name: Western Thrace (San Remo decision and Thrace treaty of Sevres)
line: As 1919-interallied-thrace, without the Karaağaç triangle (recorded separately as 1920-karagatch-award because that part of the award was superseded at Lausanne).
basis: Decision of the Supreme Allied Council at San Remo (April 1920) to give Western Thrace to Greece and let the Greek Army replace the Allied troops; Treaty between the Principal Allied Powers and Greece relative to Thrace (Sevres, 10 August 1920), transferring to Greece the territory ceded by Bulgaria at Neuilly; Lausanne Protocol XVI (24 July 1923) put it into force and restricted its Article 1 by Article 2(2) of the Lausanne peace treaty (the Karaağaç cession).
event: The Allied Powers assigned Western Thrace to Greece; Greece occupied it in May 1920 and the transfer treaty, signed in August 1920, entered into force in August 1924.
signed: 1920-08-10 (Treaty between the Principal Allied Powers and Greece relative to Thrace, Sevres)
in_force: 1924-08-06 (with Lausanne; UK treaty record: ratifications UK 10 July 1924, Dominions/India/Italy 6 August 1924, France 30 August 1924, Japan none listed)
date_note: Start: 'late April 1920' (en.wikipedia Western Thrace: San Remo conference; the conference sat 19-26 April 1920). The Thrace treaty was signed at Sevres on 10 August 1920 but came into force only when its ratifications were deposited together with those of Lausanne (Protocol XVI of Lausanne), i.e. 6 August 1924; on that day this award ends and becomes de_jure (1924-western-thrace-de-jure).
sources: en.wikipedia Western Thrace ('In late April 1920, as per the San Remo conference ... Western Thrace was given to Greece'); army.gr ?p=58120 ('April 1920: the San Remo Conference authorised the Hellenic Army to replace the allied troops'); fhw.gr chronos 13 foreign_policy/institutions/07 ('A separate treaty concerning Thrace ratified the annexation of western Thrace to Greece'); api.parliament.uk/uk-treaties/treaties/6814 (Treaty between the Allied Powers and Greece Relative to Thrace, signed 10 August 1920, Treaty Series 013/1921, ratifications 1924); mfa.gov.tr Lausanne Protocol XVI.
note: This award was carried out (not superseded), so it overlaps the de_facto events of May 1920 and turns into de_jure on 6 August 1924. Shown as 'awarded' only because the title was a signed but unratified treaty from 1920 to 1924; the film may simply ignore it under the de_facto layer.
editorial: The award was carried out: Greek administration from May 1920 and the Thrace treaty in force from 6 August 1924. Kept as a note; the land is drawn as held from 1920 and as recognized from 1924. Status changed from 'awarded' to 'note'.

name: Xanthi district (Western Thrace west part)
line: Between the Nestos (west) and the Xanthi-Rhodope regional-unit boundary (east); north = Greek-Bulgarian border.
by_whom: Greek Army (Army Corps of National Defense, Maj. Gen. Emmanouil Zymvrakakis)
basis: Greek military occupation authorized by the San Remo decision (April 1920), replacing the inter-Allied administration
event: The Greek Army took over the Xanthi district from the Allied administration.
date_note: No date found for the Greek takeover of Xanthi itself. The Greek move into Western Thrace culminated on 14 May 1920 (as given, probably Old Style = 27 May Gregorian), when the Serres Division, coming from the west, entered Komotini, so Xanthi was Greek-held by then at the latest. Allied (Entente) troops had entered Xanthi on 4 October 1919 (elisme.gr; calendar not stated). End: de_jure from 6 August 1924.
sources: army.gr ?p=58120 and ?p=44441 (HAGS); elisme.gr dossier (4 October 1919 Allied entry into Xanthi).
note: Possibly earlier: the HAGS page mentions a Greek 'Xanthi Division' whose XV Infantry Regiment landed at Alexandroupoli on 14 May 1920 (OS), which suggests Greek troops were stationed in Xanthi during the inter-Allied period; not confirmed. Xanthi's local liberation day (4 October) refers to the 1919 Allied entry.

name: Komotini district (Rhodope)
by_whom: Greek Army: Serres Division (Army Corps of National Defense, Maj. Gen. Emmanouil Zymvrakakis); Greek gendarmerie
basis: San Remo decision (April 1920); handover by the inter-Allied administration
event: The Serres Division entered Komotini, seat of the inter-Allied administration, which General Charpy handed over to the Greek Army.
handover: 1920-05-27 (OS 14 May): General Charpy and General Zymvrakakis at Komotini (dcstamps photo dated 14 May 1920)
date_note: Sources: 'In the morning of 14 May 1920, the Serres Division entered Komotini' (HAGS); the Greek newspaper Makedonia (issues of 14-17 May 1920, compiled on elisme.gr) gives about 09:00 on 14 May, after Greek gendarmerie units. Neither states the calendar. Greece used the Old Style in 1920 and the Greek-derived dates for the July 1920 advance are Old Style (dcstamps: Greek HQ in Adrianople 12 July = 25 July Gregorian in Turkish sources), so 14 May is read here as Old Style = 27 May 1920 Gregorian. If the source date is already Gregorian, start = 1920-05-14. End: de_jure from 6 August 1924.
sources: army.gr ?p=58120, ?p=44441 (HAGS); elisme.gr 'Apeleftherosi Thrakis' dossier (Makedonia, 14-17 May 1920); dcstamps.com Western Thrace Inter-Allied page; greekcitytimes.com 14 May 2020 (centenary).
note: (Julian 14 May 1920 - calendar inferred, see date_note.) Komotini commemorates its liberation on 14 May.

name: Dedeağaç / Alexandroupoli and the lower Evros (Feres)
line: East boundary = the Evros from about Kipi to the sea.
by_whom: Greek Army: XV Infantry Regiment of the Xanthi Division
basis: San Remo decision (April 1920)
event: Greek troops landed at Dedeağaç and relieved the French garrison; the town was later renamed Alexandroupolis after King Alexander's visit in July 1920.
date_note: Dedeağaç: occupied at 06:00 on 14 May 1920 by the XV Infantry Regiment (Xanthi Division), landed from the sea, replacing French troops; Feres (Feredjik) at 18:00 the same day (HAGS; Makedonia). Read as Old Style 14 May = 27 May 1920 Gregorian (see 1920-komotini). End: de_jure from 6 August 1924.
sources: army.gr ?p=58120 ('the XV Infantry Regiment of the Xanthi Division disembarked in Alexandroupoli'); elisme.gr dossier (Dedeağaç 06:00, Feredjik 18:00, 14 May 1920); TUBA ch10 (King Alexander visited Dedeağaç after Raidestos in July 1920; the town was renamed Alexandroupolis).
note: (Julian 14 May 1920 - calendar inferred.)

name: Middle and upper Evros valley (Soufli, Didymoteicho, the later Orestiada district)
line: East = the Evros up to the Arda confluence near Adrianople, then the Bulgarian frontier of Neuilly; the Karaağaç triangle across the Arda is recorded separately.
by_whom: Greek Army (IX Infantry Division in the north, per HAGS for Karaağaç)
basis: San Remo decision (April 1920)
event: Greek troops moved up the Evros railway, taking Soufli, Didymoteicho and Kuleli Burgas.
date_note: Makedonia of 16 May 1920: the towns were occupied 'successively Feredjik, Soufli and Didymoteicho ... from this morning' (Pythio/Kuleli Burgas also listed); on 14 May Didymoteicho had 'not yet been announced'. So 15 or 16 May 1920 as printed; read as Old Style = 28-29 May 1920 Gregorian. HAGS: occupation of Western Thrace completed on 20 May 1920 (OS) = 2 June Gregorian. End: de_jure from 6 August 1924.
sources: elisme.gr dossier (Makedonia, 14 and 16 May 1920); army.gr ?p=58120 (completion 20 May 1920).
note: (Julian 15/16 May 1920 - calendar inferred.) The exact day for Soufli versus Didymoteicho is not separable from the sources (same communique).

name: Karaağaç triangle (Adrianople suburb west of the Evros, with Bosnaköy)
line: Lausanne Art. 2(2) (the line that later made it Turkish): from the confluence of the Arda and the Evros 'upstream along the Arda, up to a point on that river to be determined on the spot in the immediate neighbourhood of the village of Tchorek-Keuy: the course of the Arda; thence in a south-easterly direction up to a point on the Maritza, 1 kilometre below Bosna-Keuy: a roughly straight line leaving in Turkish territory the village of Bosna-Keuy'. So the triangle is bounded by the Evros (north and east), the last stretch of the Arda (north-west) and that straight line (south-west); it is the part of present Adrianople Merkez west of the Evros. From the present boundary data the straight line runs from about 41.653 N 26.490 E (Arda) to about 41.610 N 26.595 E (Evros).
by_whom: Greek Army: IX Infantry Division
basis: Part of Western Thrace (Bulgarian 1915-1919 under the Bulgarian-Ottoman convention of 1915); Greek occupation under the San Remo decision; stayed Greek under the Armistice of Mudanya (Greek withdrawal only from east of the Evros); ceded to Turkey by Lausanne Art. 2(2), in place of war reparations.
event: Greek troops took Karaağaç, the Adrianople railway suburb, completing the occupation of Western Thrace; renamed Orestias; ceded to Turkey at Lausanne and handed over on 15 September 1923.
date_note: Start: occupied by the IX Infantry Division on 16 May 1920 (HAGS); 'at midnight of the 15th [16th?]' (Makedonia); read as Old Style = night of 28/29 May 1920 Gregorian. End: handed over to Turkey on 15 September 1923 (Lausanne Protocol XV, para I: 'shall be handed over to the Turkish authorities on the 15th September, 1923, at the latest', provided Greece had been notified of the Turkish ratification; the Turkish Grand National Assembly ratified on 23 August 1923; the Adrianople Governorship publication 'Edirne isgal altinda' confirms that Karaağaç was evacuated on 15 September 1923).
sources: army.gr ?p=58120 ('the occupation of Karaağaç by the IX Infantry Division followed (16 May)'); elisme.gr dossier; en.wikipedia Karaagac, Edirne ('When Greece held the town (1920-1923), Karaagac was renamed Orestias'; 41 39 20 N 26 31 30 E; with Bosnaköy one of the two Turkish settlements on the right bank of the Evros); en.wikipedia Treaty of Lausanne ('The major issue of the war reparations ... was abandoned after Greece agreed to cede Karaagac to Turkey'); Lausanne Art. 2(2) (rastko.rs text); Protocol XV (mfa.gov.tr); edirnevdb.gib.gov.tr 'Edirne isgal altinda' (15 Eylul 1923).
note: (Julian 16 May 1920 - calendar inferred.) TUBA ch10 (citing The Times of 24 July 1920) speaks of a 'French zone' at Karaağaç shelled on 22 July 1920, so a French detachment (probably at the railway station) may have stayed there after the Greek entry. Lausanne left the village of Tchorek-Keuy to a population test by the Boundary Commission (its present identity was not established). The Greek inhabitants left for Greece and founded Nea Orestiada across the river.

name: Karaağaç triangle (Thrace treaty award, superseded)
line: As 1920-karagatch.
basis: San Remo decision (April 1920) and Thrace treaty of Sevres (10 August 1920), superseded by Lausanne Art. 2(2) and Protocol XVI
event: Karaağaç was part of the Western Thrace awarded to Greece; at Lausanne Greece gave it up in exchange for Turkey dropping its claim to war reparations.
date_note: Start: San Remo decision, late April 1920 (signed as part of the Thrace treaty, 10 August 1920). End: Lausanne signed 24 July 1923, Art. 2(2) gave the triangle to Turkey and Protocol XVI restricted Art. 1 of the Thrace treaty accordingly (in force 6 August 1924; actual handover 15 September 1923).
sources: mfa.gov.tr Lausanne Protocol XVI para 3 ('the application of Article 1 of the Sevres treaty on Thrace is restricted under Article 2(2)'); en.wikipedia Treaty of Lausanne; en.wikipedia Western Thrace ('Karaagach and its environs became part of Turkey after the Treaty of Lausanne').

name: Western Thrace (Lausanne frontier)
line: East: Lausanne Art. 2(2): 'From the mouth of the River Rezvaya, to the River Maritza, the point of junction of the three frontiers of Turkey, Bulgaria and Greece: the southern frontier of Bulgaria as at present demarcated. Thence to the confluence of the Arda and the Maritza: the course of the Maritza; then upstream along the Arda ... the course of the Arda; thence in a south-easterly direction up to a point on the Maritza, 1 kilometre below Bosna-Keuy ... thence to the Aegean Sea: the course of the Maritza.' Art. 6: in waterways the frontier is the median line of the waterway or its principal branch. North: Neuilly frontier with Bulgaria (present border). West: the Nestos (Greek since 1913 on the west bank).
basis: Treaty of Neuilly (Bulgaria -> Allied Powers); Treaty between the Principal Allied Powers and Greece relative to Thrace (Sevres, 10 August 1920); Treaty of Lausanne Art. 2(2) (frontier with Turkey) and Protocol XVI (24 July 1923)
event: With the Lausanne ratifications the Thrace treaty came into force and Western Thrace became Greek in law; Lausanne exempted its Muslim population from the population exchange.
date_note: Greek sovereignty became de jure when the Thrace treaty of Sevres (10 August 1920) entered into force with the Treaty of Lausanne (Protocol XVI: ratifications deposited together with those of Lausanne), 6 August 1924. The Greek-Turkish frontier articles (Lausanne Arts. 1, 2(2), 5-11) came into force between Greece and Turkey as soon as both had deposited ratifications (Art. 143), possibly earlier; the Greek deposit date was not found. One Turkish source (makale.isam.org.tr) gives 16 August 1924 for Lausanne's entry into force (disagrees with 6 August).
sources: mfa.gov.tr Lausanne Protocol XVI; rastko.rs text of the Treaty of Lausanne (Arts. 2, 6, 143); en.wikipedia Treaty of Lausanne (in force 6 August 1924; Muslims of Western Thrace, about 129,120 in 1923, excluded from the exchange); army.gr ?p=60862 (Lausanne 'became effective on 6 August 1924'); api.parliament.uk treaty 6814.
note: Alternative readings: some would date de jure Greek rule from the formal Allied handover of May 1920 or from the Greek annexation proclaimed on 20 May 1920 (OS; dcstamps 'Greece officially annexed Western Thrace'); the brief's rule (treaty in force) gives 6 August 1924.

name: Greek garrisons on the Thracian railway under the Allied occupation (1919-1920)
line: No zone is described: the sources give Greek detachments at stations along the Constantinople-Adrianople railway (Hadımköy, Çatalca, Çorlu, Muratlı, Lüleburgaz, Uzunköprü) after the French withdrew from them; Ottoman civil administration remained.
joint_with: Allied (mainly French, Armee d'Orient) occupation forces; Constantinople itself under Allied occupation; Ottoman civil administration in place
by_whom: Greek Army detachments
basis: Allied occupation of the Thracian railway after the Armistice of Mudros (30 October 1918); Greek units replaced French ones
event: Greek troops took over railway stations in Eastern Thrace from the French in January 1919 (footnoted strengths 18-24 January: Lüleburgaz 9 officers and 300 men, Çatalca 170 men and 5 officers, Uzunköprü 95, Hadımköy 50, Muratlı 49).
date_note: TUBA ch10: 'Greek forces began settling in the places the French vacated on 14 January 1919' (another passage: entered 18 January, numbers raised until 24 January 1919); Belleten 3737: 'Hadimkoy station ... was occupied by the Greek army on 14 January 1919'; TUBA ch03: on 14 March 1920 Greek units at Lüleburgaz were moved by train toward Hadımköy. End: absorbed into the full occupation from 20 July 1920.
sources: tuba.gov.tr TUBA-978-625-8352-72-6 ch10 and ch03 (Local History of the National Struggle 1918-1923, vol. 10: Edirne-Kirklareli-Tekirdag); belleten.gov.tr full text 3737.
note: The troop figures in TUBA ch10 are not explicitly labeled Greek. Draw as points (small garrisons), not as an area.

name: Raidestos and the Marmara side of Eastern Thrace, up to the Allied zone of Constantinople
line: Eastern limit (approx): the zone of Constantinople stayed under Allied occupation. Greek sources say the Greek frontier reached 'Chatalja (Metrai)' (pemptousia) / 'as far as Chatalja' (fhw.gr); the Sevres treaty line (see 1920-sevres-eastern-thrace) runs 10-25 km west of the Çatalca lines (Black Sea near Podima - west of Istranca - 1 km west of Sinekli station - Marmara 1 km SW of Kalikratia). Whether Greek troops stood on the treaty line or on the Çatalca lines (Lake Durusu/Terkos - Çatalca - Buyukcekmece lake) is not established: draw the Sevres line and mark the strip up to the Çatalca lines as uncertain.
by_whom: Greek Army (Army of Thrace), supported by British warships
basis: Greek military occupation with Allied consent (British naval support), ahead of the Treaty of Sevres; Greek civil administration (Governor-General of Thrace at Adrianople)
event: Greek troops landed on the Marmara coast at Eregli and Raidestos and moved inland against Cafer Tayyar's 1st Corps; the whole of Eastern Thrace outside the Allied zone was taken within five days.
date_note: 20 July 1920: Greek landings on the Raidestos shore, at Eregli (taken 11:45) and Sultankoy, Raidestos taken 13:00 (Greek HQ report in TUBA ch10; TUBA ch03 gives Raidestos occupied 20 July 1920; TUBA ch10 elsewhere 21 July). Greek forces entered Muratlı before Raidestos (TUBA ch03). Belleten 3737: the occupation began on the morning of 20 July with the bombardment of Eregli. The Times, 2 August 1920: no resistance from the Bulgarian border to Çatalca. End: Mudanya in force (15 October 1922), then evacuation (1922-eastern-thrace-evacuation). Greek sources would give these dates Old Style (7 July 1920).
sources: TUBA ch02, ch03, ch10 (tuba.gov.tr, vol. 10 Edirne-Kirklareli-Tekirdag); belleten.gov.tr 3737; pemptousia.gr pdf 338729 (Governor-General in Adrianople and four nomarchs; borders reached Çatalca/Metrai but not Constantinople); fhw.gr chronos 13 institutions/07 ('as far as Chatalja'); en.wikipedia Greco-Turkish War (the Greeks had moved into Eastern Thrace 'apart from Constantinople and its region').
note: TUBA ch03: Raidestos was taken under Turkish (TBMM) administration on 13 November 1922. Allied (British) troops held the Constantinople zone and the Nicomedia peninsula throughout.

name: Adrianople and the lower Evros valley east of the river
line: West: the Evros; north: the Bulgarian-Turkish frontier of 1915 (present border).
by_whom: Greek Army (Army of Thrace), crossing the Evros from Western Thrace
battle: Kuleli Burgas bridgehead and Uzunköprü (22-25 July 1920, minor)
basis: Greek military occupation (Allied-sanctioned) ahead of Sevres; Greek civil administration
event: Greek troops crossed the Evros at Kuleli Burgas and entered Adrianople on 25 July 1920, which became the seat of the Greek Governor-General of Thrace.
date_note: Adrianople occupied on 25 July 1920 (Adrianople Governorship 'Edirne isgal altinda'; TUBA ch10: occupation of the whole region completed the same day). Greek-derived dcstamps: Greek HQ in Adrianople on 12 July 1920 (Old Style = 25 July), King Alexander in the city the next day (26 July). From 22 July Turkish artillery fought the Greek bridgeheads at Kuleli Burgas (about 35 km south of Adrianople) and Karaağaç; Uzunköprü and Karaağaç were the only places with resistance (TUBA ch10). On 25 July Cafer Tayyar's 1st Corps (about 10,000-15,000 soldiers and civilians) crossed into Bulgaria. End: Mudanya in force (15 October 1922; Turkish sources 14 October).
sources: edirnevdb.gib.gov.tr/kultur/pdf/edirne_isgal_altinda.pdf; TUBA ch10; belleten 3737; dcstamps.com 'Thrace, Greek Occupation (1920-1922)'; pemptousia.gr 338729.
note: Turkish troops entered Adrianople on 25 November 1922 (Adrianople isgal altinda). March 1922: the Paris conference of Allied foreign ministers proposed returning Eastern Thrace to Turkey except Adrianople and Saranta Ekklisies; Ankara refused (not an award to Greece, not recorded as an event).

name: Saranta Ekklisies and the Strandzha side
line: North: Bulgarian-Turkish frontier (present); east: the Black Sea coast up to the Sevres line near Podima (the Constantinople part of the coast is in 1920-rodosto-marmara).
by_whom: Greek Army (Army of Thrace)
basis: Greek military occupation ahead of Sevres; Greek civil administration (prefecture of Saranta Ekklisies)
event: Greek troops occupied Saranta Ekklisies on 25 July 1920, completing the occupation of Eastern Thrace in five days.
date_note: TUBA ch02: the Greek occupation started from Raidestos on 20 July 1920 and was completed with the occupation of Saranta Ekklisies on 25 July 1920. TUBA ch10: Saranta Ekklisies and Babaeski reported occupied in late July; Lüleburgaz and Çorlu among the towns taken before civil administration was set up. End: Mudanya in force (15 October 1922). Saranta Ekklisies celebrated its recapture on 10 November 1922 (TUBA ch02).
sources: tuba.gov.tr TUBA-978-625-8352-72-6 ch02 (Saranta Ekklisies) and ch10.
note: The Greek prefecture names (Adrianople, Saranta Ekklisies, Raidestos, Gallipoli) are the standard ones; pemptousia only says 'four nomarchs' without naming them.

name: Gallipoli peninsula, within the Allied-held Straits zone
line: The whole peninsula south of the Bolayir isthmus; under Sevres part of the European Zone of the Straits (Art. 179: 'From Karachali on the Gulf of Xeros north-eastwards ... the crest of the Kuru Dagh ... cutting the road from Rodosto to Malgara 3 kilometres west of Ainarjik ... to a point on the road from Muradli to Rodosto about 1 kilometre south of Muradli ... thence east-north-eastwards to Yeni Keui ... at a minimum distance of 2 kilometres north of the railway from Chorlu to Chatalja; thence north-north-eastwards to a point west of Istranja ... thence to the Black Sea'), i.e. also the Marmara coast of Raidestos and Silivri.
joint_with: Allied (British, French) forces holding the Dardanelles forts and the Straits zone under the Armistice of Mudros
by_whom: Greek administration
basis: Greek civil administration (prefecture of Gallipoli) in the Allied-controlled zone of the Straits; Greek sovereignty awarded by Sevres Art. 84 subject to the Straits regime (Art. 84 para 4, Art. 178-179)
event: The Gallipoli peninsula came under Greek civil administration with Eastern Thrace, while the Allies kept their troops at the Dardanelles.
date_note: Month only: the peninsula was part of the Greek administration of Eastern Thrace set up after the July 1920 occupation; no day found for the Greek entry into Gallipoli town. End: Mudanya in force; eurohoops (Greek, Old Style dates) says the residents of the Gallipoli peninsula were the last to leave in October 1922.
sources: net.lib.byu.edu/~rdh7/wwi/versa/sevres1.html (Sevres Arts. 84, 179); eurohoops.net/el 527661 (last to leave were the residents of the Kallipoli peninsula); pemptousia.gr 338729 (four nomarchs).
note: Low confidence on the extent of Greek control: the existence of a Greek prefecture of Gallipoli is the standard account but was not confirmed in the fetched pages; the Allied (British) presence at the Dardanelles is well known (Çanakkale crisis, September 1922), but its exact posts on the peninsula were not checked.

name: Eastern Thrace during the Greek evacuation (Mudanya)
line: Mudanya: Greek troops 'to withdraw from Eastern Thrace as far as the Maritza', i.e. behind the Evros; Karaağaç on the right bank stayed Greek (see 1920-karagatch). From 31 October 1922 the Greek Army stood on the Evros line from the Bulgarian frontier to the sea (the present Greek-Turkish border plus Karaağaç).
by_whom: Greek Army (General K. Nider) and Greek civil administration, under Allied supervision
battle: Dumlupınar (26-30 August 1922) - the defeat in Asia Minor that led to the loss of Eastern Thrace without a battle there
basis: Armistice of Mudanya (11 October 1922): Greek troops to evacuate Eastern Thrace to the Evros within 15 days; Turkish civil authority to take over 30 days after the Greek troops left; at most 8,000 Turkish gendarmes in East Thrace until the peace; Allied troops to stay until the peace treaty
event: Under the Mudanya armistice the Greek Army withdrew behind the Evros between 15 and 31 October 1922, followed by about 250,000 Greek refugees; the civil administration was handed to the Allies by 12 November.
handover: 1922-10-15/11-12 (army out by 31 October; civil administration to Allied missions by 12 November)
date_note: Mudanya signed 11 October 1922 by the Allies and Turkey (Greece did not sign there); Greece acceded on 13 or 14 October (en.wikipedia gives both); in force 15 October 1922 (en.wikipedia Greco-Turkish War; Turkish sources 14 October). Greek Army: withdrawal order by General K. Nider on 30 September (OS) = 13 October; withdrawal west of the Evros from 2 to 18 October 1922 OS = 15 to 31 October Gregorian (eurohoops, which gives Mudanya as '28 September (11 October New Style)', so its dates are Old Style). Greek civil authorities left 'by the end of October' (OS, about 12 November Gregorian); fhw.gr: on 12 November 1922 the Greeks surrendered the administration of Eastern Thrace to the Allies, who handed it to the Turks. The town-by-town order of the Greek departure is not known.
sources: en.wikipedia Armistice of Mudanya; en.wikipedia Greco-Turkish War (1919-1922) (in force 15 October 1922); fhw.gr chronos 13 institutions/10 (12 November 1922; 250,000 refugees); eurohoops.net/el 527661 (Old Style dates of the withdrawal, about 45,000 men in five divisions); edirnevdb 'Edirne isgal altinda' (in force 14 October 1922).
note: (Julian 2-18 October 1922.) eurohoops wrongly says the armistice ceded the 'Karagach triangle'; Karaağaç was ceded only at Lausanne. The film can show Eastern Thrace fading out between 15 October and 12 November.
editorial: The Greek Army stood on the Evros line from 31 Oct 1922 (Gregorian; 18 Oct Julian); the Allied missions then handed Eastern Thrace to Turkey.

name: Eastern Thrace under Allied missions before the Turkish takeover
by_whom: Allied (British, French, Italian) missions
basis: Armistice of Mudanya
event: The Allies held Eastern Thrace briefly and passed it to Turkish administration town by town in November 1922.
date_note: Allied missions took over from the Greek authorities in late October - 12 November 1922 and handed the towns to Ankara's officials: Saranta Ekklisies 10 November (TUBA ch02), Raidestos 13 November (TUBA ch03), Adrianople 25 November 1922 (Turkish troops entered; Adrianople isgal altinda). Mudanya: Allied troops to hand the area to Turkish forces within one month at most.
sources: fhw.gr chronos 13 institutions/10; TUBA ch02, ch03; edirnevdb 'Edirne isgal altinda'.
note: Not a Greek status: lets the map show Eastern Thrace as neutral between the Greek departure and the Turkish arrival.

name: Eastern Thrace (Treaty of Sevres, Arts. 27 and 84)
line: Sevres Art. 27 I(2), frontier of Turkey with Greece: 'From a point to be chosen on the Black Sea near the mouth of the Biyuk Dere, situated about 7 kilometres north-west of Podima, south-westwards to the most north-westerly point of the limit of the basin of the Istranja Dere (about 8 kilometres northwest of Istranja), a line to be fixed on the ground passing through Kapilja Dagh and Uchbunar Tepe; thence south-south-eastwards to a point to be chosen on the railway from Chorlu to Chatalja about 1 kilometre west of the railway station of Sinekli, a line following as far as possible the western limit of the basin of the Istranja Dere; thence south-eastwards to a point to be chosen between Fener and Kurfali on the watershed between the basins of those rivers which flow into Biyuk Chekmeje Geul, on the north-east, and the basin of those rivers which flow direct into the Sea of Marmora on the south-west, a line to be fixed on the ground passing south of Sinekli; thence south-eastwards to a point to be chosen on the Sea of Marmora about 1 kilometre south-west of Kalikratia, a line following as far as possible this watershed.' Art. 84: 'Turkey renounces in favour of Greece all rights and title over the territories of the former Turkish Empire in Europe situated outside the frontiers of Turkey as laid down by the present Treaty. The islands of the Sea of Marmora are not included in the transfer of sovereignty.' The line runs about 10-25 km west of the Çatalca lines, although secondary sources say 'up to the Chatalja line'.
basis: Treaty of Sevres (10 August 1920), Art. 27 I(2) and Art. 84; Greek sovereignty over the European Straits zone outside Turkey subject to the freedom-of-the-Straits obligations (Art. 84 para 4, Arts. 178-179)
