event: Sevres gave Greece all of Eastern Thrace up to a line some 30-40 km from Constantinople, including Adrianople and the Gallipoli peninsula; the treaty never came into force and Lausanne returned the area to Turkey.
date_note: Signed 10 August 1920 (fhw.gr: 28 July / 10 August 1920). Never ratified by the Ottoman Empire or Greece, never in force. End: superseded by the Treaty of Lausanne, signed 24 July 1923 (Greece accepted the Evros frontier by signing); Lausanne came into force on 6 August 1924 (use that if the atlas prefers legal supersession).
sources: net.lib.byu.edu/~rdh7/wwi/versa/sevres1.html (text of Arts. 27, 84, 179); en.wikipedia Treaty of Sevres ('Eastern Thrace (up to the Chatalja line)'; Greece never ratified; superseded by Lausanne); en.wikipedia Greco-Turkish War ('ceding to Greece Thrace, up to the Chatalja lines'; Turkey kept Constantinople, the Marmara islands and 'a tiny strip of European territory'; never ratified); fhw.gr institutions/07.
note: Positions of Podima, Istranja, Sinekli and Kalikratia are my identifications with present villages (Yalikoy, Binkilic, Sinekli, Mimarsinan) and approximate coordinates; Kapilja Dagh, Uchbunar Tepe, Fener and Kurfali were not located. The Marmara islands stayed Turkish.

name: Imbros and Tenedos (Sevres Art. 84)
basis: Treaty of Sevres Art. 84 para 3: 'Turkey further renounces in favour of Greece all her rights and title over the islands of Imbros and Tenedos'; both islands also in the demilitarized Zone of the Straits (Art. 178)
event: Sevres awarded Imbros and Tenedos to Greece; Lausanne returned them to Turkey.
date_note: Sevres signed 10 August 1920, never in force. End: Lausanne signed 24 July 1923 (Art. 12 excepts Imbros, Tenedos and the Rabbit Islands from the islands confirmed to Greece; Art. 14: 'The islands of Imbros and Tenedos, remaining under Turkish sovereignty, shall enjoy a special administrative organisation'); in force 6 August 1924.
sources: net.lib.byu.edu Sevres text (Art. 84, Art. 178); en.wikipedia Imbros ('granted the island to Greece'); rastko.rs Lausanne text (Arts. 12, 14); makale.isam.org.tr (Lausanne negotiations on Imbros and Tenedos).
note: Overlaps the de_facto events 1918-1923-imbros-greek and 1918-1923-tenedos-greek.

name: Dodecanese except Rhodes (Venizelos-Tittoni agreement)
basis: Venizelos-Tittoni agreement (Paris Peace Conference): Italy to 'transfer the Dodecanese to Greece, except for the island of Rhodes'; Rhodes to stay Italian until Britain ceded Cyprus to Greece, then a referendum; Italy to support Greek claims in Northern Epirus, Greece to support Italy over Avlona and Albania and in Aydın/Menteshe
event: Italy secretly promised the Dodecanese (except Rhodes) to Greece; it renounced the promise in mid-1920 and renewed it at Sevres.
date_note: Signed 29 July 1919 (en.wikipedia Italian occupation of Adalia; en.wikipedia Venizelos-Tittoni gives only 'July 1919'). End: Foreign Minister Carlo Sforza's secret note renouncing it - July 1920 (en.wikipedia Venizelos-Tittoni) or June 1920 (en.wikipedia Italian occupation of Adalia); replaced by the Italo-Greek treaty of 10 August 1920 (next event).
sources: en.wikipedia Venizelos-Tittoni agreement; en.wikipedia Italian occupation of Adalia ('signed on 29 July 1919 by Tittoni and Venizelos'; Italy 'renounced Antalya and the islands of Dodecanese except for Rhodes'; Sforza denounced it in June 1920); hephaestus.nup.ac.cy (promise 'with the possible exception of Rhodes').
note: Island list = Lausanne Art. 15 list (Stampalia, Rhodes, Calki, Scarpanto, Casos, Piscopis, Misiros, Calimnos, Leros, Patmos, Lipsos, Simi, Cos 'and the islets dependent thereon') minus Rhodes. Kastellorizo was French-held from 1915 and passed to Italy only in 1921; whether the 1919/1920 texts covered it was not found. The Dodecanese were under Italian occupation throughout (no Greek control).

name: Dodecanese except Rhodes (Italo-Greek treaty of Sevres)
basis: Italo-Greek treaty signed at Sevres on 10 August 1920 (renewing the Venizelos-Tittoni terms); the Treaty of Sevres itself gave the Dodecanese to Italy
event: Italy agreed to cede the Dodecanese except Rhodes to Greece, with a later plebiscite for Rhodes; it never did and denounced the treaty in 1922.
date_note: Signed at Sevres on 10 August 1920 (fhw.gr: 'By a special Greco-Italian treaty, the Dodecanese islands, except Rhodes, were ceded by the Italians to Greece'; Rhodes to decide its fate 'after the elapse of fifteen years'). Never carried out ('remained a dead letter', hephaestus). End: denunciation by Italy - 8 October 1922 as given in the task, not confirmed in the sources found; en.wikipedia Venizelos-Tittoni says 'Italy formally renounced it in August 1922'. Legally superseded by Lausanne Art. 15 (24 July 1923), by which Turkey ceded the islands to Italy.
sources: fhw.gr chronos 13 foreign_policy/institutions/07; hephaestus.nup.ac.cy ('Greek-Italian Treaty of Sevres' repeated the promise, which 'remained a dead letter'); en.wikipedia Venizelos-Tittoni agreement (formal renunciation August 1922); dodecaneso.org (Lausanne: 'all Turkish titles and rights to the Dodecanese were transferred to Italy', Castellorizo included).
note: Denunciation date unresolved: 8 October 1922 (task) vs August 1922 (en.wikipedia).

name: Northern and eastern Aegean islands (confirmed by Lausanne Art. 12)
line: Art. 12: 'The decision taken on the 13 February 1914 by the Conference of London, in virtue of Articles 5 of the Treaty of London of the 17-30 May 1913 and 15 of the Treaty of Athens of the 1-14 November 1913, which decision was communicated to the Greek Government on the 13 February 1914, regarding the sovereignty of Greece over the islands of the Eastern Mediterranean, other than the islands of Imbros, Tenedos and Rabbit Islands, particularly the islands of Lemnos, Samothrace, Mytilene, Chios, Samos and Nikaria, is confirmed, subject to the provisions of the present Treaty respecting the islands placed under the sovereignty of Italy which form the subject of Article 15. Except where a provision to the contrary is contained in the present Treaty, the islands situated at less than three miles from the Asiatic coast remain under Turkish sovereignty.'
basis: Treaty of Lausanne Art. 12 (Turkish recognition of the 1914 Great-Power decision); Art. 13: no naval base or fortification on Mytilene, Chios, Samos and Nikaria, and Greek military aircraft forbidden to fly over the Anatolian coast; Straits Convention: Samothrace, Lemnos, Imbros, Tenedos and the Rabbit Islands demilitarized
event: Turkey recognized Greek sovereignty over the Aegean islands taken in 1912, except Imbros, Tenedos and the Rabbit Islands.
date_note: Lausanne signed 24 July 1923, in force 6 August 1924. Confirmation only: the same islands are already de_jure from 13 February 1914 in GB3 (1914-aegean-islands-de-jure); no change on the map. Sevres Art. 84 para 3 had confirmed the same decision in 1920 (never in force).
sources: rastko.rs text of the Treaty of Lausanne (Arts. 12, 13); makale.isam.org.tr (Straits Convention Art. 4); en.wikipedia Treaty of Lausanne (Arts. 6 and 12).
note: Thasos is not named in Art. 12 but is covered by the 1914 decision ('particularly' list is not exhaustive). Art. 6: islands within three miles of a coast belong to the coastal state.

name: Treaty of Lausanne: what Greece gave up and kept
line: Greek-Turkish frontier = Lausanne Art. 2(2) (the Evros, with the Karaağaç triangle to Turkey); traced on the 1:1,000,000 maps attached to the treaty (Art. 4) and on the ground by a Boundary Commission (Art. 5). Convention respecting the Thracian frontier (same day): demilitarized zones of about 30 km on both sides; the Greek zone runs from Cape Makri (village excluded) north, roughly parallel to the Evros, to Tahtali and the Bulgarian frontier about 15 km west of Kuchuk-Derbend.
basis: Treaty of Lausanne (24 July 1923) with Protocol XV (Karaağaç, Imbros, Tenedos), Protocol XVI (Sevres Thrace and minorities treaties) and the Convention respecting the Thracian frontier
event: Lausanne replaced Sevres: Greece kept Western Thrace and the 1914 islands but gave up Eastern Thrace, Karaağaç, Imbros and Tenedos and its claims in Asia Minor.
date_note: Signed 24 July 1923; Turkey ratified 23 August 1923; all others by 16 July 1924; in force 6 August 1924 (en.wikipedia; HAGS). makale.isam.org.tr gives 16 August 1924 (disagrees). Art. 143: between Greece and Turkey, Arts. 1, 2(2) and 5-11 entered into force as soon as both had deposited ratifications, even before the general proces-verbal.
sources: rastko.rs Lausanne text; mfa.gov.tr Protocols XV and XVI and Convention III; en.wikipedia Treaty of Lausanne; army.gr ?p=60862.
note: Context event for the film caption; the area changes are in the individual events. The 1913 titles (Macedonia, Epirus, Crete, the islands) were not reopened: Art. 12 confirms the 1913-14 instruments for the islands and Art. 16 has Turkey renounce all territory outside its new frontiers.

name: Mount Athos (Agion Oros)
basis: Greek since 1912-13 (GB3); minorities treaty of Sevres via Lausanne Protocol XVI
event: Greek sovereignty over Athos was not touched at Lausanne; the minorities treaty that came into force with it guaranteed the rights of its non-Greek monasteries.
date_note: No change of status in 1918-1924. Lausanne does not mention Athos (checked in the full rastko.rs text). The Sevres treaty for the protection of minorities in Greece (10 August 1920), put into force by Lausanne Protocol XVI on 6 August 1924, contains (in the standard text, Art. 13 - not verified here) Greece's undertaking to respect the traditional rights of the non-Greek monastic communities of Mount Athos.
sources: rastko.rs Lausanne text (no mention of Athos); mfa.gov.tr Protocol XVI (puts the Sevres minorities treaty into force, abrogating its Art. 7 para 2 and Art. 15).
note: Recorded only because the task asks; no map change.
editorial: Greek sovereignty over Mount Athos, with its autonomy, was recognized at Lausanne (in force 6 August 1924); the research recorded it as a note, which left Athos undrawn from 1924. Drawn as part of the recognized state from that date. Status changed from 'note' to 'de_jure'.

name: Corfu (Italian occupation 1923)
line: Whole island of Corfu. The sources fetched speak only of 'Corfu'; they do not say whether Paxoi or the Diapontia islets (Othonoi, Ereikoussa, Mathraki) were also occupied, so treat those as NOT occupied unless another source says otherwise.
basis: Decision of the Conference of Ambassadors (terms announced 8 Sep 1923, accepted by Greece 8 Sep and Italy 9 Sep; on 14 Sep the Conference told Mussolini to evacuate by 27 Sep; 26 Sep indemnity of 50,000,000 lire awarded to Italy)
event: After the murder of General Enrico Tellini and his staff on Greek territory near Kakavia on 27 Aug 1923 and the Italian ultimatum of 29 Aug, an Italian squadron bombarded Corfu town and landed 5,000-10,000 troops on 31 Aug 1923. The Italians evacuated on 27 Sep 1923.
sources: en.wikipedia Corfu incident
note: Gregorian dates (Greece had already switched calendar on 1 Mar 1923).

name: Petrich border zone (Greek advance into Bulgaria, Oct 1925)
line: The sources fetched name no village other than Petrich and give no depth in km. Greek troops crossed the border on 22 Oct 1925 to occupy Petrich (about 8-10 km north of the border on the Beles crest); the League ordered a ceasefire 'hours before the Greek army was due to attack Petrich', so the Greek line lay between the frontier and the outskirts of Petrich. Greek-side press claimed Petrich was taken; Bulgarian sources say it held. Draw a shallow strip (up to ~10 km deep) along the frontier from the Beles crest south-west of Petrich to the Strymon valley at Kulata, stopping short of Petrich town.
by_whom: Greek Army (III and IV Corps ordered to the border), government of Theodoros Pangalos
battle: Incident at Petrich ('War of the Stray Dog')
basis: Military occupation in a border war; League of Nations ruling (ceasefire, Greek withdrawal, £45,000 compensation to Bulgaria) accepted by both states
event: Border shooting at Demir Kapia on Beles on 18 Oct 1925; Greek 48-hour ultimatum; Greek troops entered Bulgaria on 22 Oct to occupy Petrich and nearby villages; fighting with Bulgarian troops and IMRO chetas; League-ordered ceasefire and withdrawal; status quo ante.
handover: Greek withdrawal observed by French, Italian and British military attachés sent by the League
date_note: Entry 22 Oct 1925 (en.wikipedia). End = last day of the conflict in the Wikipedia infobox (19-29 Oct 1925); no source fetched gives the exact day the withdrawal was completed. Recalled (not verified here): the League Council met in Paris on 26 Oct and demanded withdrawal orders within 24 h and withdrawal within 60 h; check Barros, The Greek-Bulgarian Incident of 1925 (1964).
sources: en.wikipedia Incident at Petrich (infobox 19-29 Oct 1925; ~20,000 Greek v. ~10,000 Bulgarian troops); warhistoryonline.com 'Stray dog sparked war' ('occupied the town of Petrich and nearby villages'); balkanhistory.org 'War of the stray dog' (says the League intervened BEFORE Greek troops crossed, contradicting the others)
note: Sources disagree whether Petrich itself was entered. Villages occupied are not named in any source fetched.

name: Thesprotia north of the Kalamas (Italian advance 1940)
line: From the 1940 Greek-Albanian border (Konispoli - Filiates sector) south to the Kalamas (Thyamis) river, which Greek covering units withdrew behind on the first day of the war.
basis: Italian invasion from Albania (Greco-Italian War)
event: Italy invaded on 28 Oct 1940; Greek covering units were forced south of the Kalamas on the first day; the Siena Division was directed on Filiates.
date_note: End month only: Greek forces stood again on the Kalamas along its whole length on 13 Nov 1940 and the counter-offensive began on 14 Nov; the day the Italians were cleared from Filiates and the border area is not in the sources fetched (protothema.gr says all Greek territory up to the border was freed by 26 Nov 1940).
sources: en.wikipedia Greco-Italian War; en.protothema.gr (25 Nov 2025) 'November 22 1940 ... Koritsa'

name: Igoumenitsa - Margariti bridgehead south of the Kalamas (Nov 1940)
line: Coastal strip south of the lower Kalamas from the river to Igoumenitsa and inland to Margariti, the deepest Italian point (7 Nov 1940).
basis: Italian invasion
event: Igoumenitsa captured 6 Nov 1940; Margariti reached 7 Nov; Italians pushed back behind the Kalamas by 13 Nov.
date_note: Italians crossed the Kalamas on the night of 4/5 Nov; end = 'by 13 November the Greek forces once again stood at the Kalamas river along its entire length' (date by which the bridgehead was gone).
sources: en.wikipedia Greco-Italian War

name: Pogoni / Kakavia - Kalpaki corridor (Italian advance 1940)
line: From the border at Kakavia south-east along the Ioannina road to the Greek Elaia-Kalpaki position, which held (main Italian assault from 2 Nov repulsed; Italians pulled back on 8 Nov).
basis: Italian invasion
event: Greek covering forces fell back to the Kalpaki line by the night of 29/30 Oct; Italian contact 1 Nov; main assault 2 Nov repulsed; Italian pull-back 8 Nov.
date_note: End month only: cleared in the Greek counter-offensive of 14-23 Nov 1940; exact day not in the sources fetched.
sources: en.wikipedia Greco-Italian War

name: Konitsa (Italian capture, Nov 1940)
line: Konitsa town and the Aoos valley between the border at the Perati bridge and Konitsa.
basis: Italian invasion
event: 'On 1 November, the Italians managed to capture Konitsa.'
date_note: Captured 1 Nov 1940; retaken in mid-November (exact day not in the sources fetched).
sources: en.wikipedia Greco-Italian War

name: Northern Pindus (Julia Division thrust, Oct-Nov 1940)
line: A narrow tongue from the border at Grammos south-east along the upper Sarantaporos and Aoos valleys through Samarina and Distrato to Vovousa (captured 2 Nov), about 30 km short of Metsovo, which was never reached.
basis: Italian invasion
event: The Julia Division advanced over the Pindus towards Metsovo, took Vovousa on 2 Nov, was surrounded and driven back to roughly its start line within a week.
date_note: Most villages retaken 3-4 Nov (Julia surrounded by 3 Nov); by 13 Nov the Greeks had reoccupied the Grammos and Smolikas ranges (end date = 'by').
sources: en.wikipedia Greco-Italian War

name: Korytsa and the Korytsa plateau
line: Whole Korytsa plateau, controlling the Devoll valley approaches; entire plateau held by 27 Nov 1940.
by_whom: Greek III Corps / Western Macedonia Army Section (9th Division entered Korytsa)
battle: Battle of Morava-Ivan / Battle of Korytsa
basis: Military occupation in war (Greco-Italian War)
event: Offensive from 14 Nov 1940; Morava summit taken 19-21 Nov; Italians withdrew to the Devoll valley and the 9th Division took Korytsa on 22 Nov; whole plateau by 27 Nov.
date_note: End = Italian re-entry into Korytsa on 14 Apr 1941 (Greek retreat ordered 12 Apr). Morava/Ivan point is approximate.
sources: en.wikipedia Western Macedonia Army Section; en.wikipedia Battle of Korçë; en.wikipedia Battle of Morava-Ivan; Kathimerini 23 Nov 1940 headline via fhw.gr ('Korytsa was taken yesterday'); en.wikipedia April 1941 Italian offensive in Epirus (Korytsa taken 14 April)

name: Devoll (Bilishti) district
line: Between the Greek border at Kapeshtitsa and the Korytsa plateau.
by_whom: Greek III Corps
basis: Military occupation in war
date_note: Start month only: taken in the Morava-Ivan battle (14-23 Nov 1940); exact day not in the sources fetched. End: Italians took Bilishti on 15 Apr 1941.
sources: en.wikipedia April 1941 Italian offensive in Epirus (Bilishti 15 April)

name: Kolonia (Erseka, Leskoviki)
by_whom: Greek Army (Epirus and W. Macedonia sections)
basis: Military occupation in war
date_note: Start month only (Greek counter-offensive of mid/late Nov 1940; days not in sources fetched). End: Erseka fell to the Italians on 17 Apr 1941 after Greek resistance; Leskoviki was an Italian objective in the following days (Ponte Perati, 18-22 Apr).
sources: en.wikipedia April 1941 Italian offensive in Epirus; en.wikipedia Battle of Ponte Perati

name: Moschopolis
by_whom: Greek 10th Division
basis: Military occupation in war
date_note: Taken 24 Nov 1940 (10th Division; Kathimerini of 25 Nov reports it). End: Greek withdrawal from the northern sector after the GHQ order of 12 Apr 1941 (Korytsa re-entered by the Italians 14 Apr); exact day not found.
sources: en.wikipedia Western Macedonia Army Section; Kathimerini 25 Nov 1940 via fhw.gr

name: Pogradets and the Kamia massif
line: Town of Pogradets on Lake Ohrid and the heights to its north-west (Kamia massif), where III Corps stood through the winter.
by_whom: Greek 13th Division (III Corps)
basis: Military occupation in war
date_note: Entered 30 Nov 1940 by the 13th Division after the Italians evacuated it (Kathimerini 1 Dec). End: withdrawal after 12 Apr 1941 (exact day not found; Korytsa fell 14 Apr).
sources: en.wikipedia Western Macedonia Army Section; Kathimerini 1 Dec 1940 via fhw.gr

name: Premeti
by_whom: Greek II Corps
basis: Military occupation in war
date_note: Taken 4 Dec 1940 'after a raging battle' (Kathimerini 5 Dec). End: re-taken by the Italians in their April advance (between Klisura on 17 Apr and the border on 21 Apr); exact day not found.
sources: Kathimerini 5 Dec 1940 via fhw.gr; en.wikipedia Battle of Ponte Perati (Premeti among positions recaptured)

name: Agioi Saranta ('Porto Edda' to the Italians)
line: Coastal district from the Greek border to Agioi Saranta, incl. Konispoli and Finiki (Finiki/Konispoli taken in the same advance; exact days not found).
by_whom: Greek I Corps
basis: Military occupation in war
date_note: Taken 6 Dec 1940 by I Corps (en.wikipedia 'Battle of Himara'; himara.gr). End: April 1941 withdrawal (exact day not found; himara.gr gives the Italian return as '8 October 1941', evidently an error for April 1941).
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Himara; himara.gr almanac 'liberation of Saranda'; Kathimerini 7 Dec 1940 via fhw.gr

name: Delvino
by_whom: Greek I Corps
basis: Military occupation in war
date_note: Day approximate: abandoned by the Italians and entered at about the same time as Agioi Saranta (Kathimerini 7 Dec 1940: 'Argyrokastro and Delvino abandoned by the Italian army'). End: April 1941 withdrawal.
sources: Kathimerini 7 Dec 1940 via fhw.gr; himara.gr

name: Argyrokastro and the Drinos valley
line: Drinos valley from the Greek border at Kakavia north to the Greek line short of Tepeleni.
by_whom: Greek I Corps
basis: Military occupation in war
event: Held for about five months.
date_note: Entered 8 Dec 1940 (Kathimerini 9 Dec; en.wikipedia 'Battle of Himara'). End: April 1941 withdrawal; the Italian XXV Corps crossed into Greece on 21 Apr, so Argyrokastro was given up shortly before (exact day not found).
sources: Kathimerini 9 Dec 1940 via fhw.gr; en.wikipedia Battle of Himara; greekcitytimes.com 8 Dec 2021

name: Chimarra coast
line: Coast from Lukovo/Porto Palermo north to beyond Chimarra; inland the Kuç saddle giving access to the Shushitsa valley.
by_whom: Greek 3rd Division (I Corps)
basis: Military occupation in war
date_note: Battle 13-22 Dec 1940; the Italians abandoned the town and the Greeks entered on the morning of 22 Dec (Kathimerini 24 Dec says 'yesterday', i.e. 23 Dec: minor disagreement). End: April 1941 withdrawal (exact day not found). Kuç coordinates approximate.
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Himara; Kathimerini 24 Dec 1940 via fhw.gr

name: Klisura and the Trebeshina - Tepeleni front
line: Klisura gorge and the heights north and north-west of it: Bubesi and height 802 (2 Feb 1941), Mount Shendeli and heights 1647, 1260, 1178 of Trebeshina (13 Feb 1941); the advance stopped short of Tepeleni.
by_whom: Greek II Corps (5th Cretan Division, 15th Division)
battle: Capture of Klisura Pass; Battle of Trebeshina
basis: Military occupation in war
date_note: Pass taken 10 Jan 1941 (operation 6-11 Jan; Kathimerini 11 Jan). Bubesi 2 Feb; Trebeshina heights 13 Feb 1941. End: Klisura fell to the Italians 17 Apr 1941.
sources: en.wikipedia Capture of Klisura Pass; en.wikipedia 15th Infantry Division (Greece); Kathimerini 11 Jan 1941 via fhw.gr; en.wikipedia April 1941 Italian offensive in Epirus

name: Ostravitsa - southern Tomoros sector
line: Mountain sector linking II and III Corps: Mount Ostravitsa (taken 12 Dec 1940) and up to the southern approaches of Mount Tomoros (Dec 1940).
by_whom: Greek Cavalry Division (OMK)
basis: Military occupation in war
date_note: Ostravitsa taken 12 Dec 1940 by the Cavalry Division (OMK); Tomoros reached later in December. End: April 1941 withdrawal (exact day not found).
sources: en.wikipedia Western Macedonia Army Section
note: Municipalities marked (?) are inferred from geography, not stated in sources.

name: Greek-held southern Albania at its greatest extent (Feb - mid-Apr 1941)
line: FRONT LINE held from mid-February to mid-April 1941 (stable through the Italian spring offensive of 9-24 Mar 1941), from the Adriatic to Lake Ohrid: Adriatic coast north of Chimarra -> Kuç saddle (head of the Shushitsa valley; Greek forces about 16 km from Avlona) -> heights south and east of Tepeleni (town Italian) -> Mount Shendeli -> Trebeshina ridge (heights 1647/1260/1178) and Hill 731 (Mount Trebeshina, 'about 20 km north of Klisura', between the Osum and the Aoos) -> Bubesi -> across the Osum valley in Skrapar -> southern slopes of Mount Tomoros -> Mount Ostravitsa -> Devoll valley -> Kamia massif -> west shore of Lake Ohrid north of Pogradets. Coordinates below are approximate positions of the named features, not surveyed front positions.
by_whom: Greek Army: I Corps (coast/Drinos), II Corps (Klisura-Tomoros: 17th, 5th, 1st, 15th, 11th Divisions in March), III Corps/W. Macedonia Army Section (Korytsa-Pogradets)
battle: Italian spring offensive (Battle of Hill 731), 9-24 Mar 1941
basis: Military occupation in war
event: The front stabilized from 6 Jan / Feb 1941; the Italian spring offensive between the Osum and the Aoos (main blow on a 32 km front, Hill 731) failed; the Greek retreat began after the German invasion.
date_note: Start = last significant Greek gains (Trebeshina heights, 13 Feb 1941; 'final Greek advances until 8 March' per en.wikipedia). End = GHQ order to retreat (12 Apr 1941); the area was then given up from north to south between 13 and 21 Apr (Korytsa 14, Bilishti 15, Erseka and Klisura 17, Italians on the Greek border 21 Apr).
sources: en.wikipedia Greco-Italian War; Italian spring offensive; Battle of Hill 731; Battle of Ponte Perati (16 km from Avlona); Battle of Himara; 15th Infantry Division (Greece); Western Macedonia Army Section; April 1941 Italian offensive in Epirus
note: No source fetched gives the full front line; it is reconstructed from the positions named in them. Check against the Hellenic Army General Staff maps (An Abridged History of the Greek-Italian and Greek-German War 1940-1941). Spring offensive end: infobox 16 Mar, text 24 Mar.

name: Epirus front after the Greek capitulation (Italian entry into Greece, April 1941)
line: Italian XXV Corps crossed the border on 21 Apr 1941 (Perati bridge - Kakavia sector) behind the retreating Epirus Army; German SS troops had taken Ioannina on 21 Apr. Epirus then fell into the Italian occupation zone.
occupier: Germany, then Italy (zone, 1941 - Sep 1943), then Germany (Sep 1943 - Oct 1944)
basis: German invasion and Greek capitulation: protocol of Tsolakoglou with Sepp Dietrich signed 20 Apr 1941 18:00 (near Metsovo / Votonosi), second protocol at Ioannina 21 Apr, final armistice with Germany and Italy (Tsolakoglou, Jodl, Ferrero) 23 Apr 1941 (Thessaloniki per en.wikipedia Military history of Greece in WWII)
event: GHQ ordered the retreat from Albania on 12 Apr 1941; II Corps divisions began to disintegrate 15 Apr; Epirus Army capitulated 20-23 Apr.
date_note: End month only: Epirus was evacuated by the Germans in October 1944 (exact days by town not in the sources fetched). See the zone events for the change of occupier.
sources: en.wikipedia German invasion of Greece (Ioannina 21 Apr; armistice 23 Apr); Western Macedonia Army Section (protocol 20 Apr 18:00); Military history of Greece during WWII (near Metsovo 20 Apr, Ioannina 21 Apr, Thessaloniki 23 Apr); Greco-Italian War (surrender to Germany 20 Apr, to Italy 23 Apr); April 1941 Italian offensive in Epirus (XXV Corps on Greek soil 21 Apr; capitulation 22 Apr)
note: Sources disagree on the capitulation day (20, 21, 22 or 23 April) because there were three successive protocols.

name: Eastern Macedonia and Western Thrace east of the Strymon (German conquest phase)
line: Everything east of the Strymon to the Evros (Turkish border).
basis: German invasion (Operation Marita)
event: The Germans crossed to the Thessaloniki railway on the evening of 7 Apr; the Greek line capitulated on 9-10 Apr.
date_note: Start = German attack on the Metaxas Line from Bulgaria; the Eastern Macedonia Army Section's surrender took effect at 13:00 on 10 Apr 1941 (some forts held a few days longer). Dates of German entry into each town are not in the sources fetched. End = Bulgarian entry (20 Apr), except the Evros strip, which stayed German (separate event).
sources: en.wikipedia German invasion of Greece

name: Bulgarian occupation zone (annexed as 'Belomorie')
line: West: the Strymon river from the Bulgarian frontier at the Rupel gorge to its mouth near Amphipolis; territory west of it stayed German. East: a line from Svilengrad (on the Bulgarian-Turkish-Greek frontier) south-south-west to Alexandroupoli, west of the Evros, leaving a strip along the Turkish border to the Germans (separate event). Islands: Thasos and Samothrace.
basis: Axis partition of Greece; unilateral Bulgarian annexation 14 May 1941
event: Bulgarian occupation and annexation (12,363 km2 of Western Thrace counted by Bulgaria; Thasos 443 km2, Samothrace 184 km2); harsh Bulgarianization; deportation of the Jews of Belomorie in 1943.
date_note: Bulgarian Second Army entered Greek Thrace 'without firing a shot' on 20 Apr 1941. Annexation declared 14 May 1941 (Filov to the National Assembly; never formally ratified, never recognized by Germany or Italy). Withdrawal: rapid evacuation began 10 Oct 1944 and was completed 26 Oct 1944, when a delegation under Dobri Terpeshev handed authority to ELAS (Bulgarian rule article; the Axis article says 'about two weeks' after 10 Oct). Moscow Armistice of 28 Oct 1944 then required Bulgaria to leave the 'Aegean region'.
sources: en.wikipedia Axis occupation of Greece (entry 20 Apr 1941, annexation 14 May 1941, prefectures Drama, Kavala, Rhodope, Serres; 'between the Strymon and a line through Alexandroupoli and Svilengrad'); en.wikipedia Bulgarian rule of Macedonia, Morava Valley and Western Thrace (1941-1944) (Strymon to Evros minus the German strip; withdrawal 10-26 Oct 1944); en.wikipedia The Holocaust in Bulgarian-occupied Greece (Alexandroupoli, Komotini, Xanthi, Kavala, Drama, Serres, Thasos, Samothrace in Belomorie)
note: The en.wikipedia page 'Bulgarian occupation of Greece during World War II' does not exist (url_not_found); the Bulgarian rule article was used. Sources disagree on the eastern boundary: the Axis occupation article says the zone excluded 'the Evros prefecture', the Bulgarian rule and Holocaust articles put the line at Alexandroupoli-Svilengrad with Alexandroupoli Bulgarian. The Strymon line cuts Serres and Sintiki municipalities: whether Sidirokastro lay on the Bulgarian side should be checked on a map of the river.

name: Evros border strip (German zone along the Turkish frontier)
line: Strip between the Evros (Turkish border) and the line Svilengrad - Alexandroupoli.
occupier: Germany (police and administrative staff only; Greek collaborationist administration remained; Bulgarians barred)
basis: Axis partition; strip 'reserved for possible transfer to Turkey'
date_note: Start: German arrival in April 1941 (day not in sources). End: German withdrawal in autumn 1944 (not dated in sources fetched).
sources: en.wikipedia Axis occupation of Greece; en.wikipedia Bulgarian rule of Macedonia, Morava Valley and Western Thrace
note: If the Axis article is right that the whole Evros prefecture was excluded from the Bulgarian zone, this strip should be the entire Evros regional unit except Samothrace.
editorial: The research gives April 1941 and 1944 only; drawn from the division of Thrace on 20 April 1941 (when the Bulgarian army entered) to mid-October 1944 (approximate).

name: Thessaloniki and Central Macedonia (German zone)
line: From the Strymon west to the Italian zone in Western Macedonia and Thessaly (boundary roughly along the eastern borders of Florina, Kozani and Larissa regional units; not given in the sources).
basis: German invasion; Axis partition
event: Kept by Germany as its outlet to the Aegean and as leverage against Bulgarian and Italian claims.
date_note: Start = German armored advance guard entered Thessaloniki on the morning of 9 Apr 1941 (rest of the zone in the following days). End = Thessaloniki, 'the last German escape port', freed 30 Oct 1944; the last German troops left Greek territory in the first days of November (by 4 Nov 1944).
sources: en.wikipedia German invasion of Greece; Axis occupation of Greece; pvgriekenland.nl 'British troops in Greece 1944-52' (Thessaloniki 30 Oct 1944; most Germans gone by 4 Nov 1944)
note: Pieria's zone is not stated in the sources (assumed German); check a zone map (e.g. Mazower, Inside Hitler's Greece).

name: Central Macedonia between the Strymon and the Axios (Bulgarian military occupation under German command)
line: Between the Strymon and the Axios; coastal defense from the Epanomi lighthouse (about 25 km south of Thessaloniki) to the mouth of the Strymon; the city of Thessaloniki and Chalkidiki excluded.
occupier: Bulgaria, under overall German control (area remained in the German zone)
basis: German-Bulgarian arrangement (not annexation)
date_note: Start: 7th Rila Division took over the coastal defense on 5 Jul 1943; the wider occupation of the Thessaloniki region followed later in 1943 at German invitation. End: Bulgaria began pulling out of central Macedonia in late August 1944 and left after the coup of 9 Sep 1944 (day not given).
sources: en.wikipedia Bulgarian rule of Macedonia, Morava Valley and Western Thrace (1941-1944); Axis occupation of Greece ('From 1943 ... between the Strymon and Axios rivers')
note: Overlaps the German-zone event; use it to tint the area, not as a change of sovereignty. 'joint' here means two Axis occupiers, not a Greek joint occupation.

name: Western Macedonia
battle: Battle of Vevi (Klidi pass); Battle of Klisura pass
basis: German invasion; Axis partition
date_note: Germans crossed the border near Florina 10 Apr; Vevi/Klidi 11-12 Apr; Klisura pass 13 Apr; Kozani 14 Apr. Kastoria and Grevena fell during the Greek retreat from Albania (days not found). End: German withdrawal through the Florina area in late Oct / early Nov 1944 (by 4 Nov 1944 at the latest).
sources: en.wikipedia German invasion of Greece; Military history of Greece during WWII; Bulgarian rule ... (Kastoria and Florina taken over by the Germans after Sep 1943, i.e. formerly Italian); pvgriekenland.nl
note: Bulgarian-backed Ohrana militias operated in Florina, Kastoria and Pella in 1943-44.
editorial: The research gives November 1944 only; the last German troops left Greek territory by 4 November 1944 (GB5), so drawn until 2 November (approximate).

name: Thessaly
basis: German invasion; Axis partition (Italian III Army Corps zone)
date_note: First German troops entered Larissa 19 Apr 1941. End: German evacuation in October 1944 (days not in the sources fetched).
sources: en.wikipedia German invasion of Greece; Axis occupation of Greece

name: Central Greece and Aetolia-Acarnania
basis: German invasion; Axis partition
date_note: German attack on the Thermopylae position at 11:30 on 24 Apr 1941, held all day; the Allies then withdrew, so the area fell on and after 25 Apr (days by town not found). End: October 1944.
sources: en.wikipedia German invasion of Greece

name: Athens, Piraeus and Attica
occupier: Germany and Italy (Italian zone with German enclaves: Kalamaki airfield, parts of Piraeus port, Salamis, Aegina, Fleves; southern Attica German until Sep 1942, then Italian); all German from Sep 1943
basis: German invasion; Axis partition
date_note: Germans entered Athens at 08:25 on 27 Apr 1941 (Kathimerini 28 Apr). German troops evacuated Athens on 12 Oct 1944; British troops (Scobie) arrived 14 Oct; the Greek government returned 18 Oct.
sources: en.wikipedia German invasion of Greece; Axis occupation of Greece; Kathimerini via fhw.gr; pvgriekenland.nl
note: 'joint' = joint Axis occupation, not a Greek joint occupation.

name: Peloponnese (with Achaea and Elis)
basis: German invasion; Axis partition (Italian VIII Army Corps zone)
date_note: German airborne seizure of the Corinth Canal bridges 25 Apr 1941 (most other sources say 26 Apr); evacuations from Nafplio 25-27 Apr; Kalamata fell 30 Apr; the Germans reached the south coast on 30 Apr. End: the Germans left in Sep-Oct 1944: Patras evacuated 3 Oct 1944 ('first town liberated in the Peloponnese'; often given as 4 Oct), the rest by mid-October.
sources: en.wikipedia German invasion of Greece; Military history of Greece during WWII (Kalamata 30 Apr); pvgriekenland.nl (Patras 3 Oct 1944)
note: Sources disagree on the Corinth Canal date (25 v. 26 Apr) and on Patras (3 v. 4 Oct 1944).

name: Kythira
basis: Axis occupation
date_note: Start: occupied after the fall of the Peloponnese (date and occupier not in the sources fetched; month approximate). End: British 9th Commando landed 16 Sep 1944 (first step of Operation Manna).
sources: pvgriekenland.nl

name: Euboea and Skyros
occupier: Germany (Apr - Oct 1941), Italy (Oct 1941 - Sep 1943), Germany (Sep 1943 - Oct 1944)
basis: Axis occupation
date_note: A German motorcycle battalion crossed to seize Chalcis in late April 1941 (day not given). Allotted to the German zone, handed to Italy in October 1941; German again from Sep 1943. End: October 1944 (days not found).
sources: en.wikipedia German invasion of Greece; Axis occupation of Greece
editorial: The research gives April 1941 only; drawn from 30 April, after the fall of Athens (27 Apr), when the Axis took over the islands (approximate).

name: Northern Sporades
basis: Axis occupation
date_note: Months approximate (dates of the Axis arrival and of the German departure not in the sources fetched). The Sporades were in German hands by 19 Sep 1943.
sources: en.wikipedia Dodecanese campaign (Sporades and Cyclades German by 19 Sep 1943)
note: Zone (Italian) inferred: 'the rest Italian'.

name: Ionian Islands
battle: Massacre of the Acqui Division, Kefalonia (Sep 1943)
basis: Axis occupation; Italian de facto annexation prepared but never formalized
event: Greek civil authorities replaced by Italians; 'Ionian drachma' introduced early 1942. After the Italian armistice the Germans attacked the Italian garrisons; more than 4,500 Italians were executed on Kefalonia.
date_note: Months approximate: the Italian landings of late April / May 1941 and the German departures of autumn 1944 are not dated in the sources fetched.
sources: en.wikipedia Axis occupation of Greece
editorial: The research gives April 1941 only; drawn from 30 April, after the fall of Athens (27 Apr), when the Axis took over the islands (approximate).

name: Cyclades (except Milos)
basis: Axis occupation
date_note: Start month approximate (Italian occupation in spring 1941, not dated in the sources fetched). German by 19 Sep 1943. Liberation: Syros 13 Oct, Naxos 15 Oct, Santorini 18 Oct 1944 (end = last of these; other islands not dated).
sources: pvgriekenland.nl; en.wikipedia Dodecanese campaign

name: Milos (German stronghold)
basis: Axis occupation
event: One of the German garrisons left behind after the withdrawal of October 1944.
date_note: Start month approximate (German zone, staging point toward Crete). End: the isolated garrison surrendered after the German capitulation of 8 May 1945 (day not found).
sources: en.wikipedia Axis occupation of Greece; Military history of Greece during WWII
editorial: The research gives May 1945 only; drawn until the German surrender in the Aegean (8-9 May 1945; approximate).

name: Lemnos, Agios Efstratios, Lesbos, Chios (German 'Salonica-Aegean' command)
basis: Axis occupation
date_note: Months approximate: the German landings of late April / May 1941 and the departures from Lesbos and Chios in autumn 1944 are not dated in the sources fetched; Lemnos freed 15 Oct 1944; German withdrawal from the Aegean islands began in August 1944.
sources: en.wikipedia Axis occupation of Greece; pvgriekenland.nl; britishmilitaryhistory.co.uk Chronology of Events Aegean Islands
editorial: The research gives April 1941 only; drawn from 30 April, after the fall of Athens (27 Apr), when the Axis took over the islands (approximate).

name: Samos, Ikaria and Fournoi (Italian)
basis: Axis occupation (Italianization without formal annexation)
date_note: Start month approximate. End = announcement of the Italian armistice.
sources: en.wikipedia Axis occupation of Greece

name: Samos, Ikaria and Fournoi (Allied-held after the Italian armistice)
by_whom: Italian garrison (co-belligerent after the armistice) with British liaison parties
event: Not 'occupied' in the brief's sense (Allied forces), and not Greek control either.
date_note: Ikaria and Fournoi (with Patmos) occupied by the Germans 18 Nov 1943; British left Samos on the night of 19/20 Nov; the Italian garrison surrendered 22 Nov 1943.
sources: en.wikipedia Dodecanese campaign

name: Samos, Ikaria and Fournoi (German)
date_note: Ikaria/Fournoi from 18 Nov 1943, Samos from 22 Nov 1943. End: German departure in autumn 1944 (not dated in the sources fetched).
sources: en.wikipedia Dodecanese campaign

name: Western Crete ('Fortress Crete' enclave)
line: After the Axis evacuated eastern and central Crete in winter 1944/45, the Germans held a western enclave around Chania and Souda; its exact boundary is not in the sources fetched (draw the Chania regional unit; check whether it included western Rethymno).
basis: Axis occupation
event: Generalmajor Hans-Georg Benthack surrendered all German forces on Crete to Major-General Colin Callander.
date_note: Airborne landings 20 May 1941; Maleme 21 May; Chania 27 May; the island under German control on 1 Jun 1941. End: German surrender after VE Day; the surrender document gives the cessation of hostilities as 10 May 1945 10:00 GMT, signed at Knossos (preveli.org); other accounts give 9 or 12 May 1945 (Fortress Crete article: 'its surrender of 12 May 1945').
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Crete; Fortress Crete; Hans-Georg Benthack; preveli.org Chronicle of the Battle of Crete; ww2wrecks.com 'The last bastion: the surrender document ... 10 May 1945'
note: Sources disagree on the surrender date (9, 10 or 12 May 1945).
editorial: Drawn from the fall of Chania (27 May 1941), not from the first German landings of 20 May: the Battle of Crete was fought on Greek-held ground until then.

name: Central Crete (Rethymno and Heraklion)
basis: Axis occupation
date_note: Rethymno and Heraklion fell 29 May 1941. End year only: the Axis evacuated eastern and central Crete 'during the winter' after the general retreat of October 1944, handing it to a weak Anglo-Greek garrison; no source fetched gives the day or confirms that Rethymno lay outside the final German enclave.
sources: preveli.org; en.wikipedia Fortress Crete
editorial: The research gives only the year of the end (1944); drawn until mid-October 1944, when the Germans left central and eastern Crete for the Chania enclave and withdrew from Thrace (approximate).

name: Lasithi (Italian sector of Crete)
basis: Axis occupation
date_note: Italian troops from the Dodecanese landed at Sitia on 28 May 1941 and occupied the prefecture; they met German troops on 30 May. German from Sep 1943. End year only (evacuated with central Crete in winter 1944/45; day not found).
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Crete; Fortress Crete; preveli.org
editorial: The research gives only the year of the end (1944); drawn until mid-October 1944, when the Germans left central and eastern Crete for the Chania enclave and withdrew from Thrace (approximate).

name: German occupation zone (1941 - Sep 1943)
line: Zone layer: overlaps the per-area events, which carry the dates of conquest and liberation.
basis: Axis partition of Greece
date_note: The zones took shape as the Axis advanced (April - June 1941); sources date the partition only to 'mid-1941'. Changes: Euboea and Skyros to Italy October 1941; southern Attica to Italy September 1942. After 8 Sep 1943 the Germans took over the Italian zone too.
sources: en.wikipedia Axis occupation of Greece; Fortress Crete
note: Kythira's zone is not stated in the sources.

name: Italian occupation zone (1941 - Sep 1943)
line: Zone layer: 'the rest' of Greece outside the German and Bulgarian zones.
occupier: Italy (XXVI Army Corps Epirus/west, III Thessaly, VIII Peloponnese)
basis: Axis partition of Greece
event: Thesprotia (Chameria) was promised to Albania after the war; the 'Principality of the Pindus' (see note event) was declared in the Italian zone.
date_note: Italian troops took over their zone between late April and June 1941 (dates not in the sources fetched). End = Italian armistice announced 8 Sep 1943 (signed at Cassibile 3 Sep); German takeover over the following weeks.
sources: en.wikipedia Axis occupation of Greece

name: Former Italian zone under German occupation (Sep 1943 - autumn 1944)
line: Zone layer.
date_note: Start = Italian armistice; the Germans disarmed or fought the Italian garrisons in the following weeks (Sporades and Cyclades in German hands by 19 Sep 1943; Kefalonia after fighting). End = liberation, area by area, September - early November 1944 (see per-area events).
sources: en.wikipedia Axis occupation of Greece; Dodecanese campaign

name: 'Principality of the Pindus' (Italian-sponsored Aromanian entity)
by_whom: Alcibiades Diamandi
event: Pro-Italian puppet entity inside the Italian zone; no change of sovereignty.
date_note: Years only; the article says it collapsed in 1942 when Germany took over Italian positions.
sources: en.wikipedia Axis occupation of Greece
note: Map faintly if at all.

name: Liberation of Greece (sequence)
event: German withdrawal from the Aegean islands began August 1944. Kythira (British commandos) 16 Sep; Araxos airfield paratroops 23 Sep; Patras 3/4 Oct; Bulgarian evacuation 10-26 Oct; Megara airfield paratroops and German evacuation of Athens 12 Oct; Syros 13 Oct; British in Athens 14 Oct; Naxos and Lemnos 15 Oct; Santorini 18 Oct; government returns 18 Oct; Thessaloniki 30 Oct; last German troops gone from the mainland in the first days of November. Left behind: the Crete enclave (to 9-12 May 1945), Milos (to May 1945) and, in the then-Italian Dodecanese, Rhodes, Leros, Kos and others (to 8 May 1945); the Axis article adds that some Aegean garrisons surrendered only in June 1945.
date_note: End = 'most German troops had withdrawn by 4 November 1944' (pvgriekenland.nl); the Axis article says the mainland was clear 'by the end of October'.
sources: pvgriekenland.nl 'British troops in Greece 1944-52'; en.wikipedia Operation Manna; Axis occupation of Greece; Bulgarian rule ... (1941-1944)

name: Dodecanese and Kastellorizo (Italian Islands of the Aegean)
basis: Treaty of Lausanne, Art. 15
date_note: Context only (not Greek). Italian since 1912 (provisional), sovereignty confirmed by the Treaty of Lausanne (in force 6 Aug 1924, recalled, not in the pages fetched; the Italian Islands article says 'formally annexed in 1923'); Kastellorizo French-occupied 1915, Italian from 1921. End = Italian armistice.
sources: en.wikipedia Italian Islands of the Aegean; Corfu incident (garrison reinforced 1923, annexed 1925)
note: Earlier history and the Venizelos-Tittoni award belong to the previous batch.

name: Kastellorizo (British-held)
by_whom: United Kingdom
date_note: Italian garrison surrendered to a British detachment on 8 Sep 1943; the only island the British kept after the Dodecanese campaign (most of the garrison taken off 28 Nov 1943); part of the British administration until the handover to Greece on 31 Mar 1947.
sources: en.wikipedia Dodecanese campaign
note: Continuous British hold is implied, not stated outright, in the article.

name: Dodecanese under German occupation
line: Taken island by island: Rhodes 9-11 Sep 1943; Karpathos and Kasos by 19 Sep; Kos 3-4 Oct; Leros 12-16 Nov; Patmos 18 Nov 1943.
date_note: Context (Italian territory, nominally under the Italian Social Republic, de facto German). Allied forces took Karpathos 29 Oct 1944 and Symi (main force) in mid-December 1944. End: General Otto Wagener surrendered the Dodecanese to the British on 8 May 1945, at Symi (pvgriekenland.nl, argophilia.com) or on Rhodes (en.wikipedia Dodecanese).
sources: en.wikipedia Dodecanese campaign; Italian Islands of the Aegean; Dodecanese; pvgriekenland.nl; argophilia.com 'Symi celebrates end of WW2 on May 8th'
note: Sources disagree where the surrender was signed (Symi v. Rhodes).

name: Dodecanese under British Military Administration
by_whom: United Kingdom
basis: Allied military occupation of enemy (Italian) territory
event: Civil affairs largely left to the islanders; informally linked with Greece.
date_note: From the German surrender (8 May 1945; HQ Dodecanese moved from Symi to Rhodes 10 May 1945) to the transfer to Greek administration on 31 Mar 1947. The Italian Islands article gives only '1945-1947' ('Military Administration in the Aegean').

name: Dodecanese and Kastellorizo (Greek military administration)
line: All the islands ceded by Art. 14 of the Treaty of Peace with Italy, with adjacent islets.
by_whom: Greek military administration (military governor recalled as Vice-Admiral Pericles Ioannidis: not verified in sources fetched)
basis: Transfer of administration by the United Kingdom pending entry into force of the Treaty of Peace with Italy
date_note: Greek control in fact from the British handover (31 Mar 1947), after signature (10 Feb 1947) but before the treaty entered into force (15 Sep 1947): sovereignty was still Italian in law, so de_facto until 15 Sep 1947, then de_jure.
sources: pvgriekenland.nl (transfer 31 Mar 1947); en.wikipedia Paris Peace Treaties, 1947 (signed 10 Feb, effective 15 Sep 1947)

name: Dodecanese and Kastellorizo (ceded by Italy)
line: Treaty of Peace with Italy, Art. 14(1): 'Italy hereby cedes to Greece in full sovereignty the Dodecanese Islands indicated hereafter, namely Stampalia (Astropalia), Rhodes (Rhodos), Calki (Kharki), Scarpanto, Casos (Casso), Piscopis (Tilos), Misiros (Nisyros), Calimnos (Kalymnos), Leros, Patmos, Lipsos (Lipso), Simi (Symi), Cos (Kos) and Castellorizo, as well as the adjacent islets.' Art. 14(2): 'These islands shall be and shall remain demilitarised.' (UNTS vol. 49; the Greek Ministry of Foreign Affairs quotes the same article.)
basis: Treaty of Peace with Italy (Paris, 10 Feb 1947), Art. 14
event: The islands 'became part of Greece on 7 March 1948' (pvgriekenland.nl), when the military administration ended.
date_note: de_jure from the treaty's entry into force (15 Sep 1947), because the cession of sovereignty takes effect when the treaty is in force; the formal incorporation of 7 Mar 1948 was the Greek domestic act ending the military administration and annexing the islands to the state, not the transfer of sovereignty. Some Greek accounts date 'union with Greece' to 7 Mar 1948.
sources: en.wikipedia Paris Peace Treaties, 1947; Dodecanese; Italian Islands of the Aegean (ceded 10 Feb 1947); pvgriekenland.nl (7 Mar 1948)
note: Including Imia (Limnia), east of Kalymnos: see '1947-imia'.

event: Since the end of the civil war (and, for the borders, since the Dodecanese took effect in 1947), no area has been added to or lost from Greek control. The land borders are those of 1913-1923 (Albania, North Macedonia, Bulgaria, Turkey on the Evros) and the Dodecanese of 1947.
sources: en.wikipedia Greek Civil War; Paris Peace Treaties, 1947

name: The Imia crisis, 1995-96
basis: Imia is Greek territory, part of the Dodecanese. Turkey renounced the Dodecanese 'and the islets dependent thereon' in favor of Italy at Lausanne (1923, Art. 15); the Italian-Turkish convention of 4 January 1932 and its protocol of 28 December 1932 placed Imia on the Italian side of the boundary (point 30 of the protocol); Italy ceded the Dodecanese 'as well as the adjacent islets' to Greece by the Treaty of Paris (10 February 1947, Art. 14).
event: A Turkish freighter ran aground on Imia in late December 1995, and Turkey then claimed the islets. On 27-28 January 1996 Turkish journalists replaced the Greek flag with a Turkish one, and the Hellenic Navy restored it; on the night of 30-31 January Turkish commandos landed on the western islet. A Greek Navy helicopter crashed during the crisis, killing Christodoulos Karathanasis, Panagiotis Vlahakos and Ektoras Gialopsos. Both sides withdrew under US mediation on 31 January. Greek sovereignty did not change.
date_note: From the grounding (26 December 1995 in the Greek Ministry of Foreign Affairs' account; 25 December in the CRS report) to the withdrawal of 31 January 1996. The flag was replaced on 27 January (MFA) or 28 January (CRS).
sources: mfa.gr, 'Turkish claims' and 'Zones grises' (Lausanne Art. 15, the 1932 convention and protocol, Art. 14 of the 1947 treaty, the events of 1995-96); US Congressional Research Service, 'Greece and Turkey: The Rocky Islet Crisis' (report 96-140, 1996); greekcitytimes.com (the three officers)
note: A note: the map does not change. Imia is drawn as part of Greece from 1947 ('1947-imia'). Turkey's claim, raised in 1996, is part of its claims to 'gray zones' in the Aegean.
editorial: Rewritten 27 Oct 2026: the first version named the islets by their Turkish name beside the Greek one and described Greek sovereignty as a claim.

name: Imia (Limnia)
basis: Imia is Greek territory, part of the Dodecanese. Turkey renounced the Dodecanese 'and the islets dependent thereon' in favor of Italy at Lausanne (1923, Art. 15); the Italian-Turkish convention of 4 January 1932 and its protocol of 28 December 1932 placed Imia on the Italian side of the boundary (point 30 of the protocol); Italy ceded the Dodecanese 'as well as the adjacent islets' to Greece by the Treaty of Paris (10 February 1947, Art. 14).
